HOW to manage bachelors.— To Miss-manage 'Mena Con-Dacron "Madam, these are the smokers' seas." Fair Passenger: "Yes, but I haven't anything to smoke." AN advertisement in a Swiss paper says "Wanted, a servant who knows how to cook and take care of children." Jr is said that a lady in London can talk the Arabic language. Many a girl in New York can chew the Arabic gum. A RAILWAY traveller of our acquaintance in- forms us that he recently caught cold through sit- ting, next to a wet-nurse. PEDESTRIAN ITEM: A Boston fellow has kissed Ms girl 450 times in two hours and one lap, and claims the belt—and all there is in it. IN the case of a man who died from having had all his teeth knocked out with a hatchet, a jury returned a verdict of "Death from ax-i-dental causes." "THERE is a ring in those tones," shouted the girl who had been listening to the sweet whispers of her lover, as she caressed the ring-finger of her left hand. EASY and pleasing lesson in punctuation—" Dear aunt, I should certainly have been with you had I been well; even now I am in great pain while I write with my nose." YOLTAiG Lady—" It was rather bold of Captain Blazer to kiss my hand, wasn't it, aunty. Aunty —" Bold ! I should think m. I should like to catch him kissing mine !" A FOND parent, anxious that his infant son ahould be sharp in his wits and profound in his thoughte, has sent him to sea, so that he may be "rocked in the cradle of the deep." A YANKEE editor says that a man came into his office to advertise for a lost dog, and that, such was the wonderful power of advertising, the dog walked into the office while he was writing out the advertisement. ITS all very well to advise people to "live within their incomes," but the true benefactor of his race is the economist who will arise and show the young men in this locality how to live without any income at all. AT a college examination a professor asked— " Does my question embarrass you rj" Not at all, sir," replied the student—' not at all. It is quite clear. It is the answer that bothers me." ONE man rebuked another for smoking. The culprit replied that he used the weed in modera- tion. " What do you call moderation ?" inquired the other. "Why sir," said the offender, "one cigar at a time." A NEW BOOK is entitled "What we really Know about Shakespeare." What we really know about Shakespeare is that he can't achieve as long a run and draw as big houses as the " Mikado" or an English ballet. A FRENCH marquis was riding out one day, when he passed an old priest trotting along contentedly on a quiet donkey. "Ha! ha !" exclaimed the marquis, "bow goes the ass, good father ?" "On horseback, my son—on horseback," replied the priest. MANY persons who enjoy considerable proficiency in the popular game of croquet, have not the slight- est idea by whom the pastime was introduced; but, though we have no means of determining the locality, we are positive that the frogs were the first to croak —eh A GENTLEMAN, in narrating to a wag the excess- ively penurious habits of a well-known Bostonian, remarked that he had recently gone from his home on a tour of the Southern States with but one shirt and a single fifty-dollar note. " Very likely," replied the facetious fellow; "and he'll not change either till he comes home again." Two men were conversing the other day, and one of them asked the other when he intended to go back home, the person addressed having come from America. He replied—" If I live till I die—and Heaven knows whether I will or not—l intend to visit my native land mace more before I leave this country." WrscoNslN paper says that one of their smart girls, wishing to prevent her lover going to California, stole all his skirts from the line on which they were hanging to dry. He wonld do well to go to the golden State, in a matrimonial state, this girl being the other party. She would be sure to take care of him. IT certainly betokened a very cloudy matrimonial life, and yet the poor widow's remark was quaint enough to make a smile. When her friend con- doled with her she heaved a deep sigh and mutt:lured : " Wall, there is one consolation, at any rate. I know where poor John is now o' nights, and that is something I could never find out before." "Why, yes," plied he; "but in my opinion we shall accomplish what our parson has endeavoured to do for the last thirty years in vain." " What is that?" said the gentleman. Another brother, Mr. Henry Pitman, is located at Manchester, while a third, Benjamin Pit- man, long since emigrated to America, finally pitch- ing his tent at Cincinnati, Ohio. Of the Manchester Mr. Pitman it is related that in the intensity of his ,1 horror of tobacco, he would stop pipe-smoking boys in the street, and pay them handsome prices for their pipes, which afterwards came to an inglori- ous end in the anti-tobacconist's fire. But the boys were not sincere in their promises not to buy new pipes with the sixpences so obtained ; and at last Mr. Pitman, from fear of bankruptcy, had to abate the vigor of his campaign. • ' • .

: FOOTLIGHT FORTUNF3. The "Chicago Times" has been reckoning up the incomes derived from "the actor's calling," which, "all things considered, is one of the best paid busi- nesses that a bright man or woman can engage in." A few " items " from our American contemporary presents some points of general interest The average leading man or woman in America receives from 100dols. to 300do1s. a week. The second man or woman (juvenile) in a first-class com- pany is paid from 75 dols.to 100 dols.a weekend the comedian and soubrette about the same. The leading people of the variety stage are all well paid. Harry iieruell,when in health,was always sure of 150 dols. weekly, and Gus Williams, before e became a star, used to demand and receive a salary of 150 dols, a week. Carmencita's legs earn her 200 dole, a week, and the late Pat Rooney, the prince of improvisa- tores, for a long time commanded 400 dole. a week. But it is upon the kings and queens of the legiti- mate that the golden rewards of the theatrical pro- fession are bestowed. Daniel Frohman,three or four years ago, paid Modjeska 1,730 dols. a week for her personal services, and considered that he made a profitable investment. Booth and Barratt, at the end of the first season they appeared together, di- vided up 362,000 dols. Henry Irving, on his first American tour under Abbey's management, played to 405,000 dole. in 27 weeks • one of Bernhardt's American tours netted her 300,000 dols., and Lily Langtry made her first American tour on a guaran- tee of 2000, dols. a week. The earnings and invest- ments of Joseph Murphy made him a millionaire. Denman Thompson often makes from 3,000 dole. to 4,000 dols, a week, and Evans and lloey in seven years have made 300,000 dole. Jos.Jefferson,who for several years paid William J. Florence 1,000 dole, a week ; Stuart Robson, William E. Crane, Neil Bur- gess, Nat Goodwin, Sol Smith Russell, Edward Her, rigan, Oliver Duod Bryon, James H. Wallick, and Richard Mansfield, are all large and steady money makers, and are all well to do, Jefferson being pro- bably the richest of the loc. Comedy, with few ex- ceptions, always pays better than tragedy, and Francis Wilson,of comic opera famc,is probably the largest and steadiest money maker before the Ameri- can public. Ile relinquished a salary of 800 dole, a a week to become a star,and his starring tours have all been immensely profitable. Wilson is economical in his ways,and if lie lives ten years will lie a very rich man. Mary Anderson,before she left the stage, frequently made 4,000 dols.a week, and Lillian Rus- sell,Pauline Hall,Lotta,Modjeska, Fanny Davenport, ' Maggie Mitchell,Clara Alorris,and Annie Pixley each made a comfortable fortune every year. Lotta is worth close to a million, and is the richest actress , living. But the earnings of the most popular players fall far below those of the great opera singers. Patti never sings for less than 5,000 dole. a night ; Serabrich has often received 1,500 dols. for a single performance; Campanini has been paid 8,000 dole. a month, and Jean de Reszka, during his American ' tour last year, was paid 1,500 dots. For each perfor- mance and 20 per cent. of the box receipts. His brother Edouard was paid 500 dole, for each perfor- mance. Playmaking, when one succeeds at it, is one of the most profitable of callings. Bronson Howard, Charles H. Hoyt, Henry C. DeMille, David Belasco,aml William 11. Gillette each makes not less than 25,000 dols, every year, and Howard's income in some recent years has often trebled that amount.

Mr. Henry Matthews, M.P., recently spent an evening in the Sydney Parliament. The report ers were not prepossessed in his favour. One of them unflatteringly sums him up as" a hungry-looking gentleman with a greedy chin, and a mouth that closes like a rat-trap." They seem to be going in for realistic journalism in the colonies just now.

A Dublin picture dealer has found himself in luck's way. At a recent sale of books and pictures belonging to the late Earl of Charlemont, he pur- chased to old portfolios for a trifle. On examining them he found in one a pocket filled with etchings; these bore the inscription. " Drawn by Albert, etched by Victoria. Presented to Lady Charlemont by Victoria." It is supposed they were given by the Queen to the Countess of Charlemont as a souvenir of her one solitary visit to Ireland, but it is said that the question of their authenicity will be submitted to her Majesty.

-- -- The Rev. Wiliam Purcell, who has been connected with the Roman Catholic Church, Maiden-lane, Strand, for several years past, but who has been re- called by Archbishop Croke to resume duty in the diocese of Cashel, is to be presented with a testi- monial from his many friends on Thursday even- ing in the Catholic School, Macklin-st., Drury-lane. The Rev. Fenwick Skrimshire, the rector of the .31aiden-lane church, is to preside, and Mr. Justin 3PCarthy, M.p., and that Hon. Edward Blake, M.P., have intimated their intention to be present. Father Purchell has been a conspicuous standard-bearer of Home Rule in London,and has done good organis ing work amongst his countrymen in the metropolis.

Mr. Lilly, the author of the new book " The Great Enigma," is, as is well known, one of the most brilliant Roman Catholic controversialists. Ile is by profession a barrister and a member of the Inner Temple. lie knows something of science, but his tastes are mediaeval, and his views almost those of a Crusader. In literary society he is most popular. Unlike some Roman Catholics, he recog- nises kindred spirits in earnest Angelicaus, and has known intimately the late Canon Liddon and Vis- count Halifax, president of the English Church Union, to whom he dedicates his book. He was an intimate friend of the late Cardinal Newman. of whcm he has published some interesting remin- iscences, and the Cardinal often sought his advice on theological points.

Colonel Nicol, the editor of the" war Cry," whose conscientious objection to vaccination found him before the Highgate Bench, is a Scotsman. Be joined the Salvation Army in a remote Scotch country town ten years ago, and by energy and cnpacity has climbed to his present place in the organisation. For some time Colonel Nicol had charge of the foreign department at the Interna- tional headquarters, in Queen Victoria-st. Then he went round the world with General Booth—writ- ing many graphic letters to the " War Cry "—and since his return he has become editor of the Salvationists' thriving weekly. Cohnel Nicol is still quite young ; he is slightly built, and has fair hair and a beard.

The Fawcett memorial tablet in Westminster Abbey, and some chains of office which he has ex- hibited, give evidence of the special attention which Mr. Gilbert has devoted to designing anc.l working in metal. His most important work in point of size will before long be a familiar sight to Londoners. This is the bronze fountain to the memory of Lord Shaftesbury, which is in course of erection at Piccadilly-circus. The design is a charming one—dolphins, mermen, and mermaids sport in the water and there are nets in which all the fish cf the sea are tumbling over and over. In appearance Mr. Gilbert is youthful, almost to boy- ishness, and his manner is as unassuming.as it is kindly. He has a country retreat at Goroshall, a pretty village in that delightful bit of country which lies between Guildford and Dorking.

There are few men so well known in the medical world es Mr. Jonathan Ilutchinson. He belongs to an old Yorkshire Quaker family, and in that county he was born and educated. Roinoving in early life to London to commence practice as a surgeon, he soon made his mark, and was appointed surgeon to the London Hospital, Whitechapel. Taking a great interest in skin diseases, he joined the late John Startin, at the Blackfriars-road hospital for skin diseases, where he worked hard for many years. lie is now the leading authority on these diseases. In person Mr. Hutchinson is tall and thin, with a thought-worn face, modest in manner, and simple in mode of life. He is at work from early morning until late at night, and notwithstanding his large practice, finds time to get through a large amount of museum and literary work. His writings are known thrcughout the world.

-- Mr. H. P, °libel-, who was stricken down with paralysis on Monday morning on his way to busi- ness, and was conveyed to the Pantheon, the offices of the firm, in Oxford-st., in a condition from which he never rallied, and was the eldest of the three brothers who made the name of Gilbey a household word. In early life Mr. H. P. Gilbey was a wine merchant in the City,but when his two brothers, Waiter and Alfred, started at the West- end he joined them, and the phenomenal success of the great house was to no small extent attributable to his energy and ability. The deceased gentleman, who was sixty-eight years of age, was as remark- able for his unostentatious modesty as he was for his constanl and unobtrusive charity. Mr. Alfred Gilbey has been dead some years, and Mr. Walter Gilbey—so well known in connection with the breeding of horses in England—is now the last of three brothers. He has numerous sons and nip- hews.

Mr. Alfred Gilbert has " arrived "; be can now write R.A. after his name. The " immortals" of Burlington Rouse have done well in electing the talented sculptor, for in him the true feu sacrti • burns bright and clear, and although his exhibits to the Royal Academy shows can almost be counted on the fingers of two hands, their quality fully justifics the distinction which has lust been con- ferred unnn him. • Alr. Gilbert was born in London thirty-eight years ago, and after studying his art under Boehm, he went to Paris, and under M. Cavalier, of the Ecole des Beaux Art, became ac- quainted with the work of Palquiere, Premier, and Mercie. It was,however,during his long stay in Rome that he produced the works which have placed him so high up the ladder of fame. Of these may he mentioned "The Kiss of Victory," "Icarus," and a pleasing group " Mother and child." A small bronze head which he exhibited caused a great flutter among the artistic fraternity and was pur- chased by Mr. Luke Fildes. •

Ilerr Poznanski, the great violinist, is of Polish and English parentage and American birth. He developed a talent for the violin before attaining his fourth year, and soon became known iii his native city, Charleston, as• a musical prodigy of extraordinary promise. Later on:the great violin- ist Vieuxtemps, while touring in Americai with Thalberg, heard the boy play, and at once recog- nised his genius. For six years young Poznanski studied with Tieuxtemps, during which time he ' appeared with great success before Paris and Vienna audiences in concerts given by his master. He studied composition under S. Bagge, a pupil .of Lechter, and, after completing his musical educe- tint), played in the principal towns of Germany and France, where his grand tone and technique made his tour a series of triumphs. In 1866 he and his brother Joseph, pianist, gave an extended cbncert tour through the United States, and he -was ;after- wards appointed Director of the Illinois Coriserva- tory of Music, a pest he held till 1881, when be returned to Europe. Herr Poznanski is also a pro- lific composer of violin music. He and his charm- ing wife have a picturesque house overlooking the Thames at Ravenscourt-park.

'Everyone appreciating the benefits of shorthand will wish Mr. lkaac Pitman a speedy recovery from h.is illness. The "inventor of phonography." ;as he , likes to be called, is ordinarily one of the halt and heartiest of octogenarians. To this Mr. Pitman's methodical habits have largely conduced. He lives an ascetic life, and goes through his daily task like clockwork. Rising regularly at six, he goes break- fastless to -work at the " Phonetic Depot," ,as his place at Bath is called, and before the rest of the world is awake he has transacted ne• email propor- tion of his work. Ile is a non-smoker, a non- drinker, and an uncompromising vegetarian. i They i say also that he s a Quaker,,and certainly his dress and appearance give color to the statement. Two energetic sons assist Mr.Pittnan in his work at Bath, and two nephews—Messrs. Clarence and Gilbert Pitman—manage his London depot.

div.head: A. GLIMPSE OF SAN FRANCISCO.
div.p: A. GLIMPSE OF SAN FRANCISCO.

--- Mr. Hugh Ilarting, in an article in the " gives an interesting account of San Francisco. The city is built on a hilly formation,so unique (he says) that only some primeval convulsion could account for its appearance. Precipitous ascents and descents a ho:.ind to the north, and from the higher points a fine view spreads southwards across tiers of yellow wooden buildings to ranges of mountains rising up in mysterious and misty sequence. The chief th•rough- fare, Market-street, itself a level highway, separates the hilly from the flat portions of the city. The difficulty of public transit has bees overcome by the introduction of the cablecar system,the most perfect in the States. I have experienced nothing more delightful than a ride in, the head of one or these cable carsonaking steep ascents toppling over, and gliding swiftly down, only to rise once more like a switchback railway. Before I became accustomed to the tremendous ups and downs and the rapidity of this cars, I used to held on tight, momentar- ily expecting a collapse; but I soon got to regard thi. precipitous hills with indifference and enjoyed leaning back while breasting a rise or viewing a descent from the summit. The steepest descent in Sas Francisco is made on Washington-street, a residential quarter to the north, and the angles here assumed by the car throws one considerably out of the perpendicular. Stoppages are only made at street-corners, and, while waiting to take up stray passengers, or drop them,as the case may be, you hear the gables grating hoarsely beneath the track. They never cease their running day or night, and the sound suggests the rapacious gabbling of coins imprisoned monster. During his stay in San Francisco, Mr. Harting ex- plored the Chinese quarter, and paid a visit to the thea- tre there. One by one (he writes) we descended into a dimly lighted passage, off which were partitioned tiny hovels, the abodes of dozens of the Chinese race. Skirt- ing a series of side galleries, we entered a low kitchen, where a couple of Chinamen were attending to the great ovens, preparing a meal. Stairs led up from this dimi- nutive space, and as we began to aece.nd a medley of strange sounds proceeded from above,in which the clash of a symbal predominated. Oa reaching the top we found ourselves in the green-romn ot the Chinese theatre, surrounded by a gibbering mob of actors,attirecl in most gorgeous costumes, while the cymbals clashed and drums thundered close at hand. Pushing our way through the crowd, beyond a curtained doorway, we suddenly found ourselves on the stage. All was bewil- derment. Amid a terrific noise a wild skirmish was go- ing on.between a Chinese warrior (the star actor) and half a dozen armed men. Swords crossed, spears waved, and the warrior, after repeatedly tumbling over for no apparent reason, drove back his assailants through the curtains into the green room ; whereupon out filed a fresh body of men, and the battle was renewed with even greater vigour than before. The square theatre was filled with Chinamen, who, with upturned yellow faces, soft felt hats, and dark dresses, formed an odd assembl- age. Upstairs in the gallery were the ladies, their faces partially conclealed with bands of white linen. This strange audience seemed much impressed by the perform- ance, especially when a song was sung, accompanied very sweetly on yee-yens or stringed instruments. Some of the make-ups were very grotesque. The strangest of all were the Chinamen impersonating ladieso.vith smooth 1. neat hair and highly rouged cheeks. The theatre began to empty before the pageant ended, and our guide led us back by the way we had come.
THE MISSING WOlO COMPETITION.

At Bow-at. Police Court, on Tuesday, Mr. H. Reichardt proprietor, publisher, and editor of" Pick-me-up." and Mossrs. Wertheimer, Lea, and Co., the printers, were summoned for infringing the Lottery Adis in connection with the " missing Ford " competition. After a pro- tracted hearing Sir John Bridge decided that the Icomnetition was a lottery, and convicted the defendants fining them a shilling in each case. judgment was stayed for a week in view of an appeal. The decision of Sir John Bridge will, it is thought, have the effect of putting an end to missing-word com- petitions without t urther question. Mr. C. A. Pearson, proprietor of " Pearson's Weekly" and other pqhliCa- tions who was associated with the proprietors of " Pick Me Up "in defending the test case, states that he does not intend to appeal against the magisterial decision. Indeed, he expressed himself pleased with the result of the action, as the work of dealing with the competitions has of late become terribly exacting, and after those already in progress and arranged for have been finished the competitions will no longer continue. As illustrating .the popularity of this missing4vord feature of " Pearson's Weekly "and the enormous amount of work involved, its conductor declares that this week they have received £20,000, involving nearly 500,000 of separate shilling entries. He has been run- ning the competitions for the last twelve months, hut it was not until within the last three months that replic's became overwhelmingly numerous. Latterly the circu- lation of" Pearson's" had enormously increased, and last week 1,050,000 copies were printed. In oilier to deal with the competitions alone 350 per week for , salaries had been spent. '

CHAPTER XXXVIII. THE HAND OF DOODi. "This is one of the strangest and most intricate cases on record," muttered the chief, thoughtfully, long after Arthur had left him. "I will detail two of the best men we have to hunt Lyons down, and bring him to justice." Bet if the earth had opened and swallowed him, he could not have been more completely lost to the world. At length a very cunning device was resorted to. An item was sent to the leading journals, in which it was stated that a very disgraceful street brawl had occurred on Lexington Avenue, and the participants, two well-known young society gentlemen—Mr. Frank Lyons and a Mr. Smith—had both been placed under immediate arrest, and were then "in durance vile." As had been expected, one of these paragraphs met Frank Lyons's eye, and he presented himself at the office of the paper to demand a retraction. He was invjted into the private office to await the coming of the editor, and word was immediately sent to the detective bureau. The chief, with one of his men, lost no time in making Lyons their prisoner. They had wisely concluded to say nothing about the Pittsburgh affair, until they had learned the whereabouts of lonie Lawrence. As the officer stepped forward, placed his hand upon Lyons's shoulder, and said: "You are my prisoner," Lyons wheeled suddenly about, and exclaimed. "May I ask upon what charge?" "Upon the charge of abducting Miss lorrie Law- rence," was the quiet reply. "At whose instigation ?" he demanded. "Mr. Arthur Rochester's," was the reply. At first he tried bravado, and declared it was all a mistake; but that failed him, and when he saw the handcuffs he fell back like one half fainting. "You say it was Arthur Rochester who caused my arrest ?" he asked, bitterly. The man nodded. "Then that is one more item added to the account I have to settle with him," he said, with an insolent

laugh. "Mr. Rochester is, or Was, the young lady's lover," the detective went on. "Poor fellow he has been driven almost mad over the affair. Losing her almost ruined his life, he loves the girl so dearly." Again that insolent, sneering laugh fell from Frank Lyons's Tips. "It ruined his life did it?" he repeated. "I am right well pleased to know that; I wish it had killed him. He shall never know from my lips the whereabouts of lonic Lawrence." Those words assured the detective two things: that Lyons knew where the girl was, and that she was Miss Lawrence still.

"Where are you taking me?" cried Lyons, aghast, as they stopped before the Tombs, and the officer invited him to enter. "Where you will in all probability remain until you disclose the whereabouts of Miss Lawrence. I cannot answer.now further than that." "Then I shall die here," responded Frank Lyons, with a harsh, discordant laugh. "I am master of the situation, and I intend to remain so." "W' shall " returned th. fficer

,e si see, urn. e officer, grimly; when three days passed, and Lyons was still obdurate, matters were assuming a serious aspect. To Arthur Rochester those hours that passed were like the agonies of death. Anothe- :k of tortur- 0 again, upon

It was a shock to Lyons when he discovered the double charge on which he was to be triFd—for that murder committed in Pittsburgh on that bitter winter night, as well as for the abduction of lonia Lawrence.
A RUNCORN Bb:ERHOUSE KEEPER SUMMONED.

Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Clara Marsh, a widow, licensee of the Sailors' Home, Regent-sr.. was summoned for unlawfully permitting drunken- ness. Mr. B. Wynne Humphreys prosecuted for the police, and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. It appeared that on Friday night, the 2114 inst.,lnspec- tor Cooper Was passing down Regent-street, about half past ten, when he heard a considerable noise emanating front the Sailors' Home, and five minutes later he entered, in company with P.C. Gregory. Both officers were in plain clothes Proceeding through the bar into aa inner room, the officers found 8 or 9 men and one woman, and without exception, they were all under the influence of drink more or less, and two men named John Wilkinson and Charles Botterill, were "dis- gustingly drunk." The disturb rice in the room was so great that it could be heard across the street, and the utmost confusion prevailed. There was a vast amount of liquor on the floor. With much difficulty Inspector Cooper obtained the names of Bet terill and Wilkinson, and he then called Mrs. Marsh's attention to the fact that these men were drunk, and she replied " I know they are, but what can I do ?" He also pointed out the general disorder of the house, and to this she made no reply. Wilkinson and Botterill were taken into the taproom on their way to bed by several women, and here they com- menced to wrestle, but were separated by two or three women. Mrs. Marsh informed the police that the men were boarders and had only come from Rio Grande that day. Inspector Cooper informed the Bench that he was under the impression that Williamson had been about the town for several weeks. Evidence was given by Inspector Cooper, P.C.'s.Gregory, Ridgway, Morris, and Worth.— For the defence Mr. Knowles said he would not contend that these two men were perfectly sober, hut witnesses would prove that they were not drunk. They had come off a vsssel that day, and Wilkinson had paid for a fort- night's "lodge " in advance, while Botterill, who was also staying in the house, had not been paid off. They had tea in the house, and afterwards Wilkinson and Botterill and several others had between them two Ina gallons of beer. They then went out, and on returning Mrs. Marsh saw they had had some drink, and asked them to go to bed, but they refused to do so, until they had had their supper, which was cooking in a pan on the lire. TheY'were not served with any drink, and when the police canto in they. were simply waiting for their supper. As to the disturbance, Mr. Knowles said sailors,when they came ashore after a long voyage, were very merry and ivial, and amused themselves and their friends by larking and singing. It would have been a gross interference with the liberty of these sailors had Mrs. Marsh when they returned home to sleep, refused to admit them, and sent for a. pence- II to place them in the cella, for which they would have had to pay 153. for one night as much as she would keep them a week for. He argued that these circum- stances did not come- within the charge of permitting drunkenness.—The defendant and several other wit- ' messes were called in support of this statement, and the ! Bench dismissed the case.—The charges of drunkennese against Wilkinson and Botterill, were also dismissed. -41 r,

slipped - to freedom. "We will capture him sooner or later," declared the chief, energetically. "Our men will all be active in the search, the reward is BO great." "It will not matter much," replied Arthur I Rochester, gloomily. "He would not divulge Miss Lawrence's whereabouts. He would take the secret Into the grave with him." The chief smiled. "Rest assured he has gone directly to Miss Law- rence," he said; "and by tracking him down, we shall be sure to find her." But when a fortnight rolled by, and he was not yet traced—nor even the faintest clue to his where- abouts discovered—then, indeed, did Arthur begin to despair. His friends advised him ',to abandon the search, but he turned ftlim them angrily. "Never l" he cried. "I shall never rest, day or night, until I have solved the terrible problem." When Frank Lyons found himself free, he lost no time in leaving New York city; and, contrary to expectations, he did not go near lonie, but made his way at once to Boston, waiting there for an ocean steamer whtch he knew would sail early the following week. "I can never take lonic with me. They are watching me too closely for that," he thought, as he watched the tall spires of the city fade away in the, dimness of the oncoming night. "I will leave her. where she is for a month or so; and when the ex- citement has partially blown over, return for her. It is perfectly safe leaving her where she is. She I cannot escape." Taking an ocean steamer had been a very clever plan; but executing,ft was not so easy. Ho found each and every one under close surveillance of the police. "It would never do to remain in Boston," he con- cluded; and made preparations to take the evening train to an interior town, quite off therein line, and accessible only by stage. He did not feel quite safe until the train was under headway, steaming out of Boston. Perhaps there is no sensation in life more terrible than the knowledge a man has that there is a price on his head—the feeling that he is hunted like a wild beast, that the man who gives him to eat or I drink, looks in his face, and, if he knew him, would betray him. Lyons's bravery was lessening. He had grown nervous from continual pursuit. And in that hour in which he was leaving Boston a terrible depression came over him. His vile, adventurous life, full of evil deeds, rose before him, and he owned to himself the truth of , those words, that there was no hell so terrible to any man as the reproach of his own conscienoe. Night was setting in with sullen sultriness, pre- saging a corning storm. Night fell over the beautiful city he was leaving, ever the blue sea beyond and the golden sands; night, with a lowering sky and rising wind, in which the shrill whistle of the departing train was heard more plainly than ever. Silence fell over the land, broken only by the boding voice of the coming storm. More than one Man on that ill-fated aain felt the strange depression—a half warning—a presentiment of coming evil. As the train reached the first station, it was, by. some unaccountOle reason, found to be twenty minutes behind time. The fireman heaps more coal into the furnace, watching covertly out of the corners of his eyes the engineer, John Doan, who stands thoughtfully before the window, with his hands on the lever, while the train, puffing and panting, dashes on through the darkness of the night. And as he looked the engine whirled with light- ning-like rapidity around an abrupt curve. There was a terrible, hoarse cry from the en- gineer.

It was, he said, highly improper that one man„ like _the lord lieutenant, should hold the ap.: pointment of justices in his own hand. Ni' property qualification was required in the case of a workingman magistrate being appointed in a boronal•, but the working-man could not be Made a county justice. What was more ridiculous still, by 'a ludicrous etiquette a retail shopkeeper could not be made' county justice , while his cousin the wholesale wine' and spirit merchan could be appointed one. What he desired was o see qualification abolished so that all classes—shopkeeper, working-man, and professional man—would be eligible. Mr. Dodd was heartily received by his political oppon- ents, and they passed a vote of thanks to him, and also approved the principle of his bill.

1 CHAPTER XXXIX. KETRIBUTLON ALWAYS FOLLOWS THE WICKED. Quick as a lightning's flash the train whirled around the fatal curve, where the dark object lay across the track, and terrible was the crash that followed.

It was the greatest holocaust known for years. People always spoke of it afterward with a shudder. There was fearful loss of life; scores were mangled, scores wounded unto death. Luckily a village was near, and the unfortunates were quickly carried thither as soon as they were extracted from the debris of the wreck; among them was Frank Lyons. He had been taken to the nearest house—a farm- house—and soon the farmer's wife was busied in making him as comfortable as his intense pain would permitthim to be. "Will he die, Doctor?" asked the good woman, looking up into the physician's face as she followed him out into the hall. "His head is not injured, but his spine is broken," was the answer. "Then there is no hope for him," said the farmer's wife. "Not the slightest," was the reply. "You will have little to do," he went on, "but your work will be tiresome. The young man utterly refuses to believe that he lies in any danger. There is no earthly aid for him. There is nothing to do but to watch him, cheer him, soothe him. Give him wine, brandy, cordial, but make him understand, as soon as possible, that he has to die! Men hear such news better from women than from us. He may last till sundown to-morrow," he added. "Not longer." So human lives are measured off. Then the doctor went away, and the farmer's wife returned to her patient; and, turning down the night-lamp, was about to resume her watch by his bedside, when he called out to her sud- denly. "Don't lower the light. I never could endure darkness. What was that I heard the doctor saying to you? It is their business to croak and make people miserable." "He has left me a difficult task," said the farmer's wife, gently. "They always leave the hardest part to other people,' said the sick man, grimly. "What is your task?" "To give his message to you," she replied; "but, perhaps I need not fear. Brave men do not fear death. You may be brave." "You look as though v- believe me seriousl

volc as though you 1y u_ jured," he said, impatiently. "Such nonsense I would not believe the doctor if he said so; would you? Do I look like a man likely to die 7" "I cannot tell. The doctor is wiser than I. He believes you will. You are not afraid of death 7" "I am not quite sure whether I am or not," he said. "I have never troubled myself to think mach about it. I have never realised it. If I thought, really that I had to die, there is—" He stopped abruptly. "If you thought you had to die, there are matters you would attend to 7" sire said. He nodded. "Yes, if I were sure I was.to die," he repeated at

length; then he began to fail, and understand that It was indeed death. She saw a great fear was coming over him, and when the grey dawn broke, he called to her eagerly: "Is there a clergyman near? IT so; bring him to me." It was quite ,half an hour before the Reverend Mr. Merrill entered the room. "You wished to see " he said, kindly, taking
me, . his place by the sick man. "Yes," replied Frank Lyons. "I want you to bear witness to a story I have to tell, and then to help me die." This quite disconcerted the good man. It was

....as quite not an easy thing to help a man die. "I do not know much about death," continued Lyons, brushing with his weak right hand the dark, damp curls back which clustered about his fore- head. "I have only seen one man die, and he was murdered," he whispered; "murdered one snowy stormy night in the suburbs of Pittsburgh." The words ended in a shudder and a long-drawn, gasp-

_ _ "It will be all up with me anyhow," he told him- lug breath. _ self, with a laugh horrible to hear; "and if I have "Revenge and malice are not worth much to a to face the gallows, it will be a glorious revenge to dying man—a man who is leaving the world behind me that I will carry the secret down to the grave him," he added. with me. Arthur Rochester will never And his "You are very right," said the clergyman. "They 'arlinit." are stumbling blocks in the path that leads to The trial of Frank Lyons was one of the most heaven." celebrated that, was ever tried in the metropolis, "It is not fair," muttered Frank Lyons to himself. owing to his hitherto high social position. "After all, I have had but a very short life of it, He was found guilty of murder, and sentenced to and it has been a miserable failure. be hanged. "I need not inflict the story of my life, and youth On the morrow the whole city was startled by the upon you." he said. "I was left an orphan at an news of his daring escape. For a time no one could early age, and when I became one-and-twenty I find the slightest ' clue as to how it had been came into the fortune I inherited. The whole effected; then at last it came out that an old secret of my mined life lies in these words. If I friend of Lyons's had aided • him by securing with had been put out into the world to earn my own Influential aid, a position in the prison, and had livelihood, I might have turned out an honourable, - him the keys that had unlocked Industrious the doors man...ln less than three years I ran

through three noble fortunes which hid been left me, and at the age of four-and-twenty I found my- self a bankrupt, heavily in debt, and pressed by creditors. "I had met a true and noble girl, whose life might have been happy enough if I had not drifted across her path. She learned to love me, and I encouraged her. When I broke with Barbara Law- rence, calling our friendship only a pastime, her heart broke, she had so truly believed I was sincere in my attentions to her. She never named me. Not even to those nearest and dearest to her was it over known that she even knew me. •.,(" I tried to camfort myself for many a day after Barbara Lawrence died with the thought—' A 'woman should not infer if a man speaks pleasantly to her for a few times that his object is matrimony.' I tried to forget her, but her face haunted me. "The day of retribution came after I met Bar- bara's younger sister, lonie, who, I felt sure, knew nothing of Barbara's love affair. "I cannot tell you what she was like—gloriously beautiful, with a beauty which has driven more men than myself mad with love for her. "From the first moment I saw her a strange, subtle fascination drew me toward her. I grew to love her with a love that was my doom. "I won her love, but lost It; for she had found out, In some way, what a graceless spendthrift I had been. "She learned to love another—one who had in by-gone days been my friend. "I made the mistake of my life when I took a solemn vow that I would take her from him by fair means or foul. An opportunity came. It has always seemed to me since that an evil fate ordained in that way. "I heard her uncle, who was under the influence of wine, quarrelling with an enemy of mine, a man for whom I had entertained a life-long hatred. My heart beat strangely when I heard them quarrel- ling, and, lonie's uncle turned away with the reck- less words on his lips: 'Keep away from me! Keep out of my path for ever, .or I will kill you P—words spoken in the heat of the moment, but never meant. "That night, quite by chance, I met my enemy In an isolated spot; words led to an altercation, and—Heaven help mel—l slew him in the frenzy of the moment." Here followed a brief account of Lyons's plot- tings until he fled from the church with lonie in his arms, as stated in a previous chapter. " I bore the senseless girl to my carriage," Lyons continued, "and drove rapidly away. "Illy every effort to arouse her was without avail. 'Was she dying ?' I asked myself, in agony. "I drove across the country to the nearest village, and upon the outskirts of it I observed, before a small white cottage, a doctor's sign. "I drove up to the piazza and was met by the doctor, who assisted me into the house with the inanimate form of lonie. ." Is she your wife?' he asked, and the question was pat to me so suddenly, I did not have time to consider whether it would be best to claim her on that half-concluded ceremony or not, and I answered —'No; my fiance.' "I was invited into an adjoining room, and be called upon his wife, a stately, gentle lady, to assist him with his new patient. "Was it only my fancy, or did I hear blood- curdling-laughs and hushed cries through the hours that followed? "At length I beard the doctor's footsteps ; the gravity of his face startled me. ...Are you prepared for a great shook?' be asked ; and I replied that I could nerve myself to bear it, Inquiring, in I he same breath, if there was anything serious the matter? "'I almost fear to tell you,' he replied; but I presume it is best gotten over quickly. The young lady is hopelessly insane, sir.' " I wonder the words did not strike me dead whare I stood.

" For an hour or more she was quite violent,' he went on, gravely, 'but now she has sunk into a state from which no power can arouse her. She is more helpless than the most helpless child, and she will be like this through life.' "No mortal man ever suffered what I suffered when I followed him into the adjoining room and

The babblings that she uttered would soon have driven me mad, too. Leaving a well-filled purse, with the instructions she should have every care that money could procure, I went away. I wan- dered up and down the face of the earth the most wretched man that ever lived. "You have not heard all yet," he said, turning his feverishly bright eyes on the clergyman. "I came back to New York, and there a trap had been laid for me by lonie's friends. "To be brief, I was arraigned for that murder, in Pittsburgh on that winter right. Then an e?e- witness was produced. I was convicted, and the jury passed sentence of death upon me. I escaped —it matters little now how—and fled to Boston, intending to take the out-going steamer for Europe, • but I saw it so closely watched by the officers ef the law I dared not make the attempt, and on the Impulse of the moment took the train back into the interior. You know the result.
"I suppose," said Frank Lyons, looking into the rector's distressed face, "you consider mine a bad case ? "

" I have never heard a worse series of crimes," said the clergyman, sadly. "I do not speak of forgiveness, for I believe there Is none for me; I have sinned too grievously for that. I can make but this reparation before I die: Send to the man from whom I parted lonic, rind who is wearing his life out searching for her, and tell him where she is."

"His name I" said the clergyman, seeing he was sinking fast. "Arthur Rochester, No. Lexington Avenue, New York," was the faint reply. "Is there anything else you would like to say r was asked Lyons. "Yes," he muttered; "lonie—l—onie—" With the name on his lips, Frank Lyons pagsed through the portals of death to the unknown. beyond. Before noon the neat day the Reverend Mr. Mer- rill's letter to Arthur Rochester, telling him of lonie's whereabouts, was on its way to New York. In it was a faithful statement, word for word, of all Frank Lyons had said. Arthur Rochester's emotion, upon reading that letter, can be better imagised than describod. lonie lying ill, her reason entirely dethroned, and for ever 1 The words seemed to scorch their way into his brain. "Heaven keep me from going mad myself at such intelligence as this!' he cried, raising his white, desperate face to the night sky. Procuring two of the most famous medical experts in insanity cases, Arthur hastened on at once to the little village of Braulea. He lived years instead of hours, it seemed to him, before the train dashed up and stopped at the little depot. There was no conveyance, and the three started on foot for the doctor's cottage, on the outskirts of the village. He had been telegraphed to; he would be, expecting them. As they opened the white gate, Arthur turned suddenly to his companions. "There is one favour I insist upon," he said, "and you will not, I am sure, find it in your hearts to refuse me. I must see lonie at once.

"OH, MAMMA, WE'RE GOING INTO THE DARK!" The little girt stood on the seat of a first-clas com- partment on the London underground railway, looking out of the window. The writer of these lines sat on the opposite seat watching the child, who was taking huge delight in what she saw and heard at the station where she and her mother entered the coach. Presently the train started, passed through an open space or two, then plunged into the tunnel. As All outside objects vanished, and the window became a mirror in which she could see nothing but the dim lines of her own sweet face, the little one cuddled down to her mother's side, and said, with a note of anxiety in her voice, " Oh mamma, we're, going into the dark! I don't like the dark, do you?' " No, dear," answered the mother, her words being ac centuated by the mourning dress she wore; "no, dear, nobody likes the dark, but we shall see the light again at the next station."

"There's nothing in that," do you say? Possibly you have followed the sun around the earth and never been in the dark. If that is the case, this trifling incident about the child in the tunnel has no significance for you. But it goes stiai,ght to the hearts of most of us, for we an men and women who have known what it is to wait long for a morning that has been slow, so slow, to come. I have before me now a woman's letter, in which she . tells the simple story of an illness. " All my life," she says, " I have been subject to racking headaches and bilious sickness. Almost every week I would have an attack, with a dreadful pain at the temples and a weight over the eyes, so that I could scarce Multitudes of women will understand this. These tormenting headaches, accompanied as they norno°l3lV are, with great nervous prostration and distress of mind, have often driven good women to despair, and not infrequently to suicide. It is going into the dart, indeed. She continues : "At these times I felt so dizzy that I was obliged to lie on the couch constantly, and but for necessity of caring for my family, should have been con- fined to my bed. In the morning in particular my mouth tasted badly—a disgusting metallic taste that often made me shiver with the loathing I had for it. With this there would be a thick, tenacious phlegm GI mucus which I rinsed out as well as [ could W th vvaten. I ate next to nothing, because I had no desire for food, no appetite. Still I took something, of course, to sustain life, yet even that often made me so sick that I threw it up again." Now, the fact that this lady's experience is the experience of millions doesn't make it any easier to bear in the case of an individual, does it ? When you burn your fingers at the fire the pain isn't a bit the less because it is an everyday occurrence with some- body. Death comes to some human being every second, yet death remains a terror to all, and will, until there is not a breathing manor woman in the world. You ad" mit this. Well, then, read the rest of the letter. "At times," says the writer," I threw up a quantity of green fluid, and had a heavy, dull, sinking pain in the right side. After every successive attack I felt stitl more weak, languid, and tired, and had an increasing difficulty in getting about. This in substance was my condition for years, during which time I underwent medical treatment and also took many medicines that were recommended to me ; but I grew worse in spite of all. "One day in April, 1890, I happened to read in a pamphlet of a case like my own haying been cured by Mother Seigel's Syrup. All the symptoms were so fully described that I felt very hopetul, and procured a bottle of the medicine from Mr. John Beckett, the chemist, at Monkgate, and after taking it but a short time, Comp , surprise and joy the headache and sickness loft me, and I never felt so well. It was like coming into the day- light after a tedious night.—(Signed) Emz.a WARE, 65, Newboro'-street, York. April 23rd, 1891." The ailment vs hich so long destroyed this woman's health and happiness was indigestion and dyspepsia, from which, sad to say, very few of her sex are free. Imagine the bulk or mass of suffering they endure, with its evil consequences pervading all their relations with others. Why may not the remedy which cured her do the same for all her pain stricken sisterhood ? It will. it will ; and is doing it daily. It helps them out•of the dark tunnel of disease into the brightness of health and natural usefulness and enjoyment,

RE-OPENING OF THE BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CiiA.PEL, WARRINGTON. Sunday was the occasion of the re-opening of Bold-st., Wesleyan Chapel, after undergoing decor- ations. The work of decoration was carried out by Messrs. H. and S. Mendley, Bridge-st., Warrington, under the direction of Mr. T. Silcock, and it has produced a most pleasing change intim- sacied edi— ice. The building has been elaborately adorned with artistic colouriug. The ceiling has been tinted in colours of create and blue, and the stiles and beams are of a fawn colour, the rich plaster freeze being relieved by ' a full vellum tint. The walls have been treated as de- corative masonry, with straw-coloured broad points or banda on a rich dark green background. The main' walls en each side of the orgati have been divided into decorative arches in harmony with the idea of the -existing arch, across each being placed a'sert of decent.; tire curtain surmounted by a frieze. Over each there had , been left a space of .azure and gold, being a conven-,' tionalised representation of a starlit sky. The stiles is the gallery front have been stained a colour more is-, harmony with that of the pulpit, and have been revar- nished. The work has been carried out in the short,' period of five weeks, and has been exeepted in a man:Y nor which is most creditable to those who bad it in hand. Sermons were preacned on Sunday morning and even- ing by the Rev. T. House, of Liverpool. There was a I large congregation in the evening, when the rev. gentle- man, prior to the delivery of his sermon, made a short financial statement. He said the recent bazaar realised, after payment of expenees,£47l. There was a chapel debt of some £209, and after this £262 was left towarclothe renovation. This had cost £420, and, considering the size of the building and what had been done, he thought it had been done economically. He knew something of what it cost to renovate chapels, having had experience of three or four such cases in his last three or four • cir- cuits, and he thought the work had been carried out with due economy. In order to meet the balance of ex- penditure, £l5B was required, and the collections that day, the receipts at the lecture the following evening, and the collections next Sunday would be applied to the payment of the debt. He understood that in the pre- • sent circumstances of Warrington, the recelpts of many of those present were not so great as was ordinarily the case, but he appealed to them to give RS generously as they could. The chapel would not need any further re- novation for many years to come. The trustees would like them to help them by assisting in the matter of pew rents, fora person who took a pew in a Methodist Chapel contributed to the funds of the place. He pointed out that as yet pew tents could Hot be dispensed with, but advised all those who could to take sittings in the chapel, as he himself had been in the habit ,of doing in those chapels at which he had been a minister. —The rev, gentleman subsequently preached an excel- lent sermon from Job xxxiic., Bv., But there is a spirit In man : and the inSpiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding." Ile described his text as a thunder- bolt against materialism. We lived,he said;between two completely antagonistic ideas—one that man was simply a material being, the other that he had a spiritual nature. If a Man took the materialistic view the horizon of his being was narrowed down to the present time he was a superior gifted animal, that was B. If he took the spiritual view, his horizon enlarged and swept range upon range, height above height. The Bible teaching in this matter was summed up in the verse of the text— there was a spirit in man and, there was a God who in- fluenced that spirit. Materialism said therowas no spirit in man, and no Almightly Being that inspired him—that his only inspiration came from his brain tend his brain was affected only by its environments. 'This was very simple, but did not touch the great problem of life. The main tenet of materialism was that there was nothing in the universe but matter and force, and that all things were explainable by the properties contained in them. There was a third thing, consciousness, which was a machine whose springs were adapted to produce certain results. All men were maiehines. fia..Patil talked of a divine law that was written on every man's heart, but our materialistic philosophers told :us that the idea of independent consciousnesswas an .obsolete notion. Ac- cording to them, the present crodePand vulgar theories regarding morality, religion, Divine Providence, God,the soul of man, and will, apart from organisation was pure nonsense : there could be no angel, no spirit, no mind,no God,apart from organisation. MriJohn Morley said a good man was a machine whose springs were adapted so to fulfil their functionsAs toproduce bene- ficial" results—no credit tothe man-for any right-doing, but a great deal of credit to whoever made the springs. Professors Clifford, Huxleyeilerbert-Speneer,and others, taught that the laws of thought were inducedaendencies of the nervous system. Prefeseor flualey said that con- sciousness was a function of nervous matter, when the matter had attained a certain degree of • oiganisation, consequently, when the organisation-ceased, -conscious- ness ceased. Mr. Frederick flarrisonsaid,to talk to him of organization being swept away and the.coasciousaess remaining the same was nonsense. Thatheory of develop- ment of these' men was a scheme in which thamud of the earth under certain chemical conditions generated mag- gots,whicaa grew bigger because they could not help it,and these ancestral maggots had produced our present phil- osophers. Wonderful maggots'! But that was &scheme in which there was no arehaugelano • God, no:spirit world, no inspiration of a human soul. The rev, gentleman dealing further with the materialistic theories of man's origin, asked wild made the atom from which he was said to have sprung, and said the woiald sooner take the testimony of the searing spiritseeking to,find its waybaek to Godah an that of the spawn of some stagnant pool, and the reptile's trail in the mire.—Anthein3 were sung by the choir at each service. Collections were made, by which a sum of about £2B was realised. LECTURE ON SPORORON. On Monday evening the Rev. S. T. Houae delivered a lecture in the chapel on C. H. Spurgeon. Dr. Starkey Smith, in the absence of Mr. William Barlow, who had been announeed as chairman, but as mitering from a cold, presided. The audience was only small. "there were also present on the platform the Revs. T:Kittlan, A. Freeman, and T. Ross. A hymn haying been sung, and prayer offered by the Rev. A. Freeman, Mr. House delivered his lecture. He said a few years ago there were in the world three great preachers, Henry Ward Beecher, Dr. Parker, and Charles Haddon Spurgeoe, and of these Mr. Spurgeon held the highest place. Without the wide culture and the intellectual penetration of the great American -preacher he had a congregation quite as large. He was heard by more peopae than any other' preacher of the century, and his sermons had been more widely read than-those of any living man. ells name was to multitudes eif families a household word, and to the churches of Christ it was a tower of streggth. • • character was as massive as that of OfiverOsomwell. The great preaching friars of the middle ages and George 'Whitfield preached occasionally to larger audiences than, 'Mr. Spurgeon ever saw, but no other man than Spargeon had gathered and heldtogether for more than 30 years a :congregation of 5,000 to 8,000 people weekly. There was no music, no highly creanised ritual to attract them ; the service was simple Sand unadorned; they went to hear the man alone. Be had to endure the lot of all reformers. When a young preacher he was denounced in some quarters and lampooned in others, said to be ignorant, uneducated, half-educated, without polish, or a University career. The,press, notably the" Saturday Review" and the " Daily 'Telegraph," sought to crush bimeinder the mountain of their malediction. Press- men who probably never went to a place of worship said he was irreverent, and they declared he was a bag of wind, soon to be forgotton. These writers were for- gotten and unknown while the young preacher found a place that would be his for ever in the history of the Christian Church. Thomas I3inney declared that he would not occupy a pulpit which Spurgeon had occupied, until six months had intervened ; it must be purified. But the more he was thus spoken and written against, the more people went to hear him, and in the long run it was proved that the critics were wrong and the com- mon people right, as in such a case they generally were. His sermons had been published weekly since 1855, and had had a circulation of 50 millions in this country, and been widely circulated in America and the colonies, and translated into many of the languages of Europe and some of the languages of Asia. He was one of the most prolific of authors and gave some 60 volumes of instruc- tive literature to the world. He might have become rich, but lavished his money on the Tabernacle and its agencies. His people gave him £8,248, and four or five Years later £4,500, and he spent both sums upon work connected with his place of worship. The personalty of hie will was proved at £lO,OOO. £B,OOO of that, it was fair to say, was the estimated value of his sermons and books, which of course he could not have been expected to part with. He died worth next to nothing in cash. The lecturer, enumerating some of the elements of Spurgeon's success mentioned his perfect and command- ing voice,his thoroughly English style,his hard work,and great reading, his earnestness, and his godliness.—The Rev. A. Freeman proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer, and the chairman, mentioning that he had been acquainted with Spurgeon's father in Essex.—The Rev. T. Ross seconded, and the Rev. T. Rirtlan supported the motion, which was heartily carried and acknow- ledged, and the proceedings concluded in the-usual de- votional manner.

He regarded the central conference as far more important in respect to what itanight do. than in respect to what it actcally did, and probably at no period of our history had poor law legislation, I assumed sixth grave aspects as at present. One impor- tant subject was the)question of;pensions to old people. THE REDUCED QtaiIIMICATION FOR GI7ARDIENS The Oteurread a circular from the Basford rUnion inviting the Bcard to join the Guardians of that'Union in proteeting,in the strongest terms possible to the Local Gemernment'Beard against their freduction of the rated able qualificatien of elected Guardians to ES. They. consideredthat there was no necessity for so veat change. (Rear, heart) The inevitable result .of it would be to increase the distribution of the poor rataby causing the election on 'Boards of Guardians of persons haying little responsibility ,and small interest in what theyadministered.—Mr. Sutton remarked that when the. Board had previously had this subject before theinthey did not think it necessary to interfere, and the Local Government Board had by their action in the matter simply been acting in accordance with the will of the country, as erproseed by the doing away of like qualifi- cations. There was now no ,gualification for Parlia- ment, or for Town Councils. There ,was none forthe borough magistracy, and a bill was tote introduced to dispense with quedificaticon 'for the county maais- tracy. It was for the .Board -to say whether it was necessary to take any steps •ict the matter. —Mr. Mum proposed that the 'Beard accede to the in •a-itation of the circular letter.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON

1-wconded.—The Cnaixerats thought it wodd be a waste ol: strength on the part of the Board to do as propesed. It did not matter to them whetherthe qualification was Bd. or £6O. They as old-fashioned people -might think it did, but they must bear in mind that .the rising gen- eration thought different., and considered they had been kept out of their rights bythese old-fasbioned,people with their large assessments. They were determined to have their share of the representation ; they could not be prevented.—Mr. DIGNITY Don't you think that if Boards of Guardians throughout the country were to express an opinion it would iafluence the LocadGovern- mentSoard in their future determination about matters P —Mr. Mum n thciught the reduction of qualification , would do more injury to the ratepayers than the like so' far as the borough and county magistrates and Town. Councils put together would do, because there would be• dispensation of the monies of the ratepayers concerned, and the lower classes—he did not wish to say anything disparaging about them—men rated at £5, would be only too willing to give their compeers too much money.— Mr. Roberts: That does not by any means ensure a man sitting on a Board of Guardians. That is only ensured by the election of the ratepayers of the district.—The CHAIRMAN said supposing he did not pay any rates it would not make the slightest difference as to his being qualified to be a Guardian. He should just be as good a man if he paid lad, as if he paid £3O.—A GUARDIAN You would think of the £3o.—The CHAIRMAN : Think of the £3O ! I have a great deal more to think of.—Mr. GILL did not think it would be of much use joining in the protest ; it would have no effect on the Local Govern- ment Board. The qualification of £5 might look ridicu- lous, but for the Town Council and other public bodies there was no qualification at all. He moved an amend- ment that the circular lie on the table.—Mr. ROBERTS seconded.—Mr. A. J. JOLLIZT supported the amendment. He characterised the decision of the Local Government Board as a very just and proper one, and said it would be a very great mistake to go in the face of the whole tendency ef modern times, by opposing the decision. He did not see why there should be this apparently jealous feeling of one class against another. (Cries of " No, no.") People elected by the ratepayers were supposed to act in the interests of the commuity at large, and he did not see why a person rated at £5 could not act as honestly as a man rated at £5O. It depended on the man, not on his money value.—The amendment and ori- ginal motion were put, when 9 voted for each. The Chairman then gave his casting vote for the amendment, which was thus carried. be appointted inspectors upon the terms stated. The hos- pital reports showed that there were 11 patients in the Accident Hospital, and 8 in the Infectious Diseases Hos- pital. The medical officer reported that during Novem- ber there were 87 births and 38 deaths, being at the res- pective rates of 348 and 152 per 1,00.) per annum. Zy- motio disease caused 1 death. Notifications of infectious disease had been received as fellows :—Enteric or typhoid ' fever, 8 ' • erysipelas,l2 ; membrane croup, 3; and scarlet fever. 17; total, 38. The medical officer adds :—I am, pleased to be able to state to the Council that the death rate in this borough for the month of November,in corn- tiiarison with that of most towns in the kingdom, is very low, being only 15.2 per 1,000 of the population. In the Month of October the death rate was 164 and in the month of November last year it was 18.96. The cases Of infectious diseases notified are less numerous than during the last three months. I have regularly visited thehospitals during the month, and haee found the ad- ministration satisfactory. The surveyor is carry- ing out the recommendation of the Council dili- gently, erecting a building for the accommodation Of smallpox patients. I am glad to be able to atate that we still enjoy an immunity from smallpox atot a single case of it having occurred amongst our 'community. I would strongly recommend that every i Oerson above ten years of age be re-vaccinated, and that no unnecessary delay be made in vaccinating child- ren. All precautions have been taken in disinfecting houses where that infectious disease has been reported lrom, and in various parts of the town back passages i ave been disinfected, The insanitary property in this own requires the careful attention of the Council. That In Victoria-st. which I reported some time ago has not yet been attended to. My attention has been called to a house and shop at the corner of Brynn-st. and Travis- at. where the yard is inundated, and has been for some time and is dangerous to health. This should be imme- diately attended to. I recommend that certain diseases 'be struck eff from notification cases such as obtain in other Sanitary Authorities. 1 recommend that the state of William-st. be improved, more especially the part of at abutting on Albert-road. Resolved—lapou'the certificate of the Medical Officer of Health, that houses numbered to 12 inclusive, back Milton-road, are unfit for human habitation, that the , Town Clerk be and he is hereby instructed to take all necessary legal Steps for having such buildings closed, and themse thereof for human habitation prohibited. In moving the adoption of the minutes, Councillor G. I.Neil,expressed the hope that the public would take the doctor s advice and be revaccinaced.—Alderman Timmis seconded.—Alderman Waring asked for an explanation why the insanitary property in Victoria-street had not been attended to.—Councillor Quinn called attention to I thellooded state of Orford-street, in which the roadway was higher than the houses, rendering the homes unfit for habitation.—Councillor 'Neil replied that there had been great difficulty in deAling with the owners of pro- perty, in'lrictoria-street, who had now been served with the usual notice,that if the property was not attended to within seven days,it would be condemned. In regard to the Lower- house-lane improvement, the surveyor was instructed to arrange with Messrs. Kelsall and Hodgkinson the Amount of compensation to he paid to them, in respect of the laying of sewer across their fields, and that fail- ing such arrangement, notices be served upon them, un- der section -16, of the Public Health Act, 1875. ualderman Sadler moved, and Alderman lilleyseconded the adoption of the minutes.—Councillor Smith asked whether there was in the Highway Department a man named Peter sate' a labourer,-working as a-hricklayer at the rate of 6d. an hour. He also drew attention to the defective lighting of Mersey-road district.—Alderman ;-Sather, as to-the letter question, said it was the in- tention of the Committee of the Local Board to replace the present lamps in Mersey-road, by Bray's patents ; no doubt the present Committee would act in a similar way. As to the other-question there • had beena man working as a bricksetter at a rate of wages under the standard wage., and contrary to the resolution of the Local Board. If this was had in Oxfordcitreet, it must be [lad in Edward-street.—:Alder- man Sadler said he was surprised to hear such a remark from the deputy chairman of the ,Committee. This matter was entirely new, and ought to have been -raised at the Committee.—The minutes were passed. --•

THE .DISTRICT AUDITOR. The Town Clerk read a letter from Mr. George liastee kleurst, the district auditor, certifying that the accounts 'of the Local Board •up to November Bth, were correct; and expressing regret at the severance of his official onnection with the Board. He paid a high [compliment to the officials of the Board.—The Town Clerk was in- structed to reply reciprocating the good feelings exe -pressed. PRECAVTIONS AGM NS T SMALLPDX. There were presented for confirmation the minutes of the meeting of the Council and Committee held on the .28th November, at which it was resolved that having regard to the prevalenceof smallpox in the neighbour- hood of Widnes, the Market Inspector be instructed not to allow the sale ",of old clothing er similar articles, in the market, or 'market -places, and that the Medical L Officer of Health be directed to see to the effective [ carrying out of this resolution. The Surveyor pro- duced and explained 'plans prepared by him for the lerection of a temporary wooden hospital, for smallpox., upon part of the site adjacent to the Infectious Disease Hospital, and it was resolved that the same be approved and adopted ,and that the Surveyor forthwith proceed to .carry out the works at an estimated cost of 18360.— The Mayor said Widnes was to be congratulated upon its continued immunity from that dreadful scourge ,emallpox. If it could go forth that both the Medical etrfficer and the Corporation strongly recommended the people of Widnes to be .re-vaccinated, it would be of 'immense advantage.—The minutes were approved. The Engineer [reported that the mean rain- for the past month had been 2.215 inches. The -water pumped during the month was 63,497.655, and the water delivered 433,812,817, a decrease of 15.22 per cent. The illuminating power of the gas during the .month had averaged 1880 candles. Accounts amount- ed to £1,087 Os. 7d. on gas account, and £193 43. lid. on water account. The estimate of wages for the next four weeks amounted to £l3O per week.—On the motion of Alderman Timmis, seconded by Councillor Bullough, the minutes were passed. Neil, deputy chairman of the Technical Instruction Committee, in moving the adoption of the minutes of that Committe,said they had received a grant of £240 from the County Council for the past half-year 1892-3, the total grant being £4BO. This was the full grant. Efforts had been made to obtain a contribution front the County Council towards the erection of }the technical school, but hitherto they had not succeeded. div.head: PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE. '4O
div.p: PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE. '4O
7 SPEEOIfire:BY THE DUKE OF WESTMINSTER

AND THE BISHOP OF CHESTER. The annual prize distribution in connection with the Warrington Training tock place at that institittion (ill-Sitturdhy afeerloon. Tfla-Ettnecrehe Duke of Westminster occupied the chair, and dis- tributed the prizes. The Bishop of Chester was also present. TherDuke of Wasnrnisrest, who was received with much applause, said he was much obliged to the Principal for the kind words with regard to him with which he concluded hisepeech, as well as to the commit- tee for the opportunity thus given to him to pay a visit te the Warrington Training College, though, he must confess, it was rather late in the day to make acquaint- anise with one of the first and best colleges for mistresses in England. (Applause.) With regard to training colleges generally, he thought they ought never to forget to be grateful for the foresight and the energy which was displayed by the National Society in the beginning of the century, and also to the clergy who had from the earliest times been the .pioneers in the great work of education. That college, he understood, was the fruit of that foresight, energy, and devotion to the cause of education ; and especially of RELIGIOUS /ODIJOI.TION IN THIS COUNTRY. These colleges had naturally become more important. They had risen in importance with the increase of pop- ulation, which, as they knew, was enormous ; and with theimmense impetus given to the whole cause of educa- tion by the Act of 1570. The status of mistresses, and; cif course, of masters, had risen with the advantages given them by these training colleges. It was, therefore, only- reasonable to suppose that those young ladies, who hadaecently entered that admirable college, and who would enter it at a later period, were determined to take all the advantages they possibly could of the immense facilities, the admiral facilities given by the excellent staff•of the college to enable them to assume a very high position with regard to the training of their future pupils throughout the district. In these days the 'ques- tion e religious education was held very dear, they were happy to say, by a large number of persons. It behoved those who regarded religious education to be essential, andus one of the necessary elements in the syllabus of the College, and as necessary for the Christtan future 'welfare of England, to tale care that these training colleges were thoroughly well supported, and that they were made the strongholes-of religious life. Be under- • stood that owing to the want of room there were noday students attached to the college. It was most desirable that those who held the religious training of their chil- dren as to the highest importance should take steps to provide accommodationiorthe admission of these young ladies into their Training Colleges. In conclusion, his 'Grace said he trusted to be able to mnke amends for the past, and to take a greaterinterest in the future in the Warrington Training College. (Applause.) The Bishop of CHESTER proposed a vote of thanks to His Grace. He said he had come to Warrington at consideratfie trouble to himself. It had, ineeed, been a axed march, and they were all the more thankful to him fomomiag, because he had only arrived from London the previous evening. They were thankful to him for hie/meet-ace as Troll as for the solid support he had , - to the extension movement. The work was inaugut by the late Lord Winmarleigh, who was a good friend to that<eallege, ae well as to many other similar institu- tions, and -the Puke had gone ,very far towards making it a dear possibility for those upon whom the respon- sibility rested, to carry on the work of the extension of the college. .(Applause.) is 'Grace would find his best reward for the trouble and interest he had bestowed on the college, in all he had heard that<day, as well as from Dr. Pit& in 'Landon. It is well known that the college stood second to none of the colleges in the country. The Speaker then addressed some exhortatory remarks :to the students.--=The proposition was seconded and heartily carried, and the Duke acknowledged the com- pliment. The preceedings were interspersed with part swigs; and at the close tea was ,provided in the senior students' class room, and there was a sale of work in the junior students' class room, in aid of the fund for the enlargement of the colleze.
