div.head: PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION IN THE
div.p: THE PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION IN THE
A« t Is; • iF AIM KIKIXZW—
UNITED STATES

BY Mn. H. WRITHA.M. The mule is tired of being ridden ; it has felt the spur, and has thrown its rider. Net a very nice way of speaking of the public, yet true, none the less. Possibly readers of the " Examiner " would like it making a little clearer as to what is meant by thetpublic."-InTOIHICS; herei-nss-st home, the great mass of voters are found in what are known as the working classes, and I think there can be no doubt that these toilers and moilers do usually be- have very much after the mule fashion, yet they count when the election day comes round. I feel it a duty to say a few words to my friends in Warrington, touching the recent election for President of this great Republic, more in the wi.y of warning than anything else. First, in the way of warning, don't be too sanguine about great benefits accruing to Great Britain, because Cleveland is about to replace Harrison. The Democracy of the States is a long way short of be- ing in favour of free trade. There is precious little , difference between the two parties. A study of the two letters of acceptance' issued by the two leaders, proves beyond doubt, that the words of Statesmen are only used to hide their thoughts. And yet the world most certainly moves along, not as fast, may-be, as some of us would like, but for all we know as fast as is good for us. The McKinley Bill is not dead as yet. Whether it will die a sudden death, or will linger, and die inch by inch, none can tell. lam inclined to the opinion that its death will be a lingering one. However, that may be, I strongly advise that you do no shouting. Whatever von think touching American politics, keep it close within your own breasts. Every sign made in England, of interest as to the result of the recent election, comes over here magnified manyfold. For myself, Ido not at all believe that free trade in America means pros- perity in England—l mean, of course, in a general sense. Comparatively, her export trade is very little. Should the Democrats carry out the platform they are supposed to stand on, I expect to see it increased by leaps and bounds. It is hard to judge as to what will happen. A most unprecedented state of things has come about, and, as unexpected. Not only is there a demo- cratic President, but the Congress and Senate will be democratic. Hitherto, the Senate has been something like your own House of Lords. It represented only capital. During the campaign one speaker said, "If we lose the President,the Senate will be ours. It cannot, be taken from us. We shall hold it permanently, and however much the Democrats may hold in the HoUse, they cannot get one of their measures through while we retain the majority of which we are sure in tire Senate." How great the fall is may be seen from such cocksureness as this. Yes,the mule has kicked with a vengeance,and has hurt a few of the politicans. Why has he kicked ? ask the Republicans. Does he not get big wages ? Is he not the most well-to-do workman in the world, and so on ad infinitum ? I have long felt the desirability of something being done to break up the pernicious state into which we have grown of being divided into classes, upper, middle, and lower, and, alas, a residuum also. Its effect is to be keep one class in utter ignorance as to the condition of the other. Hence the old saying, "One half the world does not know how the other half lives." The Republicans seem dazed, completely thunderstruck, at what has happened. All sorts of reasons are given but the right one. That the people are sick of McKinley is true, but this is not all. They have had pot a few object lessons in the recent strikes, the homdstead business to wit, and yet these do not cover the ground. The workmen know that under the present High Tariff system, the manu• facturer has become nothing less than a mere blunderer and plunderer, and he saw that he was not getting his share of the plunder. Before dealing more fully with the manufacturer, let us look at the workingman. First, let me say, I believe the native American is, almost to a man,Republican in politics ; he is so thorough a schemer that he manages to get hold of all the easy jobs carry- ing good pay. The hard work, and the poor pay, fall to the foreign-born as a rule, a choice few ot the foreign- born holding many choice positions. The foreign-born are gradually, yet surely, becoming the majority. Twice recently has it been urged from the pulpit that something was wrong somewhere, that the American 1 women were refusing the duties of materniy, they marry but have no families, ors attlasst, not more than one or two. Their income thus brings material comfort. At my place of work, some 4,000 men are employed, and at a recent meeting held by a large number of the men, I was called upon to speak, and I dealt largely with the fact that those amongst them who had come to this country single men, had remained so,—That those amongst them descended from foreign-born parents did nct marry, or, if they did so, did not obey the Divine injunction, and I pointedly asked them for the reason. "They could net afford to marry, they could not afford to have any families," these were the answers. Why should they not vote for the Democratic ticket then, and bring about a change, no matter what? The usual wage is from 10 to 15 cents per hour, or from 4s. to 6s. per day. • It has been urged from Republican platform and press, that the workmen there did no more work than in Eng- land, and that all he brought into his house was as cheap and indeed cheaper than in that poor benighted land. Great pictures have been posted in every conspicuous place on which were depicted two scenes, the happy and prosperous Ameri- can workman, riding to work on his bicycle, and the .11 welt- dreseed end well fad. On the Eng- lish side misery of the most abject kind. Your Cradley Heath chainmakers, and your factory gates. have done fine duty here, or were thought to be doing so. Every arrival from England, of either workmen, or persons of mote was interviewed, and reports of the most wretched kind appeared as to the •misery of the English workmen and women. All this in consequence of :Free Trade. They have not had it all their own way: my pen has been pretty busy. It was easy to point out that England was the only Free Trade nation in Europe, yet she paid the highest wages, and sent out the least proportion of emigrants, and that the best protected countries of Europe and Asia paid the most miserable wages, had the most crimes. and daily sent near two hundred men to stand at our mill gates willing to work for anything they,could get. Large families and drunkenness are supposed to be the English workman's great drawbacks. A reasonable discrimination will show that a large and sober family is no drawback, but rather a blessing to in- dividual and State, but who can tell where the misery ends when the family is large, and the parents are drunken 2 Mr, Blaine seems to entertain a vigorous hate for the tight little island, and tried his best to get hold of the Irish vote by raising race hatred. Mr. Blaine said that he believed that where one Irish American voted for him in 1884, three or four would vote for the stational ticket in 1892. Since the break of the Irish-Americans from the Democratic party in his campaign, there had been, he said, an unfailing trend of them away from the Democracy. " Two things,.Mr. Blaine explained, had urged on the movement. One was the treatment that distinguished Irishmen had rgeeived from the administration of Pre- sident Harrison, and the other was the menace which the Irish-American race in general must see in the alliance of the Democratic party and English in- terests. Irishmen were beginning to see, he said, that the Democratic party served England in the most material way, and he thought Irishmen had not yet reached the point where they were particularly anxious to render England stronger and more competeht to pur- sue an offensive policy toward Ireland." The Catholic Church makes a strong point on the question of large families, and has hitherto been the only church that has taken a decided stand against all Malthusian ideas ; and somehow, or other Republican politics are permeated with the thought that either Leo of Rome, or the Lion of England are trying to run America. The Irish vote has gone for democracy, and 1 with the other influences referred to, has brought about the great landslide that has surprised the Republican 'party so much, The protection system, while bringing large profits to employers, has still injured both them and the nation at, large. ‘• The McKinley way was to call in one Republican manufacturer after another, ask him how much • pro- 'be' needed 'in his business, and write in the ydigeoever preposterous figures he was pleased st fi name. cturers under the pampering eamu lee! Our n iMUDI in- fluence of the high proie.!..'tive system, have been con- verted into such negligent, shiftteM inefficient Vg.siness men that their experience is valueless for throwing on most points. This incompetency is a factor to be considered, and one which complicates the whole pro- blem. Our manufacturers have not had to depend for their profits upon the closest economy in the whole ad- j ministration of their business, upon the praotiCa et the exactest and most rigid method, and upon the develop- ment of the highest skill and efficiency in their opera- tions, as British manufacturers, in competition with thel world, have beep obliged to do. Hence it is that British manufacturers can, for example, sell for 45 cents a yard a piece of goods which our own manufacturers cannot make and sell for less than 1.50 dollars. Mr. Monks in his interesting lecture on American pro- tection said, "I had information given to me, as to where I could go and buy 200,000 acres of land in one lot, with both coal and ironstone in it for £50,000 or is. per acre." I mention this to show, or point out two things. First, that the natural wealth of the country being so cheaply got at, proves either the inefficiency of the manufacturer, or,Carnegie-like,his great greed,as the cause for the existence of protection, and again what could John Bull do, if he would only get hold of the natural wealth of his conntry, instead of continuing to pay royalties? • Clarence-st., Worcester, Mass.

RITNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday afternoon. at Dutton Workhouse. There were present Messrs.Mcintyre (chairman),the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, and Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. J. Lea, S. Taylor, A. R. Norman, H. E. Heywood, J. Parr, B. Aaron, T. Baxter, C.C., J. M. Williams, James Whit- low, John Whitlow, P. Hall, R. Bratherton,T.Lewis, J. Brandreth, J. Baguley, J. W. Baguley, J. Ashton (clerk), are G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: CLERICAL ERROR.
div.p: A CLERICAL ERROR.

The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Boaz d, acknowledging the appointment of Miss Elizabeth Moran, the schoolmistress at the Workhouse. They re- marked that they observed that it• was proposed to pal, her a salary of £2O a year,whilst her predecessor had £25 per year, and asked on what ground the reduction was recommended by the Committee.—The Clerk said on re- ferring back to the minute book, he found the resolution of the Board was that the salary should be £2O a year, hut in reporting it to the Local Government Board the sum was, by a clerical error, put at £25, and they sanc- tioned that amount. The £2O a year,however, had still been paid. He had written to the Local Government Board explaining the matter.

div.head: INFECTIOUS DISEASES.
div.p: INFECTIOUS DISEASES.

The Clerk read a rep-Oa-a-U.-le-Dice—dons Diseases Hos- pital Committee, which stated that they had recon- sidered the report of the Committee that a hospital be built on the ground adjoining the Workhouse, at the ex- pense of the Union.—lt was proposed by Mr. Heywood, and seconded by Mr. Aaron, that the facts be laid before the Local Government Board, setting out what had been proposed to be done, and pointing out that the township of Runcorn as an urban Authority,and had an Infectious Diseases Hospital which was not. available for paopers except under an agreement.—Mr. Williams moved the adoption of the report. He said it simply stood this way, that they put the facts before the Local Government Board, and if they decided as Mr. Danseyintimated,they would have to begin de noro.—Mr.Aaron seconded, and the report was adopted.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Mr.Brandreth moved the adoption of the report of the Finance Committee, whish stated that there was £4,029 18s. Bd. in the bank, and that the following calls had not been paid a month ago :—Antrobus, £135 ; Partington, £2l ; Frodsham £1,73 ; Kingsley, £132; P.ingswood, £32 ; Sutton, £lbB ; Whitley Superior, £42.—alr.Taylor proposed that the Clerk write, drawing the attention of the townships to the fact that the calls were not paid.— Mr. Aaron moved that the Clerk write that if they were not paid within a fortnight there would be a summons, because it was a regular thing.—Mr.Taylor's motion was carried. A cnezersiAs COLLECTION. Mr. Brandreth made the annual collection among the Guardians for the purchase of tobacco and extras for the inmates on Christmas Day, and a SUM Of 255. was col- lected. This was all the business of importance.

div.head: TRAGEDY IN A LUNATIC ASYLUM.
div.p: TRAGEDY IN A LUNATIC ASYLUM.

Considerable excitement was caused in Birmingham on Monday owing to a report tnat a fearful tragedy had been committed in the City Asylum at Winsor Green. The authorities were reticent on the subject ; but even- tually it was officially stated that one of the inmates, Thomas Beasley, had been killed by another patient named Allsopp. On Saturday night an amateur drama- tic entertainment styled " War to the Knife" was given at the Asylum, and during the performance a saline was heard in one of the wards. The porter, going there found to his dismay that Allsopp had creatnd a more dramatic scene than the players on the stage. He bad with a piece of crockery beaten Beasley to death and peverely injured two other patients.

div.head: ruGittsT UNTENCED TO PENAL SERVITUDE FOR MANSLAUGHTER.
div.p: A ruGittsT UNTENCED TO PENAL SERVITUDE FOR MANSLAUGHTER.

-- At Ulster Winter Assizes on Saturday, Thomas Smyth, a Belfast utig,ilist, whose name has been a good deal be- fore the nubile lately, was tried for the manslaughter of his wife, Jane Anne Smyth. There was a great dual of evidence to show the cruel treatment to which the woman was subjected. The juty found the prisoner guilty, and Mr. Justice Gibson sentenced him to fifteen years' penal servitude, remarning that if the Crown had indicted prisoner for murder he jury would have been quite justified in finding him guilty of that, cha rgs.

THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY. DECEMBER 17, 1892.

Txuiu is both instruction and GoengTroersys amusement to be had from a per- usal of the proceedings at the meeting of the National Union of Conservative Associations which took place at Sheffield on Tues- day. The instruction is to be found when noting the attitude taken up by the Conference with regard to protection. Colonel HOWARD VINCENT, M.P., was again to the front with a resolutien 'calling for the protection of native industries, in- cluding agriculture, and the resolution was en- dorsed by this meeting of Conservative oleo- tioneerers. Although carried by what was • described as a " substantial" majority, the vote in favour 4 the resolution iwas not so overwhelm- ing as, for instance, at the meeting of the Union at Oxford in 1887, when there were one thousand votes to twelve, or at Birmingham last year. Nor was it passed without some remonstrance. Even Tories, badly off as they are for a" plank" in their platform which can be galvanised into even the semblance of a " popular cry," can hardly fail to soe the absurdity of taking up with a quack nos- trum which is being dis credited even in the United States, tho country in which, above all others, High Protection has had an ample inn- ings and a fair trial under the most favourable of circumstances. There are numberless directions in which useful reforms might be prosecuted;

yet so poverty-stricken in resolYrce is I the Tory party that they have to place in the forefront of their programme a mild imitation of that MCKINLETISAI which has so disgusted the democracy of America as to bring upon a great and historical party, a defeat almost unparalleled in its severity. Mr.Munnoon, an ex-M.P.for Read- ing ventured, tni dissent from Colonel HOWARD VINCENT'S proposal. He oven went so far as to suggest that the interests of the agricultural labourer and the artisan should be considered,but this, as might be expected from the character of the gathering, only excited the laughter of his hearers. That a Tory should speak seriously to Tories about the interest of the agricultural labourer seemed to strike these worthy delegates as a subject for hilarity. While the discussion on Protection, and its result, may well suggest many useful reilecLions on the development of modern Toryism, the speech of Mr. BALroun, delivered in the course of tho afternoon, cannot fail to excite some amusement. Apparently following a vagrant and unaccountable impulse, he selected to pose as a social reformer. How badly he filled the part is abundantly evident to everyone who reads his remarks. He is, he tells us, in language which is just a shade indefinite, in favour of several re- forms which, if carried out, would tend to amelior- ate the lot of the poor. But the difficulties in the way of accomplishing any one of these reforms are, at all events as sketched by Mr. BALFOUR, simply stupenddhs, not to say insuperable. In the matter of social legislation, he says, "the begin- ning of wisdom is to recognise the enormous diffi- culty and complexity of the problems with which you have to deal, the enormous risks which you run if you deal with them in a hasty and partisan manner, and not merely fix your eyes on this or that evil, and suppose that the first quack remedy will afford a complete and perfect cure." We have often heard language of this kind before, but it is not prompted by the spirit of the sincere and convinced reformer. These are not the words of the honest and zealous advocate of progress, but rather of one who would much prefer to bring into prominence the obstacles that lie in the way of progress. Descending to particulars, Mr. BALFOUR expresses a desire to improve the condition of the aged and deserving poor, but at the same time he solemnly warns us of the evil consequences of laxity in the administration of the Poor Laws. There are people who are not satisfied with the

unequal distribution of wealth, but Mr. Bal.- roux advises them to turn their attention to increased production. This is something like tell- ing the man who works fourteen or fifteen hours a day for a mere pittance that the real remedy foi his condition is not to be found in the lessening of his hours and the increase of his pay, but in adding an hour or two extra to his day's labours. Mr. Bsixorn also warns the advanced labour party against driving capital out of the country. In these days, he says, capital moves at the stroke of a pen, and by the mere writing of a cheque. He did not condescend to explain in what way or by what process all the immense applied capital of this country—the railways and tramways, the machinery and coal mines—were to be transferred to a foreign shore by the mere writing of a cheque. But we must not press too hardly upon Mr. BALrouR for trifling omissions of that kind. When figuring as a reformer he is not in his ele- ment. His proposals of reform, as compared with his warnings against the dangers of any step in advance, bear pretty much the same proportion to each other as did Falstaff's bread to his wine.

STILL they go. The Conservative member for Rochester has been eliminated from the Parlia- mentary minter roll in the same way as the member for the Hexham division—that is to say, two election judges have declared his election void because of the corrupt practices of his agents. In this case the judges have gone further than in previous petitions, for they declare that they suspect that corrupt and illegal practices exten- sively prevailed at the election, and they will report to the spe lker of the House of Commons accordingly. Mr. Justice WILLIAMS once more denounced the practice of providing cheap "refreshments 'S for electors. No one—no mat- ter what his political opinions may be—who places the slightest value on the purity of elec- tions will regret the result of either the Rochester or the Hexham petition. In each instance there was evidence of the misuse of wealth, directly or indirectly, for the purpose of securing votes. The decisions of the judges will be a wholesome reminder to those who show a desire to use the old vile instrument of bribery in a new way, that they are liable to detection and punishment.

A few weeks ago a medical journal gave some salutary advice to witnesses and others who are called upon to " take the oath." In England, as most people know, the usual method of doing so is by "kissing the book," hut in Scotland they havo a better way—that of simply uplifting the right hand. The " book " which does duty at Police Courts or County Courts has usually a smooth and greasy and well-worn exterior which indicates only too plainly that it has been in many hands and pressed to many lips. Its appearance is not prepossessing, and oven those who are not particularly fastidious often enough feel that they would rather be excused the osculatory rite. Besides merely sentimental objections thero are ' reasons of a prudential and even sanitary character why a book should not he passed indiscriminately from band to hand—it may be at times from a person who is himself suffering from, or who has been in 'contact with those who are suffering from, an infectious malady, to one who is healthy but still susceptible to contlgion. It has, for the most part, been overlooked that there is an Act of Parliament which gives jurors and others the right to take the oath in the Scotch fashion, and it was to this fact that the medical journal referred to called attention. Since then, wo notice that the permission given by the Act has been taken advantage of on several occasions.

Warrington Board of Guardians is almost entirely cpmposed of Tories, and, therefore, it was not altogether unfitting that it should be invited at its meeting on Wednesday to makeitself ridicu- lous by protesting against the recent reduction of the qualification of Guardians to £5. It is true that some Conservatives have asserted with quite a suspicious amoun t of emphasisthat they entirely approved of the democratic action of the Liberal President of the Local Government Board. Indeed, they were careful to tell us that the only reason why the Conservative Government had not forestalled their Liberal successors was that they had overlooked this little reform. But Councillor Mom does not believe in these modern innovations. The workingman has found his way into the Town Council and even on to the borough bench, but the Board of Guardians is—figuratively speaking of course—the "last ditch," and Mr. MUIR appears determined to defend it to the bitter end against the intrusive invader. He, there- fore, moved that the Warrington Board of Guardians " protest" against the levelling edict of the Local Government Board. His reason for proposing this resolution was that the "lower classes," which seems to be Mr. MUIR'S definition of those who are not heavily rated,might not be so careful of the ratepayers' money as those who are under higher assessments. From this we may gather that Mr. Mom is labouring under a delusion. He seems to think that he is, as a mein- of the Board of Guardians, a " Guardian of the Ratepayers' Purse," whereas he is really a "Guardian of the Poor." The primary duty of a Board of Guardians, is to see that the poor who come under their care receive proper and humane treatment ; whether the carrying out of such u duty involves a large or small expenditure is, or ought to be, a secondary consideration. It is per- haps not remarkable that Mr. Muni should take an inverted view of things, but it is slightly comical that he should object to the " lower classes " find- ing a place among the Guardians of the Poor simply because they might think more of the poor than of the rates. It is to the credit of tho Board of Guardians that they rejected Mr. Munt's proposal, even though they only did it by the casting vote of the Chairman.

CONCERT AT CROFT. On Saturday evening the first of a series of con- certs, to be given during the ensuing eeasem, took place in the Board School, in aid of the funds of the Horticultural Society. There was an appreciative audience. considering the unfavourable state of the weather, and the schoolroom preseitted an attrac- tive appearance, being decorated for the occasion. The Rector, who is president of the Horticultural Society, presided. MORECAMBE AS A PLEASURE RESORT. The proposed new pier and pavilion at More- cambe, of which the prospectus is advertised in our columns is an undertaking which merits the sup- port of the general public and should prove to be a lucrative Investment. Morecambe has during the last few years grown very rapidly ; hundreds of new substantial houses and shops have been built, and each season sees a greatly increased number of visitors. But up to the present time the amuse- ments which have been provided have been totally inadequate to the growing demand for first class entertainments. The new pier is to be erected on the best possible site ; it will be a most handsome structure, and the pavilion will seat 1,200 persons. The directors propose to secure the services of high class artistes and every care will be taken to pro- vide entertainments such as have been hitherto unknown in Morecambe. Thus the one great need of this beautifully situated watering place is about to be met.

On Sunday afternoon Mr. Fred Wilson, builder and contractor, Greenwav-road, was driving to Halton, and taking the corner of Mill House at De!ph Bridge, his horse " bolted," and jumped the wall which.norders the canal. The Committee who have in hand the provision of a tea and entertainment for the aged people of the district, are making arrangernants for the treat to be given early next year. They are enoura.ged in this, seeing' the happiness afforded the young people last year. AWFULLY SUDDEN DEATII AT RUNCORN-

George Forster, aged 453 years, of Ne,w-street-,, Widnes, dropped down dead while walking along Church-street, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening at five o'clock. The deceased was a rivetter,,employed at the new gas works in Halton-road, and at four o'clock he complained to a fellow workman named George Plane of a pain in his chest. Mr. Worsiey held an inquest on; the body at the Cemetery office on. Thursday morning. It appeared the deceased had been in failing health for sometime and had been under the cars of Dr. 'MacLennan of Widnes for bronchitis. The doctor informed R.C. At Runwrn Petty Sessions on Monday, Stephen Con- stable and his wife, Bessie Constable, were charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and also with as- saulting P.C.'s Ridgway and lorris while in the execu- tion of their duty. About half-past seven on Saturday night the prisoners were drunk and creating a disturb- ance in Bridge-st. It most not be supposed that the money which has been expended in prizes and certifi- cates has been taken from the rates ; the funds have been obtained by a series of lantern entertainments andi lectures during the winter monthstand the hope of obtain- ing a reward has stimulated the young people te attend school punctually and regularly and to strive to make themselves efficient in their tasks. In no small measure r this has contributed to obtaining "excellent " reports at 1 the recent examinations and is consequently earning for the school higher grants, and to that extent saving the ratepayers money. ENTERIC FEVER AT Etntaconx.

"The Lancet" in its issue of December 10th refers to the above subject as follows :—" The Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioners have thanked their health officer, Mr. F. McDougall, for his interesting report on enteric fever. With such action we have to express concur- rence, still we trust that something more than the thanks reported by the locl nress have followed the receipt of such a report. Mr. McDougall tells of widespread fever and of conditions which are an obvious cause of nuisance and disease, and he adds that these conditions, notably those attaching to the storage of huge quantities of filth and excreta near houses and schools, are due to a want of proper building by-laws. In a town like Runcorn a very strict limitation should be placed on the capacity of all filth receptacles, and the scavenging organized by the authority should be such as to prevent the need of any- thing but small receptacles for filth and refuse. There are now model by-laws dealing with all such matters, and authorities who have brought under their notice the fact that so fatal a disease as enteric fever is due to their failure to make proper by-laws incur a very grave responsibility unless they deal with the matter effectu- ally and promptly." div.head: ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN.
div.p: ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The congregational tea party and concert in connec- tion with this church took place on Friday evening, in the schoolroom, Shaw-St. The after proceedings were presided over by the Rev. Canon Wood, who in opening the proceedings pointed out that according to the origi- nal estimates there remained to be paid on the contract for the chancel of the church £175, but the contractors had asked for £512. Thus, instead of having a surplus as anticipated,it was very probable that they would have a deficiency. The Vicar called attention to the en- larged school in which they were assembled, and spoke of the great advantages it would afford-. The clans had been stamped by the Education Department, the work had been well done by their townsman,Mr. Coward,and the cost was so'mething like £2oo'. They were looking forward to improving the National Schools at no distant ' date. A very interesting programme was gone through, in which the choir gave several part songs with consider- able effect-. Messrs. J. Littler and F. Wilkinson gave a pleasing interpretation of " Brotherly Love." Songs ' were contributed by Mr, Pownall, Miss Siinkin, Miss Branch, Mr. Smith, and Mr. Morris. Masters Outhwaite were very successful in an instrumental selection. Recitations were given by Mr. Bently. Mr. R. W. Pier. point gave a rendering of "Be the Fountain" on the cornet. The accompaniments were played by Miss E. Crosby. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watehm aker and Jewoslier. 51, High- it.. and 4, Bridge-at., Runcorn.—Adet.

div.head: – • -- TIT& ASTON FARMER AND. HIS GUN-
div.p: - • -- TIT& ASTON FARMER AND. HIS GUN-

At Runcorn Petty Sessions ma Monday, Thos. Walker Challoner, farmer, Aston Grange, was summoned on the information of Wm. Speechley, an officer of Inland Revenue, for having on the 19tk• October, carried a gun without a license.—Mr. Moore, supervisor of Inland Revenue. prosecuted, and Mr- J. Burton defended.— P.S. Costello said he saw the defendant going round a cover on a grass field carrying a gun, and attended by a sheepdog. He asked him if he had a license, and he replied in the negative, adding that he was only scaring birds. The gun was a double-barrelled breech loader, loaded with two cartridges—powder and shot, and the officer told him he had no right to use lead to scare birds. The defendant afterwards said he was looking for a shot at a blackbird.—Mr. Burton said the defendant had , wedding at his house, and he went out into the field' with some friends. In the course of the walk they came near a wheat field, and he was carrying the gun for the purpose of scaring birds from there. There was also a hedge much infested with rats from, a sewer. He had an opportunity to shoot both a pheasant and a rabbitt but he made no attempt to do so. The game on his farm was let, and the defendant was paid so much per each head of game ; there was not the slightest antagon- ism, or any desire to interfere with the spott of the landlord.—Mr. Burton called Jas.Nicholls, ef Frodsham. and Wm. Moss, of Newton, who gave confirmatory evidence.—The Bench Imposed a fine of 103. and costs.

On Wednesday evening the death of a widow named Phcebe Molyneux, 56 years of age, who resided at 57, Cross-street, which occurred under rather strange cir- cumstances, was reported to the police. Some years ago she was injured, and since then has complained of pains in her back and near the heart. On Saturday night her son came home the worse for drink. This seemed to excite the disease very much, and she became ill and died on Wednesday evening, as above stated. Dr. McLennan was called in, and gave it as his opinion that death was due to heart disease. 'I he inquest was held yesterday atternoon at the Bradley Hotel, and a verdict of "Natural Causes was returned. BRILLIANT SUCCASS OF A RUNCORN MEDICAL STUDENT. At the distribution of prizes at Liverpool University Col lege, by the Hon. J. Bryce, M P., Mr. ELE.Annettoon of Mr. H.E.Annett,of Ituncorn,was awarded the Torr senior gold medal for last year, he having obtained the junior gold medal for the same subjects, anatomy and physio- logy. Mr. Annett, who is a student in the medical school of the c,ollege, hag passed his intermediate, and is a holder of the Lyon Jones senior scholarship tenable for two years. It is a noteworthy fact that Mr. Annett's fellow students were so assured of, his carrying off the scholarship that they declined to compete against him. We heartily congratulate Mr. Annett on his brilliant suc- cess in the profession lie has choseu.

div.head: ST. EDWARDS CATHOLIC SCHOOL, RUNCORN':
div.p: ST. EDWARDS CATHOLIC SCHOOL, RUNCORN':

The annual entertainment in connectiQu with this school was held in Runcorn Public Hall on Wednesday and Thursday evenings. There was a largo audience on each occasion. A series of drills were gone through in an interesting manner by the infant b-iys and girls, and subsequently an operetta entitled " Puss in Boots " was given by the senior scholars. The caste was as fol- lows :—Puss, Master Harold Davies ; Flounit (owner of cat), Miss Fanny Whitley ; fairy, Miss Katie Reilly : king, Miss Jessie Acton ; queen, Miss Mary H. Redmond princess, Miss Rose Costello ; lady in waiting, Miss Mary Cooxan ; and ogre, Master J. Delaney. There was also an effective chorus. The childten were very prettily and anpropriatoly dressed, and performed their different parts with much credit: to their tutors, Miss Comer- ford and Miss Haigh. Mr. Korosco and his two child- ren gave a remarkable juggling performance. LOCAL COLLIERY DEVELOPMENT.

The Princess Pit, llaydock, near St. Helens—one of the pits included in Messrs. Richard Evans and Co's., Limited, sinking operations, which have been going on for some four years—has now been com- pletely " caged," and is this week winding coal. The pit is a new one, and has been sunk to a depth of 360 yards. Two very valuable seams of coal have been struck, known as the Rushey Park or Arley, and Little Delphi or Orrell, and a very considerable output is expected shortly. The cages are two- deck, and will raise six boxes at. once. The pit has _been connected with the King Pit, which Ilas been sunk about 200 yards deeper for tnts pirrpOse:—Trie- King Pit is at present winding coal, but will even- tually be used as an upcast or air shaft for the Princess Pit. The other sinking operations have been at the Nos. 4 and 5 Parr pits, St. Helens, and these have been completed. Altogether Messrs. Evans have now fourteen pits winding coal in hay. dock, Ashton, Edge Green, Parr, and Claiborne, in addition to upcast shafts.
HOUSEHOLD LINENS hemmed and marked free a chargE.- 1. W. DUTTON, Sankey-it., Warrington.—Atirt YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION CONFER- ENCE AT ST. HELENS.

On Saturday the quarterly conference of the Liverpool district Young Men's Christian Associa- tion was held at St. Helens. There were present Messrs. T. Jameson, F. A. Allen, J. D. MThail, It. H. 11. Fisher (Liverpool), F. Forsyth. J. Martin (Birkenhead), J. Thomas (Bangor), J. E. C. Else, W. Moss, W. Lightfoot (general secretary), and others representing St. Helens. Papers were read by Mr. J. D, M•Phall on " lhe Duty of the Young Men's Christian Association in regard to Reflective Christian work." and by Mr. Allen on "The Duty of the Young Men's Christian Association in regard to Aggressive Christian Work. A discussion followed. The delegates and members, to the numbcr of twenty. were then entertained to tea by Mr. Wm. Gamble, treasurer of the St. Helens Young Men's Christian Association, 'after which brief reports trona Birkenhead, Liverpool Central, Liverpool North, and Bangor Young Men's Christian Associa- tions were given, all showing progress, especially • at Liverpool.

div.head: REPRESENTATION OF it UNION.
div.p: THE REPRESENTATION OF it UNION.

A meeting of the ratepayers of Runcorn was held in Bethesda Lecture Hell, on Thursday night,under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Wood,for the pur- pose of considering the advisability of making ap- plication to the Local Government Board ta increase the number of Guardians of the Pour repres-nting the township of in Runcorn Union.—The Chairman described the present as a most opportune time to consider this question of representation, be- cause so many questions connected with the poor were coming to the front for which some solution must be found. There was that of distinction between those who became inmates of the Workhouse through their own fault and those who did so through misfortune. Then there was the subject relating to the education of the children in the schools. That was a question which Lancashire and other parts oh the country were trying to solve by a system of boarding out children. When those matters came before them it was necessary that they should have good and efficient Guardians, ane considering the importance of Runcorn it was desir- able that she should have a full share in deciding what should be done. (Applause.) Mr. W. Handley said Runcorn ought to have a propor- tionate representation of the Union. In 1858 the num- ber of guardians for the township was increased from three to five. At that time the ratable value was £28,455, and the estimated population was 10,000. At the present time the ratable value was £58,413 and the population 20,050. The population of the Union was 42,517, and tile ratable value £225,488. While there were 42 guardians representing 37 townships. Run- corn had 47 per cent. of the population of the Union and barely 12 per cent, of the repre- sentation, and isi regard to value, they had one-fourth of the ratable value and only one-eight of the representation. They had therefore good grounds for asking for an increase, and he moved "That in the opini au of this meeting it is desirable that this town- ship had a larger representation on the Board of Guar- dians of this Union, and that the overseers are hereby requested to urge the matter on the Local Goverrunent Board." _ _ - .
The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi seconded the proposition, and expressed the opinion that Ransom ought to have 12 Guardians. _

Mr. unison, in supporting the motion, quoted fie,ures to prove that their number ought to be augmented. If they anOed the test ot population, the average was one guardian to 1,000, which would give Runcorn 20 repre- sentatives ; and if they applied the teat of rateable value, the average was one to each £5,368, or 11 mem- bers. There were five townships with a population of 586, and a rateable value of £6,997, who enloyed the same representation as Runcorn, and there ought to be a re-arrangement of areas. Mr. Bisbrown and Mr. Taylor also supported the resolution, which was unanimously carried. On the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Lea, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman.

BY AN OCCASIONAL CORnESPONDENT.

The Corporation of Widnes had, what may fairly be deslribed as a pile of work at the first monthly meeting of the Council. The minutes submitted, occupied 49 ?ages of printed matter made up into a formidable--looking volume, but an hour-and-a. half sufficed to have them moved, seconded, dis- cussed. and carried. There was no subject of entrancing interest brought forward. The Town Clerk who was freely discussed at the first meeting of the Corporation, on November 9th, had again to run the gauntlet of a series of questiens on the resolution then passed, and now submitted for confirmation. Councillor Quinn contended that the resolution now presented, had not been read to the Council, but the mover of the appointment of Mr. Oppenheim, Alderman Wareing, said it comprised what he intended to convey and what the mem- bers understood at the time, and eventually the minute was confirmed. Further discussion arose on the remuneration of the Town Clerk's staff, which Councillors Shuttleworth and Christie considered was set at too high a figure, and they moved its reduction from £l7O to .£l5O. Councillor Shuttleworth made the very strong statement that Ithey were paying two men to do one man's work, but surely no one will argue that the Town Clerk should pay for his office staff out of a salary of £350, and an experienced and able chief clerk, and an assistant cannot be accounted dear at £l7O, tak- ing into consideration the responsible work they are called upon to perform.

The ratepayers will not wish their representa- tives to economise at the expense of that now much quoted, axiom, "a fair day's wage for a fair day's work." Although he allowed his motion to go to a division. Councillor Shuttleworth had not the conrage to support it by his vote, and Council- lor Christie found himself " solitary and alone." There will be many ways in which our Town Council can economise if they will, . in nautical phrase," keep their weather eye open."

I have often heard of the blind leading the blind,. though it has not been my good fortune or mis- fortune to see such a strange sight. But I should imagine that a new councillor calling another new councilhr to order was much more amusing, and that privilege has been accorded to your coriespon- pent. As a further amendment on the subject dealt with in the preceding paragraph. Councillor Quinn, proposed that the Town Clerk's staff should be placed under the direct control of the Council, and no allowance whatever paid to the. Town Clerk. Councillor Shores briskly rose in his place to a point of order, and said the amendment could not be received, but the Mayor quickly told him that the amendment was perfectly in order, and Coun- cillor Quinn retorted that his colleague was more out of order than his amendment. And a ripple of laughter went round the Chamber.

One question which came somewhat prominently before the Council was the insanitary condition of many of the streets in the borough. The streets mentioned by Alderman Williamson in Waterloo- road district, are a disgrace to any civilized com- munity, and it was gratifying to know that the necessary steps had been taken to put them in order. But, as the Alderman pointed out, there are many houses that are hiStath an insanitary condi- tion as to be unfit for ha.bitation, and it will not be sufficient to make a good roadway to such places. Drastic measures ought to be taken with all sach property as quickly aetha law will permit, and it is sincerely to be hoped that this zeal for sanitary dwellings is not a mere flash in the pan, another exemplification of the old proverb " new brooms sweep clean," bat that it will be sustained until there is not a 2 unhealthy dwelling left in the town.

There is likely to be a change in the personnel of the new School Board at Runcorn. I hear that the church candidates are to be the Vicar and Messrs E. Imison and C. Timmins, the two latter replacing Mr. A. Salkeld, who retires at his own request, and Dr. McDougall, who, iris whispered, has shown too much indepeddence of spirit to be again placed in the position he has held for the past three years. The,worthy:doctor's name may thereforebe expected to figure amongst the independent candidates. It is practially certain that-the-other returning roam- bers—Dr. Gastaldi, and Messrs. Pritchard, Taylor, and T. ilandley—will seek re-election, and pro- bably a lumber of other gentlemen will be nomi- nated, but no definite information can be gathered. The mystery will be cleared up on Monday at 4 p.m.

The appointment of a woman who is not a "pro- fessional " to take charge of the smallpox patients at Runcorn Hospital, appears to bare thrown Dr. McLennan, and if report speaks true, another pro- minent gentleman, into a fever—of apprehension,of emits°. Now, 1 have long been of opinion that our Board of Commissioners have not made sufficient use of this institution in the way of arresting the spread of infectious disease by the prompt isola- tion of the first cases, but the levelling of general charges against a wcinan, because she is not a " professional " does not seem fair to her nor to the Health Committee. Though training may do a great deal, there is much truth in the saying that nurses are born not made. The charge of incom- petence might have some weight, if Dr. MacLennan could point out an instance of neglect or wrong treatment through ignorance; and the request of the Health Committee that they would consider the question when he made such an accusation seems a reasonable one. The woman may not have seen a smallpox patient before—no doubt Dr.McLennan once had his first case—but her competency as a nurse must be judged by her ability to understand and carry out tke directions of a medical man in an intelligible and satisfactory manner. The best answer to the whole affair is that the four patients are conval- escent, and it is satisfactory to know that there has not been any fresh outbreak in the town. Stranger , to me than the appointment of an unprofessional 1 nurse is the fact that four people should be attacked , with the loathsome disease simultaneously in ad- joining houses, and that although the patients have heels removed for a period of three weeks these houses should still be quarantined, and the inmates prisoners. As an unscientific man, I feel prompted continually to ask: Why ?

div.head: OUTBREAK OF SMALLPDX AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE OUTBREAK OF SMALLPDX AT RUNCORN.

THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE HOSPITAL. In reference to the outbreak of smallpox and the administration of the Infectious Diseases Hospital, the following correspondence has taken place be- tween Dr. MacLennan and the Health Committee of the Board of Commissioners:—' 107, Church-place, Runcorn, .ith December, 1892. To the Chairman of the Runcorn Health Committee. Dear Sir,—As you are probably nware,there are at present four patients suffering from smallpox in the Isolation Hospital. , Mrs. Rowles, the nurse, is laid up with a severe ill- ness, and, in consequence, I find that two women, a mother and her daughter, are at present acting as nurses. Now, patients suffering from smallpox re- quire very special nursing and dieting, as well as continual attention in regard to external application, bathing, and other treatment. I understand that the present nurses have had no practical experience, and have previously never even seen a case of smallpox. In my opinion it was very unwise to permit these i women to assume the duties of nurses when they were both gno- rant of the work, and themselves unprotected by re-vac- cination. In a threatened epidemic, such as we have at present to deaf with, we cannct be too cautious. A couple I of trained nurses could easily be obtained from the Nurses' Institution, flops-st., Liverpool, at very short notice and without much extra expense. Mrs.Houlbrook and her daughter, who are very respectable persons and whom I very highly recommend, could be placed in the caretaker's house to cook the nurses food and make them- selves generally useful. Alter the patients are well again the services of the trained nurses coold, if necessary, then be dispensed with. I can only say,in conclusion,,that unless satisfactory nursing he obtained I cannot any : longer hold myself responsible for the treatment of the I patients at present under my care in this hospital, as I am not assured that my instructions are properly carried out under the present system of administration.—l am, yours truly, A. MacLExmaN."—'• Town Hall, Waterloo.. road. Runcorn, Bth December, 1892. Dr. MacLennan. Dear Sir,—Your letter of the sth inst., relating:to the administration of the bospital,was considered at a meet- ing of my Health Committee, held last evening. They have made inquiries with regard to the sublect matter of your letter, and they are satisfied from reports sub- mitted to them by their officers, that the arrangements made as to nursing, diet,and attention are adequate,and they consider that as the patients are progressing favour- ably, there is no necessity to engage a trained nurse. The committee desire me to say that if you have any spe- cific complaint to make, either as to diet or obedience of instructions, they will be prepared to consider the same. —Yours fakthfully, E. MAUSLIALG.
i RUNCORN AND DISTRICT PERFECT

THRIFT BUILDING. SOCIETY.. - Last night there was inaugurated in Runcoin Public Hail* a building society, under the above title. The proceedings consisted of a concert, by several artistes, and a lecture on "How to live rent free," by Mr. Win, Horsley. The registered office pf the society is in Mersey Chambers, High-st., and Mr. Thomas Latimer is the secretary. The solicitor is Mr. R. D. Maddock, and the survevor is Mr. Thomas Clegg, while the board of directors consist of eight well known local geatlemen. The object of the society is to enable its members to become the owners of their own houses by advancing the full value.of.the property, without interest, and on easy terms of repayment. In fact the repayments have not to exceed the rent ordin- arks-paid for the property; or in other svords,the house in which a member lives would be purchased by the money paid as rent. Various advantages over other building societies are claimed for the one under notice, particu- larly the rule which provides for a free- ballot at the death of a member,Nr the benefit of his widow or other legal representatives. The subscription is 6d. per week per share. This entitles the holder to an advance of £lOO, without interest, repayable by £6 per annum per £lOO. The loan would thus he repaid in 16i years. The advances are both halloted for, and sold on a system defined by the rules. The society is limited to 399 'bal- lot members and 100 purchase members.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY LECTURES •AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FREE LIBRARY LECTURES •AT RUNCORN.

The, first of a series of lectures arranged by the Runcorn Free Library Committee was delivered in Bethesda Lecture Ball, on Wednesday evening, by Mr. Thomas Ward, J.P. of Northwich. There was a moderate attendance and Mr. P. %laws 11 chair- man of the Board of Commissioners, presided. The sub*t of the lecture was the action of water in the formation of the crust of the earth, and Mr. Ward at the outset pointed out that water worked in two ways, as a solvent and as a mechanical power, and he described its three forms of liquid, snow, and vapour, fly means of water in the streams and rivers and glaziers, the face of the earth was being continually changed. Water had been the great agent which had made Cheshire as we know it to-day. The rock in the Runcorn quarries had countless years ago. been like the sand banks that were now to be seen in the Mersey, and as layer after layer of sand kept ac- cumulating, the enormous pressure formed it into red sandstone. In illustration of the power of water, Mr. Ward described the great canyons of America. The sea was perpetually encroaching upon the laud in some quarter of the globe, and towns had been destroyed by its advance in our own country. An interesting.descrip- tion of the formation of glaziers, and their action in altering the crust of the earth, the lecturer incidentally mentioned that Cheshire had once been covered with ice in the same way that Greenland was to-day. The lec- turer's remarks were illustratesi by a number of photo- graphs thrown upon a screen by a oxy hydrogen lantern manipulated by Mr. J. Rhode,,, who was subsequently complimented by the lecturer for the skill he had dis- played.—Dr. McDougall in moving a veto of thanks ba Mr. Ward for his able and interesting lecture, expressed regret that there had not been a larger audience to listen to the valuable information given in a popular makner.—Mr. Grice seconded the motion, and said he had no doubt that that interesting lecture would he the means of securing a larger audience far the future loc- tures.—The motion was carried, and Mr. Ward in re- ply, urged his hearers to obsorve what was passing around them in nature.—On the motion of Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., seconded by Mr.F. A. Lake, a vote of thanks was awarded to the Chairman.

div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY. A HYMN O 1 VRAISE.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY. A HYMN O 1 VRAISE.

More than customary interest was centred in the first eoncert of the season, given by the Runcorn Musical Society. Since last winter the society has been placed under new management, and a profes- sional conductor has been engaged, and the liveliest concern was manifested as to how these changes had operated. The result, as displayed, at the con- cert in the Public Hall on Monday evening, can only be described as eminently satisfactory. That the large audience which assembled held this view was made abundantly manifest, and at the outset we cannot withhold our congratulations to the conductor, Mr. F. H. Crossley, the ollicials, and the committee, upon the success that has attenaed their labours, begun under circumstances of not the most encouraging.discription. The Runcorn Musical Society, it is hoped, has yet before it a long and brilliant career.

Mendelssohn's " Hyman of Praise" formed the first part of the programme. This composition was written by the great musician at the age of 31. years, when he was in the zenth of his powers, to celebrate the fourth centennial of the invention of printing at Leipsie, held in 1840. In order of chronology, it was written between his two chief works" St. Paul" and " Elijah," and is described by Mendelssohn himself as a " Symphony- cantata " because the orchestra have an equal share with the chorus. It may be said that none of his creations excel it in brilliancy and charm. It was first produced in England at Birmingham, and the audience) was so impressed with the 'Chorale,' "Let all men praise the Lord," that they simultaneously rose to their feet and remained standing during the rendering of the number. The work commences with a striking phrase which forms a moeif runniteg through the entire work, and occurs in the opening symphony in one forma or an- other no less than forty or fifty times. Our local chorus may with justice he said to have ex- celled themselves. Though perphaps not so strong as usual in point of numbers, the parts were well balanced—a litte more strength in the basses would possibly have been an improvement—and there was an evidenced cohesion and a sustained power that the merest tyro in criticism could not have failed to perceive. The "Chorale" was sung as near to perfection as possible. The pitch in the unnccompanied portion was•maintained with a remarkable accuracy that spoke volumes for the training the chorus had received at the hands of Mr. Crossley, and there was an artistic finish throughout the work that unmistakably- stamped the whole performance as a fine one. In the selection of principals the Committee had been exceedingly fortunate. Miss Maggie Davies (London) possesses a very bright and " telling "soprano voice, which she used with an artistic finish that quite en- thralled the audience in the several airs and recitatives that fell to her lot. Mr. Braxton Smith (London), has a robust tenor voice of good range and splendid quality, to which is added the gift of powerful expression, and he was highly sffective, especially in the air " The sorrows of Death" and the recitative " We called through the darkness." In the duet " I waited for the Lord " Miss NI. A. Jones, a member of the chorus, joined Miss Davies, and this charming number was heard to great advantage. The secend part of the programme was as follows : Overture " Marionetteu." Song Mr. Braxton Stnitu. Song " Ah non Credea." (Sonnambula) Miss Maggie Davies. Part song " Moonlight." E. Fusing Intermezzo ...... from " Song " My dearest heart." Suilivaa Miss Maggie Davies. Song " lii sing thee Songs of Araby." Mr. Braxton Smith. Polonaise... from " Life for the Czar." Chorus and Orchestra. The operatic selection gave Miss Davies an oppor- tunity of showing the extraordinary flexibility a her voice, and lits sweet quality, and this wonderful piece of vocalisation was rapturously encored. Twice she bowed her acknowledgements, but there being no cessation of the applause, she responded with the quaint and pretty song" One morn the maiden sought the mill." An encare was also awarded her for ." My dearest heart." Schubert's sere- nade was undeubtedly one of the gems of the concert. Mr.Braexton Smith displayed a purity of intonation, and a wealth of expression, that delighted his .hearers. He was also encored foe e, songs of Araby," and lie gratified the audience with a rendering of the" Rhenish popular song" Mendelssolut. The high standard of the work of the chorus was inaintained in " Moonlight" which was a charming number effectively given. Although no mention has yet neon made of the perfor- mances of the orchestra, let it not be supposed that they were unworthy of :In yen of the performance. From first to last the instrumentalists displayed a skill and a finish that was deserving of the highest compliment,and the orchestral music was one of the chief enjoyments of a most enjoyable concert. Special intermit attached to the intermezzo from the cantata " Adele "composed by the conducter, which is to be produced shortly in War- ' rington. This was the first public performance of the selection, which is a very pretty and attractive piece of 'instrumentation, and Mr. Crossley was called upon to acknowledge the substantial plaudits of the:audience. It will be of interest to know that the orchestra com- prised :—Leader. Mr. John Roberts ; first viefins,Measrs, T. Blainplii n and W. 13. Kay; second violins, Messrs. R. H Pearson W. E. Atkin and 11. Foster; vio/as,Alessrs. E. W.Reynolds. and J. Marlow ; violoncellos, Messrs. C.R. Crossley, H. Bond, and J. Simkim ; double bass, Messrs. Cottier and IL VVhitneld ; flute, Mr.W. Oekleston ; oboe, Mr. T. Ward; clarionets, Meesrs. Hipkiss, and L. Crossley ; bassoon, Mr. limiter ; horns. Messrs. Gill and Lowe : cornets, Messrs. It. Pierpoint and Smith ; euphonium, Mr. T. Outhwaite ; and organ, dr. R. Birkett Musgrove.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THEFT OF FONVIS.-AN EXTRAORDINARY DEFENCE.

At the Warrington•Borough Police Court, on Monday, Edward Walsh, labourer, of 8 Earl-st., was charged with stealing, on Saturday evening, two fowls, the property of John Williams, 126 Longford-st.— Police-Sergeant Smith saw the prisoner hurrying along Longforclst. holding his head down in a suspicious manner. He fol- lowed him and got hold of him and found him with two fowls in his possession, one dead and one alive. He said he had got them from his father's, and the sergeant took him there, the prisoner remarking to his father as he entered " Oh, father, I got them from your hen coon." Sergeant Smith went round to the back, and found that no hens were kept there. The officer subsequently dis- covered that the poultry belonged to the prosecutor.— The prisoner now said when he took the hens he was in- toxicated and did not know what he was doing. He wanted to see a hen swim ; and as he had never seen one swim in his life before he thought he would try it.—The Chief Consable said he wondered how the dead fowl was going to swim .—The prisoner was sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour. AN AEDACIOUS THEFT.

Elizabeth Clayton, a little girl, daughter of John Clay- ton, labourer 14 Oliver-st., was charged at the Warring- ton Borough Police Court on Monday, with stealing from the shop of William Daniels, 31 Pinner's. Brew, is. ed. and a basin, his property.—The Chief Constable said the shop was generally managed by the complainant's wife. She was in the kitchen.and observed tSn the wall a shadow as of some one in the shop. She went into it, and saw the prisoner, and asked her what she wanted. She said "A halfpeth of ice cream," and added "Wait a minute," then hastened out of the shop in a suspicious manner. Mrs. Daniels noticed that the basin containing the copper was gone, and hurried after the girl, seizing her, and finding the basin containing eighteen penny- worth of copper upon her. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan was communicated with, and apprehended the girl at home.—The complainant stated that on her accusing the prisoner of the theft she replied "I could not help it."—The Bench contented themselves with merely recording a conviction against her. A TASTE FOR JAM. At Warrington Borough Court. on Tuesday, before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman), E. J. Guest, and Dr. Starkey Smith, Isaac Kinsey was charged with stealing a pot of jam. value 3d., the property of Mr. William Strange,Church-st. The evidence showed that prisoner, viho was only 14 yeara of age, lodged on School-brow with his father. The previous evening,he,together with two other youths, went with a halfpenny to Mr. William Strange's shop,for the purpose of purchasing a stale cake. He was unable to effect the purchase in consequence of Mr. Strange having no cakes of a suitable age. So Isaac pretended to walk out with a disconsolate mien, hut in- stead of that he walked out with a pot of jam. He was caught afterwards by D.S. Monaghan, and he told the Bench that the possible reason he had for stealing was, because he had nothing else to do. Mr. Garnett advised him to gat something to do, because "Satan finds some mischief still, for idle hands to do." Upon Mr. Taylor, Court Missionary, offering to take Isaac under his super- vision, the lad was discharged with a conviction re- corded against him. Mr. Strange did not appear to pro- secute.
BENT ON SOMETHING.

- Mary Bent, a respectably dressed woman, of Bolton, was charged at the Borough Court on Wednesday, with being drunk and disorderly in Suez-street, the previous evening. The woman, it seems, had come to Warring- ton at the bent of what appeared to be an inspiration. She said she wanted to be a nurse in the Smallpox Hos- pital ; but her services were not accepted. She was bent upon doing something, anyhow, before she went back, she replied. And so she went and bent all her energies in getting intoxicated. After this she was dis- covered by a constable, lying on the floor. He locked her up, and the magistrates, after hearing this story. liberated her upon exacting a promise that she would bend her steps in the direction of Bolton. She went. THE LODM NG THEY DIDN'T WANT. A tall, six foot man named Martin Mulhall,and a short man named Tommy Troy, presentedthemselves—or were presented by Sergeant Chantler—to the magistrates on Thursday. They were two more or less (possibly less) respectable members of the army of unemployed. Neither of them had been out of employment long since boyhood,though. Both,too, had alvo ays been character- ized by an ingenious trick which they had learned of picking things up sharply. And consequently the Government had recognized their merit and given them several contracts at picking up something which is called oakum. They were said on this occasion to have visited the rectory the previous evening, with the inten- tion of picking up some of the Rev. F. W. goods and chattels. But they told the Bench this was not so. They said their condition of destitution had led them to Seek the Rector and ask him to oblige , them with the price of a " fourpenny doss," because they had heard he was a good man and often paid for poor men's lodgings. After taking all the incidental particulars of the case into consideration, the Bench thought they would relieve them from the trouble of borrowing money for their lodgings. They gave them a month's free lodgings at Stramgeways.
HE WAS FOND OF GAMBOLING.

lie was a vagrant. But there was that about his humble mein, and oakum coloured hair which only sadly constrasted with the large tin button that shone forth, in resplendent glory, on his apology for a waistcoat, like a minature sun. And when the Clerk said to him, before the Bench on Friday, "Richard Melior, you are charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street last night," his glass-alley-like eyes wandered to a tuft of stocking protrudisg from his boot, a tear trickled along his little nose, and he said : " Garn ; I was'nt. Lemme go." From what a constable now stated Richard on the previous night had only indulged in a little frivolity. He wasn't naturally cut out tn. a clown, and so had to seek artificial methods of raising his spirits. And when he had consumed the sixth "pint," he felt very happy. Be went gamboling about Bridge-street like a little lamp; and when he saw another man or a child in the street he thought they would like to be happy, too; and he used to pull them down on the floor and gambol with them, lie didn't often gamble though, and once when one of the men went in for" tossing," Peter was upset • and in addition to that his head collided with a brick'. Perhaps that constable took Richard to the police station to get a license for providing this kind of entertainment. Richard seemed to think so, and he smiled all the while at the Bench, in such a funny way too, lie made one think of the lid being lifted off a cheese box when he was working the smiles up. The Bench, to encourage his love of gamboling said he could go and gambol on the "golden ladder "at Strangeways for a month. Then the an actually became ungracious and said he wouldn't come near this town, nor those magistrates again. " Never ! Never !" he repeated, with a pained look on his face. Then he gathered in his little arms the clothes which seemed inclined to leave him, and toddled down the steps into the cold, dark, cells.

THEFT FROM TANNER'S LsNN TANNERY.—Thomas Mulhall, 64, Foishaw-st., labourer, was charged with stealing four poles value Be., from the Tanner's-lane Tannery Company, on the 6th inst.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the prosecution. He said that for some time past poles had been missed from his client's works and several innocent persons had been suspected; and one man's house had been examined, much to his indignation. The suspicion of Mr. Crosfield, the manager, had been directed to the defendant on Wednesday, when he saw two poles snatched from the yard and dragged through a crevice in the wall. The, man's house was searched by D.S. Monoghan and the missing articles were found there.— Defendant pleaded guilty, and it was proved that the poles had been stolen on two different occasions.—De- fendant was fined 10s, and costs on each charge, or 14 ' days' imprisonment for each offence. THRASHING HIS Chum—John Vickers, 10, Smith-st., was charged with cruelly illtreating his child, Sarah Alice Vickers, by striking her on the head with a strap. Inspector Uphill said he had seen the child, and found a bruise on its forehead. Defendant denied having touched the child with a strap. He did it with his hand whilst suffering from ill health and want of rest.—Fined 53. and costs.

Munster OF CHILDMOC—John Fiddler, and his wife Sarah, of Fillings-court, appeared in answer to an adjourned charge of neglecting their two children.—The case was adjourned last month for four weeks, to see if there would he any improvement effected in the condition of the children.—lnspector Uphill said there was scarcely any improvement in the children, and P.C. Baxendale, who had visited the defendant's house, said on each occasion he found the woman drunk.—Mr. Browne, who appeared on behalf of Mr. Tinion, male defendant's employer, said said that Fiddler himself was a hard working, steady man.—The case was adjourned for another month, the Bench warning the female defendant to keep away from the beer, which was the cause of the whole trouble. RUGBY. CROMPTON V. WIDNES.—At Crompton. In the first portion of the game Wild, after neat passing by Clough and Henthorne, scored a grand try for Crompton. In the second portion Wall crossed the Widnes lines, the place kick failing. A grand game resulted in favour2„ef Crompton by 2 tries to nil. RUNCORN v. BURTON—This match was cancelled in consequence of the frost. RUNCORN RANGERS T. DITTON REORRATION.—This match was played at Ditton on Saturday in cold pierc- ing weather, The Rangers played with 14 men, being short of Midward, one of the halves. The visitors were represented as follows ;—Full back, C. 11. Cook; three- quarter, A. Houghton ' • J. Butterworth, (captain), H. ' Hughes half backs ; 3: W. Johnson, W. Faulkners, forwards, T. Woods, J. Brennan, W. Russell, W. Sutton, W. E. Hough, E. Chaney, S. Rawlinson, and J. flelsby. Butterworth losing the toss, Rawlinson commenced hostilities at 3.30, against strong wind. The home backs mulling the play, settled in the Recs.' quarters. The homesters got away with a dribble, which Butterworth checked and kicked to touch. The Rangers now pressed and looked much like scoring, until the home full back relieved with a kick to touch. Give and take play now ensued, and on half time arriving nothing had been scored by either side. After the restart Houghton kicked well into the Recs.' quarters,and Russell had exceedingly hard lines in not scoring, the ball being kicked dead. The kick out was retnrned by Butterworth, who sent across the field, and the Recs, appeared to have a clear run in, but Houghton dashed up and tackled brilliantly. The home forwards got away on the loose, and a race between them and Houghton ended in the latter kick- ihg dead. The visitors now pressed hard, and from some loose play Russell crossed the line, but the try was disallowed. After the drop out the Recs.essaved a rush, but Cook saved grandly. Shortly afterwards Hughes getting the ball an the bound, rounded the home backs in splendid style. and scored close to posts, but the try was again disallowed.
