ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION.—A CLINKING GAME. —OUT local association team journeyed LS Liverpool on Satur- day and encountered the Liverpool Printers in the 3rd round of the Liverpool junior bat competition. The match was played on a ground known as the Strawberry Gardens, and certainly the iron " clinkers " thereon did, though somewhat distantly, resemble that well-known fruit. The game was of a very fast and exciting nature and at half-time Warrington were leading by 3 goals to 2. Matters certainly looked promising when a short time off the finish Warrington added another goal, but it was now that they made a fatal mistake. They became too confident, and the 'Liverpudlians rushed two goals through, the score at the finish being 4 goals. Although darkness was now quickly setting in, the referee ordered the teams to play another twenty minutes, and during that time Warrington went under and retired defeated by 5 goals to 4. Before the game commenced, Warring. ton pretested against the ground and the fact that ch.; touch line was only about two feet from a building which ran the length of the field. The referee said that the ground was certainly dangerous, but nevertheless ordered the game to be played. Nothing but praise can be given to the Warrington players, who, although on a strange and dangerous ground, played up with that characteristic energy which marks Warrington foot- ballers, be they Rugbyites or Associationists. The secre- tary of the club has forwarded his protests to the Liver- pool Association. The facts are the state of the ground ,the nearness of the touch line to a building, having to play twenty minutes' extra time, and the fact that the last goal was scored in complete darkness. If the protests are successful, and it is to be hoped they will be, then the Liverpudlians will play at Warringtfon where football fields have no associations whatever with "clinkers." It may be mentioned that two of the Warrington players were rather severely cut by the above-mentioned "clinkers." Sr. WERIIIIRGH'S T. MOORI ROTHRS.—MOOTO Rovers travelled to Chester on Saturday to play the above team. The Saints were not fully represented, three substitutes being played. Callaghan started the ball,and the visitors at once bore down on the home citadel. The home backs were in form and ably responded to the sails made upon them. The Cestrians went away with their old dash, and Callaghan defeated the goal keeper with a pretty shot. This, however, was disallowed. Ten minutes later they notched their first goal, Brown doing the needful. The Rovers strove hard to score, 'but the defence of the Werburg,hs was too much for them, and half-time came with the score standing St. Werbiugh's, one; Moore Rovers, nil. On the resumption of hostili- ties the Saints got away, and had a short spell of press- ing, until the visitors' right got down, and after a pretty piece of work defeated Maguire with a splendid shot. After this the ball was alternately at each end of the field, no points being registered. A very evenly-con- ' tested game resulted—as it deserved to—in a draw of one goal each.

DEATH OF THE HON. W. H. CROSS, M.P. The Hon. W. H. Cross, M.P., son of Viscount Cross, is dead. A fortnight ago he was attacked by typhoid fever at his residence in London. At the outset his con- dition caused considerable unea.si ness, but grave sy p- toms appeared only on Friday last. The malady rapidly developed in severity, and Mr. Cross succumbed on Sunday evening at six o'clock, his wife, Lord Cross, and other members of the family being present. Lord Cross hardly left his son during his illness. Mr. Cross, who was but 38 years old, well known in the neighbour- hood of Warrington. He was born at Appleton Hall, and was a frequent visitor at the Hall, now the resi- dence of his uecle and aunt, Mr. and Mrs. Lyon. In that neighbourhood he gained considerable popularity. He was educated at Rugby, and Ustiversity College, Ox- ford, and soon after leaving the latter was called to the bar at the Inner Temple, namely,in 1882,when he joined the northern circuit. Some time ago he was chosen junior counsel for England in the Retiring Sea fisheries arbitration. Mr. Cross's first introduction to political life was in August, 1888, when he was returned unop- posed for West Derby Division, in succession to Lord Claude Hamilton, who at that time resigned owing to the condition of his health. When the deceased gentle- man sought to be returned for the division at the last general election, tie was opposed in the Liberal interest by Mr. Alderman Frederick Smith, whom he defeated by 1,182 votes. In 1880 Mr. Cross married Mary, younger daughter of the late Mr. William Newthwaite, JP., and DL., of Bromigate, Cumberland. The deceased gentle- man was a fine speaimen of young English physique, and to this material quality were joined a genial tem- perament, which exhibited itself in many considers to ways. The deepest sympathy must go out to Viscount Cross and his family in the great bereavement which has overtaken them. Mr. Cross was very popular in the neighbourhood of Pimlico, where he resided. Ho was president of the St. Gabriel's. Working-men's Club, and was one of the churchwardens of St. Gabriel's, Warwick. square, where on Sunday night the Vicar (the Rev. J. El. Ellison) announced the sad event. Chcpin's " Dead March "was played. WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVES AND MR. CROSS. At the annual meeting of the members of the Warring- ton Conservative Club, on Monday evening, the Chair- man, Alderman Francomb, said he was sure the members would join him in expressing regret at the death of Mr. W. H. Cross. Lord Cross. his father, was looked upon in Warrington as one of themselves. Some of them would remember that he lived amongst them, and he supposed 1)15 face was as well knom n in Warrington as the face of any gentleman. Tney were always delighted to see him at their meetings, and proud to read of him in the newspapers. The bright young gentleman who had just passed away seemed to have inherited a very great deal of his father's goodness and ability. He was spoken highly of wherever he was known, he was a , most excellent member of Parliament, and a man who in a few years must have come to the front. They were exceedingly sorry that death should have removed such a valuable life from areangst them awl they all sympath- ised most sincerely with his lathe,. and mother, and his widow and children. (Hear, hear.) The flag over the Conservative Club was hoisted at half-mast on Monday as soon as it became known that the Hon. W. 11. Cross, M.P., for the West Derby divi- sion, Liverpool, had succumbed to an attack of typhoid fever. Much sympathy is expressed in Warrington for Lord Cross and family upon the sad bereavement they have sustained. The news was received by the inhabit- ants of Lymin with feelings of deep regret. The flag at the Conservative Club was hoisted half-mast high as a token of respect to his memory. THE FUNERAL. The remains of the late Hon. W. H. Cross were con- veyed from Londcn on Wednesdays, and interred in Broughton-in-Furness Churchyard, amidst very deep manifestations of sorrow. At the railway station a large body of sympathisers from different parts of the coun- try had congreg,ated,and the coffin having been shoulder- ed by members of the tenantry, a procession was formed to the church. The Rev. Mr. Ellison, of Pimlico, con- dbcted the first part of the service in the church in a most impressive manner, and a portion of the tenantry, who had assembled in large numbers, wept bitterly during the performance of the solemn rite. The prin- cipal mouruers were Mrs. %V. H. Cross, Lord and Lady Cross, the Hon. and Rev. F. Cross, the Hon. J. Cross, Miss Mary Cross, and Miss Margaret Cross. The church service was choral, and at its conclusion the Dead Mareh in " Saul " was played on the organ. Amongst those present were Sir George' Baden-Powell, M.P., Mr. H. Brierley, Mr. EL Thompson, Liverpool. Conservative Association ; Mr. Cookson' J.P., and Mr. J. W. Willox, M.P. ; Mr. Damsel!, Mr. H. Cookson, Mr. W. Dillon,Mr. J. Barry, Mr. C. Holland, Mr. F. Hughes, representing the Liverpool postmen ; Captain Price, Sir Jas. Poole, and Captain Grills. Wreaths were rEceived from her Majesty the Queen, the chairman, committee, and mem- bers of the Conservative Club, Liverpool, the servants, he tenantry, dnd others.
! FRIGHTFUL ACCIDENT A.T A
WIGAN COLLIERY.

100 MEN EN TOIIBED. FIFPEEN LIVES LOST. AWFUL SCENES. On Wednesday a catastrophe of an extraordinary character occurred at the Pemberton Four Feet Mine, No. 2 pit, Bamfurlong„ belonging to Messrs. Cross, Tet- ley, and Co., colliery proprietors. Bamfurlong is a small mining village about four miles from Wigan, situ- ated in the heart of the coalfields. Its population is almost exclusively engaged in coal getting, of which there is abundant evidence in every direction. Some hundreds of men are employed at the colliers of Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Co., and on Wednesday morning close upon a hundred of them descended the shaft of No. 2 pit, in order to proceed to their work. About seven o'clock a wild cry was heard in the workings that the pit was on fire. The warning proceeded from the lips of a boy named Rowley, whose duty it was to look after a compressed air engine, situated at a point some 400 yards from the pit eye, and used for hauling tubs and buckets from various parts of the pit. It is well known to engineers that compressed air has a tendency to freeze. In order to prevent this and the:conse- quent stoppage of the engine, what is termed a " paraffin touch" is placed under the cylinder in order to keep the temperature up. The lad Rowley was discharging some duty in connection with his employment, probably cleaning the engine, when he accidentally upset the lamp, and the inflammable fluid was immediately all ablaze. It is said that he endeav- oured to extinguish the flame by throwing some cicthes upon it, but he was unsaccessful in his efforts. After sounding a shrill and terrifying warning to those around him he fled to the pit eye, and was in due course rescued. Meantime the bed of the engine, on which the paraffin had been upset, blazed terribly, and the flames spread to all the woodwork of the engine-house, which was totally consumed. The unfortunate Men] who were in the rear of the conflagration threw down their tools, and came rushing forward along the gangways towards the main level leading to the bottom of the shaft. Those within reach had been warned by Rowley's cry, but it scarcely needed such a monitor to tell them that the dreaded fire-damp had attacked them, for it spread with incredible velocity, urged on by the impetus of the devouring flames, into all the surrounding workings. Implements were dashed to the ground, and a pell-mell rush was made for life. Unfortunately, the stampede and panic, which seized on everybody, rendered the men less able to judge what was likely to prove of bene- fit to themselves. It appears that there was a conneo- tion between No. 2 and No. 1, and if it had been found, all would have escaped with their lives. Either those in danger did not think, or did not know, of thei com- munication; and, keeping only in view the main road by which they were accustomed to travel, they rushed literally into the jaws of death. The burning engine- house barred their way ; the smoke and fumes were all around them. To go forward was to be hurried alive, and to return was to be suffocated with the noxious sulphurous fumes which now pervaded the pit. Driven thus to bay, the imprisoned colliers appear to have de- cided to make a bold fight for life ;an as the only way to fresh air and safety lay throueh the fiery belt before them, they, without hesitation, rushed forward, hoping to pass right through, or at least to fall insensible on the other side, where rescue was certain. The flames, how- ever, were too fierce, and the fumes too dense. They were overpowered, and fell, singly, or in sinall groups, just as they made their last struggle. When found, their bodies were charred at the extremities, and in some instances the flesh was completely consumed, exposing the bone. All those who were not in the air-way by which the smoke and vapour travelled maeaged to gain the pit " eve." Bands of explorers were immediately organised, and a descent of the pit was made with the utmost promp e- tude. Mr. Hutchinson, manager of the colliery, led the van, superintending all the arrangements. He went down the shaft about eight o'clock in the morning, and continued at his post of danger throughout the day. All that skill and experience could suggest was done forth- with to quell the outbreak, and bring help te the survi- vors. Mr. Hutchinson's bravery was such as to evoke the admiration of men accustomed to brave deeds. The valour of the manager was well supported by several members of the medical profession, who hastened to the scene. Dr. Brayton, of Flindley' Dr. Webster, of Wigan, Dr. Dobb, of Golborne, and Dr. Mapei, shortly after arriving at the pit-brow, courageously volunteered to go down the shaft to assist the injured, donned colliers' apparel for the occasion, and were lowered by the cage, carrying with them medical iestoratives, while large jugs of warm coffee and brandy were sent down. Mean- while Dr. Bentham, of lace, and others remained above ready to render whatevor service they could as the men were wound up. The spectacle witnessed around the pit at this time was sad, but impressive. Many a time the daring volunteers were driveie back and forced to come up for breath and refreshment. ! Some of them, owing to the stoppage of the pumping apparatus, had to wade in places up to their necks in water in order to reach the workings. Many a noble deed was done, but these brave colliers appeared to reckon nothing af such heroism. They were calmly de- termined to he their fellows, and did so in the teeth of death without a thought of praise. The fight to quench the flames is described as terrible. The fear was that the conflagration might spread and catch the coal,and in any case if the entombed men were to be rescued the work had to be done at once. The rescuers, aided by the medical men, literally bombarded the flames with hand grenades, and had the satisfaction of seeing it ex- tinguished. But, even with the utmost caution, it was long before the explorers could creep along the ground, owing to the fatal after damp, to bring hope and help to their still surviving comrades, whose sufferings from cold and sulphurous vapour were protracted and in- ! tense. A touching incident was associated with the appear- anco of a lad, fourteen years old, named John Aindow. He was reached by the explorers about three o'clock, and brought to the surface, where his mother clasped , him passionately in her arms. Aindow was brought , into the carpenters' shed in a dazed condition. He was placed before the fire, and quickly revived. He had brought up his can with him, and, small though he was, , he looked a perfect picture of self-reliance and resource. Ile had saved his own life, and probably that of others,l by his presence of mind. Gathered from his own lips.' his story Was:—" I noticed something was wrong, and , at once made a leap towards a piece of bratticing. Then I got some nails from a cabin where we lads get our meals. I nailed the bratticing up, and sat down behind it. It stopped the foul air, and I was saved. It was very cold, but I did not leave the place when I found I could breathe." The boy then became silent, but pre- sently he burst into tears, and said, " My mate Billy Bates took some lamps to the far end, and he has not returned yet, and I suppose he is dead." He wept copi- ously when he thought of his woikmate and playfellow "Billy ; " and on being asked as to what he had seen, he said, "It was awful,' and with a shudder, he added, "I have passed over the bodies of four men." Aindovr was then carried on the back of a big miner to a cart and taken home. His mother left him, and went to the pit-brow to watch for the arrival of another young son, who had not then been accounted for. LIST OF, THE DEAD.

ST. JAMES'S PAROCHIAL SALE OF WORK.

It is customary, in connection with St. James's Church, Latchford, to hold a sale of work in Decem- ber, for the purposed. raising funds for some special parochial object. This year's sale took place in the schoolroom on Tuesday afternoon, the articles for sale having been provided by the lady members of the Congregation'. A large number of ladies and gentlemen attended the opening ceremony, and amongst them were the Mayor and Mayoresa (Alderman and. Mrs. Greenall), the Rev. F. and Mrs. Slater, the Rev. A. Hordern, Mrs. Beamont, Dr. and the Misses White, Mr; and Mrs. John White, Mr. and Mrs. C. S. Burgess, Mr. and Mrs. Kay, Mrs. Carleton. Mrs. Buckton, Mrs. Edelsten, Mrs. .1. A. Edelsten, Mr. H. N. Houghton, and Mr. Cogon. Before calling upon the Mayoress to open the sale, the Rev. F. Slater, ex- plained the objects which it was proposed to assist by the proceeds. He said they required £45 to balance the church accounts for the vear,and £l5 to assist in defray- ing a balance of upon alterations made to the interior of the church. The sum of £6O was the specifiod amount to clear all this, and therefore what they realized above that sum would be devoted to other necessary improve- ments, and also to the assistance of the day schools. The latter he had to confess required more assistance than they had been latterly receiving for the subscription list was not so robust as it might have been. —The Mayoress. who was received with applause, briefly declared the sale open, and alluded to the great pleasure she felt in responding to the invitation of th• Vicar to perform the opening ceremony. She felt that it was not necessary to draw the attention of the gather- ing to the many things which depended upon the success of any such parochi.il effort. They were connected with parochial work, as she herself was, and they would realize with her the importance of any such work as they were assisting in that afternoon. They were pro- bably little matters, but she would remind them that little things went to make the bulk. (Applause.) She concluded brwishingthe ladies every success in their Igenerous work.—After a vote of thanks had been passed to the Mayoress, the sale was proceeded with. The fol- lowing ladies were in management of the stalls : Mes- dames Slater, Houghton Venn, Pickton, and Marsh, fancy stall. Mesdames Houghton, and Madeley, and Miss E. , Taylor and Miss Parry, plain work stall. Miss 11. Slater, art stall. Miss Alice Burgess, Miss M. Slater and Miss ' flallwood, toy stall. Mrs. 11. Woods and Miss White, flower stall. The Misses Taylor, the china stall. Mrs. Wignall, Mrs. Brown, Mrs. Cook, and the Misses Fair- hurst, the refreshment stall. During the afternoon suit- able entertainments were provided. The sum realized by the sale was satisfactory.

div.head: WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

The annual meeting of the members of the War- rington Conservative Club was held in the Club on Monday evening. Alderman Francomb presided, and amongst those present were Alderman Wright, Councillor Hutchinson, Messrs. W. W. Westwell. C. Higginbottom, John Roberts, T. Roberts, W. Wat- son, J. Bavley, G. Jolley, D. Rawling, T. Mason, R. Daintith, G. Pining (secretary), and S. Ingham (manager). The CHAIRMAN said that was their eighth annual meet- ing, and he was pleased to congratulate the members of the Conservative Club and also the whole of the Conser- vatives of Warrington upon the splendid success the club had achieved. At the present moment he believed they had more members than ever they had. (Hear, hear.) The members seemed to thoroughly enjoy the privileges that were offered to them, and he did not think it was possible for any institution in the town to be conducted in a better way than that club was conducted. They had regular games of billiards and other amusements, they had an excellent reading room, and he believed the discipline of the club was so good that not even a shadow of gambling found its way within the walls, and drink was cer- tainly a thing out of form altogether. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. George Pilling read the annual report. The com- mittee had much pleasure in stating that the member- ship of the club was still on the increase, although there and been a number of deaths, removals from the town, had some resignations during the year. The Committee however, were of opinion that there was still a large number of Conservatives in the borough, who would be willing to become members if anproached by the right people. They therefore appealed to each member to do his best to introduce new members. The club during the past year had been well attended and conducted by all in every way that could be desired, and was in a complete and comfortable state. The Ist and 2nd class balls were held as usual in February last, and were well patronised and highly successful. Great credit was due to those gentlemen who carried them out so well. The attendance on the bowling green had been much inter- fered with on account of the very wet season, but still under the circumstances it lead done very well. There was now pending a billiard handicap, in which the large number of 140 members were taking part. The Com- mittee had to deplore through death the loss of several members, including Major Litton, Mr. George Woods, and Mr. W. Reid. In conclusion the Committee desired to record their satisfaction with the manner in which Mr. and Mrs. Higham had superintended and carried out the arrangements of the club. The report was adopted.—Mr. Pilling was re-elected secretary, and Mr. W. Owen treasurer, and a vote of thanks was accorded them for their services during the past year.

div.head: LABOUR " PEERS " IN NEW ZEALAND.
div.p: LABOUR " PEERS " IN NEW ZEALAND.
BOILERMAKER AND "COMPS," IN THE LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL.
INTERESTING EXPERIMENT.

The Christchurch correspondent of the" Standard announces that the Government of New Zealand have lost no time in availing themselves of Lord Ripon's instruction to the Governor that the lattei was to accept the advice of his Ministers in regard to the creation of new of the Legislative Council. Immediately after the conclusion of the session of Parliament, they called twelve of their supporters to the Upper House. Eight of these appointments were of the ordinary character, and call for no par- ticular comment. But in the case of the other four the Government have introduced a startling innov- tion. They have taken four working men from their workshops and—called them to the Upper Chamber of the Legislature, hitherto held sacred to the " blue blood" of the colony, or, at any rate, to large land- owners or men of personal wealth and influence, or on on account of long political services in the Lower House. The new Labour" Peers" have had no previous ex- perienle in public political life. One of them, the Hon. J. E. Jenkinson, is a boilermaker in the Government railway workshops. When the telegram arrived asking him if he would allow his name to be submitted to the Governor, he was inside a boiler engaged in riveting it, and the telegraph boy poked in the message through a hole in the cylinder. Mr. Jenkinson, not unnaturally, at first treated the affair as a hoax, and refused to take any notice of it ; but at length was persuaded to send , a reply, and did so, afterwards going i on with his ham- mering without saying a word. It s only fair to say , that he is a well-informed and intelligent specimen of the working classes of the colony, and a man of real worth and "grit." He is thirty-three years of age, and was born in New Zealand. He was successively presi- dent of the Dunedin Boilermakers' Union, and of the Christchurch branch of the same society. He was also the first vice-president of the Canterbury Trades and Labour Council. In 1879 be had a narrow escape from being killed in a large fire in Dunedin, and received special mention for his plucky efforts to save life on that occasion.

Another new councillor, the Hon. J. Rigg, is a " comp." in the Government printing office; and the Hon. William Bolt, of Dunedin, another of the new selections, is a storeman in a warehouse there. He is a native of the Shetland Islands, and in early life was a sailor. He is said to be a plodding, self-educated man, who has taken a great interest in political economy and history, and has made himself very well posted up in these subjects. The remaining Labour member, Mr. W. ' Jennings, is the foreman printer of the Auckland " Evening Star." It was generally understood that the proprietor of that journal, which enjoys a large cir- culation in the North, would have been himself one of the nominees, and great was the surprise when it was , discovered that he had been passed over in favour of the chief of his composing staff. It may be interesting to add that the appointment in each case is for seven years, and there is an honorarium of £l5O a year for the expenses incurred in attending Parliament. This new departure has caused a good deal of sensation in the colony. It is admitted that, conceding the principle that workingmen should be called to the Upper House, the Government have not made a bad selection.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLAR, CONVENTION.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLAR, CONVENTION.

--- The monthly Session of No. I Convention, S.W. Lancashire, was held on Saturday last in the Workingmen's Institute, Liverpool-road, St. llelens. The meeting was called to order at 4 p.m., when Bro. J. Lindon, P.C.C.T , presided over 0. good atten- dance, Bro. Q.M. Sergt. Roberts, C.C.T. being de- tained by military duties. The usual Credential and Press Committees were appointed, after which the reports of officers were received and considered. Bro. R. Kean, C. Sec., showed that with one or two ex- ceptions the lodges in the Convention were actively prosecuting their work, and were adding to their num- bers. The Warrington lodges were doing well, but their efforts during the past month or two had been somewhat checked by the serious smallpox epidemic, which was now happily lessening its ravages. It had seriouslyaffect- ed every institution in Warrington, as well as the trade of the town,to an alarming extent,and it was to be hoped it would very soon be amongst the memories of the past. He also referred to the the question of aD. Lodge char- ter, for No. 1 Convention, and several other itema which were dealt with seriatim.—Bro. J. Vint, C.S.J.T., gave a detailed account of the position and prospects of the juvenile temples, almost without exception active and doing excellent work, the reports showing an aggregate increase of 54 members on the month.—Bro. John Tay- lor, C.E.S., in a brief but interesting report. showed that electoral work occupied a large share of the atten- tion of Good Templars,the efforts just at this time being to influence the Government to—lst, introduce a Bill embodying the principles of the direct veto of the rate- payers, and 2nd, to prohibit county or town councils or any municipal body elected for other purposes, having any place ass future licensing authority. Many of the lodges had forwarded memorials on these lines to the principal members of the Government, and he utged those who were remiss to take steps to send them as soon as possible.—Bro. Brockbank, C. treas., was absent through serious illness, and the financial report was referred to the next session.—Bro. J. Riley C.M.'s resignation of his office, owing to other duties, was accepted, and Bro. Heywood, of War- rington, was elected to fill the vacancy. It was unani- mously resolved to forward an expression of deepest sympathy with Sister Mrs. Brockbank and family,in the serious illness of Bro. Brockbank C.Treas. A report that ' the brother was improving gave intense satisfaction. It , was unanimously resolved that memorials,on lines already indicated,be drawn up.signed by the C.E.Superintendent I and forwarded to the principal members of the Govern- ment. Thanks to the members of the " Grove" Lodge for their arrangements for the session, brought the meet- ing to a close; when a good number sat down to an ex- cellent tea. A public meeting was afterwards held, pre- sided over by Bro. R.Skaife, U.5.J.1., of St.Helens,when spirited addresses were given by the Chairman, Bros. A. Frances, L.D., J. Lindon, &c. Songs and melo- dies were given by Bros. J. Taylor and R. Ambrose., of Earlestown ; Bro. Heywood, Warrington ; and Sister Hairsnape, Wigan ; and Sister Mrs. Frances, St. Helens, contributed an excellent recitation. An interesting and enjoyable myeting closed with thanks to all taking part. BRITISH PAUPERISM.
--- WARRINGTON'S PROPORTION.

According to a report issued from Parliament upon Poor Law management the following figures explain the state of local pauperism :—First there is given the proportion of paupers for every hun- dred of the inhabitants of this Union, in-door and out-door being particularized ; also the cost of pauperism in this union, as illustrated by its being divided into so much per bead of the population. Then, by way of comparison, similar figures are given for the whole of this county, and a third set of figures show how the local numbers and cost compare with the average of the whole of England and Wales. Exclud- ing the metropolis there are but 10 unions in the King- dom where the relief is in a higher ratio than 10s, per head of the population, and the highest of these ten is Bishop Stortford, where the proportion is lie. 100. per head. Them are 25 Unions where the relief falls below the ratio of 3s. per head of population. Most of these are in Lancashire and Yorkshire, and generally the low- est rates are distant from the metropolis. The two Unions where the cost is lowest are Fylde,in Lancashire, where the rate is Is. 11. V., and Glossop 2s. In the War- rington Union the number of persons receiving relief, ha 'proportion to population is: In-door, 045 ; out-door, 113; total, 1.8 per cent. Cost of the relief 3s. (W. per head of the population. In this county tne ratio IS: In-door, 06; out-door, 12; total, 1.8 per cent. Cost of the relief, 4s. lid. per head of the population. In the whole of England and Wales the averages are: In-door, 07; out-door, 2.0 ; total, 2.7 per cent. ; and the average cost was ss. 11id. per head of the population.

div.head: SIR EDW.A.RD REED ON HOME RULE.
div.p: SIR EDW.A.RD REED ON HOME RULE.
THE MAXIMUM OF HOME RULE.

SirEdwatel Reed, M.P. for Cardiff,- has addressed a long letter to the president of the Cardiff Liberal Assoc- iation on the question of Home Rule. He commences by saying that so much has been said and written since the general election in Cardiff and elsewhere about his inten- tions concerning the Irish question that he feels constrained to put his views into definite form. The Home Rule for Ireland which he supported in 1888 was a measure which went, he thinks, as far as it was possible to go in the way of relieving the people of Ireland from harsh and capricious interference by Great Britain with their domestic affairs, or without breaking in upon the unity and authority of the Imptirial Government. Sir Edward then goes on to describe at length the state- ments made since that time concerning Home Rule, the modifications which have been made in the original pro- posal by Mr. Gladstone and others, the numerical . posi- tion of the Liberal party at - the last general election, its dependence on the Irish vote, and the statement of Mr. W. Redmond that if the Liberals did not come itp to their expectations, it would certainly be their duty to vote Against them. This, he says, brings him to the main purpose of his letter, which is to make it plain to Mr. Rees Jones (to whom he is writing), to the Government, and to all whom it may concern that he and other mem- bers of the Liberal party are under no obligation what- ever to see Home Rule for Ireland carried the length of giving to Ireland control over anything more than purely domestic and local affairs; that he has no intention whatever of assisting in any separation of Ireland from Great Britain ; that he intends to hold himself absolutely free to vote as he finds just and right when the time comes for voting., on any scheme for restoring the tenants to their holdings, and in making up his mind he will give fair consideration to all parties concerned. Finally, he will not be prepared to take part.in any pro- cess for so dealing with cruel and murderous men as to encourage people to believe either in Ireland or in England net foul crimes will go unpunished or be con- doned because the perpetrators have committed them under " political excitement." Sir Edward cannot imagine anything more deplorable, more unworthy of our country, more calculated to revolt every noble sentiment of the British people, than it will be to find a body of men composing a government, and charged with the present and future of our vast empire, accept- ing dictation from one-eighth of the home population in any matter whatever, except what are most strictly their internal concerns, and not only accepting that dictation, but accompanying its acceptance with pro- ceedings which would violate the good sense and justice of our people. He does not suggest that the Govern- ment intend going wrong on either cf these points ; yet he cannot but recognise that they are under great pres- sure to do so and that they have accepted office with full knowledge of the temptations that await them. His correspondent well knows that there is nothing in this. letter which in any way alters his attitude respecting the Home Rule question. During the laststic years his Irish supporters in Cardiff have been told plainly that, with him, Irish Honiiir Ride' has always been essentially and solely a question of the internal management of affairs in Ireland, and not a question of separating Ireland from our empire in any degree. None of his constitnents have been more cordial than his Irish friends in accepting this view. They have given no countenance to the extreme views of Messrs. Redmond. He can'see no harm likely to result to our empire, or to the world.' from Ireland being allowed— with all the forms of Parliament, and Of Executive Government in miniaturea it so pleases—to take charge of its own internal legislation and administration. On the contrary, he thinks good all round might result from extending to our Irish subjects resident in Ireland this measure of satisfaction. But he sees greet harm likely to result from subjecting any Imperial questions what- sever to the operations of a Dublin Parliament and Exe- cutive, notwithstanding the fact that these Imperial questions involve Irish interests in common with our own. Of one thing he is perfectly satisfied—and he thinks Irish members may well take note of it, and the Government, too, if that be necessary—namely, that Great Britain will never be drawn—no, not even by sympathy and the desire to please—into any sacrifice whatever of our Imperial unity, or of our sense of justice as between man and man, tenant and landlord, or whosoever he be, or of our determination to defend the peaceable people of this kingdom against the men who under any guise whatever, shed, or endeavour to shed, innocent blood. Assuredly, he cannot be drawn into any of these things, and he is confident that he will have the very general approbation of his constituents in thus disclaiming them.

div.head: DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: A DIVORCE CASE.
A STRANGE ALLEGATION.

The trial was commenced in the Divorce Court on Wednesday, of a suit in which Lady Abdy asks for a judicial separation on the ground of her husband's mis- conduct with Madame De Benites, a South American lady. It appeared that the petitioner, an Austrian, had during several years made charges against the latter of having robbed her of her husband's affections, and in 1r support of her accusations the evidence of a number of Parisian domestics and others was now read. Both Sir William Abdy and Madame De Benites deny the charges, and Madame De Benites declared in the witness-box that she had never seen Sir William till she saw him in court, and that the ;petitioner must be mad. The caee came to an abrupt close on Thursday morning. Petitioner's counsel declined to cross-examine Madame de Benites,between whom and Sir William Abdy the peti- tioner had alleged misconduct, and after the respondent had denied the accusation the Judge directed the jury to find in his favour, and the petition was dismissed, with costs against Lady Abdy's separate estate.

div.head: NATIONAL UNION OF CONSERVA-
div.p: THE NATIONAL UNION OF CONSERVA-
TI YES.

The annual Conference of the National Union of Con- servative and Constitutional Associations was opened at Sheffield on Tuesday. Mr. Stuart Wortley, M.P., pre- sided. Lord Scarborough was elected president for the ensuing year. Complaint was made that the organisa- tion of the Conservative party in South Wales did not receive sufficient consideration from the Union, and after a debate a resolutien was adopted declaring that the organisation of the party in South Wales was a " matter worthy of grave consideration" at the hands of the National Union. A resolution was next adopted favouring legislative action to give working men facilities for becoming possessors of the houses they dwell in. The subject of " Fair Trade " was introduced by Colonel Howard Vincent, and after an animated debate a resolution which he moved was carried by a substantial majority. Towards the close of the Confer- ence Mr. A. J. Balfour, M.P., entered the ball and briefly addressed the assemblage speaking chiefly upon the general principles which should guide them in dealing with those vast questions of social reform which, he said, were present to the mind of every man who interested himself in the political future of the

country. The Rev. Dr. Herber Evans was on Wednesday appointed Principal of the North Wales Congregational College. COAGULINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d. and ls. ; postage, 2d. sold everywhere, home and abroad„—Advt. , •
TEE BLACKBURN ATROCITY.
A SINTENCE OF DEATH.

The trial of Crass Duckworth for the atrocious murder - of a child named Alice Barne.p,at Witton,near Blackburn, on the Bth November, was concluded on Tuesday, at Liverpool, before Mr. Justice Grantham. Counsel for the prosecution abandoned certain evidence, which was , put forward to prove that a footprint at the scene ofthe murder, of which a cast had been taken, was made by the prisoner's boot, and later on,after the evidence of an ; expert, the Judge intimated that there was no conclu- sive evidence that a handkerchief which, the murderer had forced into the mouth of the child, and which had caused death by suffocation, corresponded with other handkerchiefs found at the house" of the .prisonei so closely AS •to warrant the inference that it belonged to the prisoner. The prosecution, therefore, relied upon the evidence of the identification by some children and one or two other witnesses, who stated that a man who was observed near the spot at the time of the murder, and who, indeed, was- seen by a little boy named Ridings, with the murdered girl in his arms. 'was the prisoner Duckworth. . For the defence an alibi was set up, and in Support of it five men were called, who swore that at the moment when the murder must have been committed the acgused was in a part of the town 1,200 yards distant and in a state of intoxication. The ! Judge In summing up pointed out that the defence was weak in the fact that, while evidence was adduced with ' a view of showing that the prisoner at the time the crime was committed was not near the spot,no evidence kad been given as to his subsequent movements. If,the learned Judge said. he was in the State of drunkenness described by the witnesses, he must have been noticed by other people, even if he had not been taken charge of by the police for being drunk and incapable. The jury, after an hour's deliberation, found the prisoner guilty, but recommended him to mercy. In reply to the usual question, the prisoner said he was not guilty of the crime. The Judge,in passing sentence of demh,said that. the prisoner had committed this diabolical act,he had no doubt, and he added that drink had broazlit hlin to the pisition in which he stood. In renly to the Judge, the foreman of the jury intimated that they had recom— mended the prisoner to mercy on the g,rouud that he bad not intentionally murdered the child. •
THE REV. H. P. HUGHES ON TEMPERANCE LEGISLATION.

The Rev. Hugh Price Hughes, at his conference at St. James's Hall on Sunday afternoon, continued his consi- deration of the Bishop of Chester's proposals, apropos of coming temperance legislation. If the Government, he said, had only the moral courage to put more faith in what is best in man, instead of fearing what is Worst in him, he could assure them that the whole nation would as heartily applaud a brave and generous attempt to deal with tlUs gigantic curse as Mr. Gladstone's-vast Liverpool audience applauded the sentiments *Bich he expressed on the question. In order to deal with this many-sided and complicated evil they must tolerate a great variety of experiments in the name of local option. Foreseeing this, the speaker proceeded to expound the solution according to the precedents of the enlightened Swedes and still more enlightened Norwegians. Briefly, the following were Mr. Hughes's " points." The Swedish or Gothenburg scheme, which Mr. Chamberlain brought betore the House of Commons in his maiden speech, provided first that the element of private gain should be eliminated from the traffic; and,secondly,that the trade should be municipalized and the profits sho4d go to the relief of the local ratepayers. Thonei the first tenet , was such a, good stride in the right direction, the second resulted in every citizen hav- ing a direct pscuniary interest in the prosperdst of the traffic. Any attempt to bring aboet; such a result in England, Mr. Hughes asserted, would be sternly and unflinchingly opposed by the tem- perance party. The Norwegian or Bergen scheme provided for the prevalence of local option everywhere, and in such a form that it might be carried out to the ex- tent of totally prohibiting the trade. This was one of the demands of the Temperance party in England. The Bergen scheme, which only applied te the retail trade and the sale of Spirits, as that was the main cause of drunkenness, though it had since been discovered that it ought equally to apply to wines and beer, legalized by the Norwegian Parliament in 1871, took the traffic out of private hands, paying no compensation, though allowing a year's grace, and placed it in the hands of philanthropic companies, controlled by the municipal authorities. These philanthropic companies were com- posed of ladies and gentlemen,who subscribed what capi- tal was needed,and received five per cent.and no more of the profits, the remainder being devoted to the support of benevolent societies which were not subsidized from the local rates or the imperial exchequer. One of the argu- ments against compensation used in Norway, was that the spirit business was not a skilled trade, is-relying the expenditure of time and money to prepare a man to enter. it. The supervision of the philanthropic companies was in the hands of the licensing authority, partly made up of magistrates and partly of town councillors. That might do in Norway, but if in England it was taken out of the hands of the magistrates the temperance party would fiercely oppose any-other method than putting it in the hands of the representatives of the people, who would be elected ad hoc, and have the moral authority which they needed to do their work. It was a matter of extreme gratification to Mr. Hughes to find that in Norway the public-houses opened at eight in the morning and closed at half-past twelve, re-opening at-half-past one in the after- noon and closing at eight in the evening on each week- day except Saturday,when the closing time in Bergen was five o'clock in the afternoon. He hoped that a great united effort would be made to secure the closing of the public-houses of this country at ten p.m., for he believed that the worst drinking was done between ten and twelve at night. 'Another feature of the Bergen scheme was the employment of men only behind the bars. He knew nothing more discreditable, cowardly, and mean than that the men of England should allow pure, innocent, good-looking young women to serve in these places. The Bergen barmen were all dressed in uniform and had a number ; and to secure strict compliance with the regulations detectives were employed. Public-houses were also not decorated and made attractive. No seas were provided,and no one was allowed to loiter about. They were conducted strictly on the cash system, no credit being allowed,and it had been made illegal to serve children under 16 years of age with liquor. Mr. Hughes hoped that Mr. Convtreare's Bill to secure this last provision in England would receive the support of every honest man. The Norwegians, he con- tended, had made two important discoveries. Firstly, that the mischief lay in the alcohol itself ; and, secondly that to sell such articles as eggs, milk, coffee, tea, Scc., in the same places as liquor was sold did not mitigate, but accentuated the evil. It was on this result that he joined issue with the Bishop of Chester, and hoped that Dr. Jayne would weigh well this fact. The sum total which Mr. Hughes deduced from this very enlightened precedent was to eliminate all attractions from houses in which liquor was sold, and set up gorgeous coffee palaces beautifully decorated, and made as attractive as flowers and music could make them. In fact, he believed that the only remedy for the abuse of the gin palace was to split it in halves—to have the gin in one place and the palace in another.

div.head: STRIKE IN THE MALLEABLE IRON
div.p: STRIKE IN THE MALLEABLE IRON

TRADE. A further meeting of the employers of Birmingham and Coventry engaged in the malleable iron trade was held at the Colonnade Hotel, New-street, on Monday night, to consider the dispute with reference to the weighing of sand in castings. The masters at first de- cided that all castings must be weighed-in free of sand, 1 but the men raised an objection, and threatened to strike. Several conferences between the representatives of both sides have been held with a view of arriving at a compromise, and at Monday night's meeting, over which Mr. W. Jones, chairman of the Masters' Associa- tion, presided, it was resolved :—" At a meeting of the Birmingham and Coventry Malleable fronfounders' Asso- ciation for a final consideration of the sand allowance, it is fairly considered that as the sand weighed in by casters ranges from 41b to 181 b. per cwt., they can- not accept a less concession than 5 per cent, allowance per cwt. "—A deputation from the men attended, and stated that these terms could not be accepted, and they would refuse to work. About nine firms and between 50 and 60 men are affected. The strike practically be- gan on Monday, as none of the men went to. work- They state that they will remain on strike until their terms are conceded.

div.head: ... STARVED TO DEATH.
div.p: ... STARVED TO DEATH.
A PITEOUS TALE.

- A piteous story comes from Dublin. At an inquest relative to the death of Annie Flynn, aged nine, it was stated that the girl had died from starvation. Her lather was in prison, her mother helpless with fever, and there were no bedclothes, no fire, no food in the house. OnSunday a neighbour, hearing a child's cry. entered the dwelling, and found Annie Flynn lying across the bed dead. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the girl died from acute pneumonia, and in a rider said the tene:nent the family occupied was unfit for human habitation.

div.head: MANNERS FOR BOYS
div.p: MANNERS FOR BOYS

Bat lifted in saying good-bye' or 'how de MI no?' Hat lifted when offering a seat in a car or In acknowledging a favour. Keep step with any one you walk with. Always precede a lady upstair4 and ask her if you may precede her in passing through a crowd or public place. Hat off the moment you enter a street door, and when you step into a private hall or office. Let a lady pass first always, unleys she asks you to precede her. In the parlour stand still till every lady in the room is seated, also older people. Rise if a lady comes in after you are seated, and stand till she takes a seat. Look people straight in the face when speaking or being spoken to. Let ladies pass through a door first, standing aside for them. In the dining-room take your seat after ladies and elders. Never play with knife, fork, or spoon. Do not take your napkin in a bunch in your hand. Eat as fast or as slow as o.hers, and finish the course when they do. Rise when ladies leave the room, and standstill till they are out. If all go out to_ether. gentlemen stand by the door till ladies pass. Special rules for the mouth are that all noise in eating and smacking of the lips should be avoided. Cover the mouth with hand or napkin when obliged to remove anything from it. Use your handkerchief unob- trusively always. Always knock at any private room door.

div.head: HINDOO GAMBLING STORY,
div.p: A HINDOO GAMBLING STORY,

Mr. Wheeler, in his "History of India from the Earliest Ages," gives a most graphic account of a Hindoo legend of two Rajahs playing for days sur- rounded by all the pomp and splendour of their barbaric courts, until one of them not only lost all he possessed, but sold himself, his wives, and his children as slaves to the winner. The two Rajahs, seated on thrones of State, at down and began their gambling duel. Yudhisthira was such a constant loser that there is no doubt his opponent. Sakuni, had "something up his sleeves," as the sharps have it. He first lost a beautiful pearl; next a thousand bags, each containing a thousand pieces of geld; next a piece of gold so pure that it was soft as wax; and so on, until last of all he staked his brothers, his wives, and himself, and lost the lot. This was a pretty square gamble, and it ended by his favourite wife, Draupadi, letting down her back hair, which was very long and black, and, adopting the prophetic vein, vowing that her hair should remain dishevelled from that day until Bhima, a friend of hers, had slain the winner and drunk his blood. The avenging battle which followed gave Bhima his opportunity, and when he had struck down his adversary with a terrible blow of his mace, he cut off his head, and holding his two hands to catch the blood, drank it off, crying out, "Ho, ho. Never did I taste anything in this world so sweet as this blood." This was doing the thing in true Eastern fashion. Women being marketable commodities in those days, it was no uncommon thing for them to form the gambler's stake as the most valuable chattel he possessed.

div.head: PRIDE OF ANCESTRY.
div.p: PRIDE OF ANCESTRY.

An anecdote is told of Mr. Roger of Werndee, rn Slonmouthshire, which exhibits the pride of an- cestry in a striking point of view. His house was In such a state of dilapidation, that the proprietor was in a danger of perishing under the ruins of the ancient mansion, which he venerated even in decay. A stranger, whom he accidentally met at the foot of the Skyrrd, made various inquiries respecting the country, the prospects, and the neighbouring bouses, and, among others, asked, "Whose is this antique mansion before us?' That, sir, is Wern- dee, a very ancient house; for out of it came the Earls of Pembroke of the first lilts, and the Earle of Pembroke of the second line; the Lords Her- berts of Cherbury, the Herberts of Coldbrook, Ramsay, Cardiff, and York; the Morgans of Acton; the Earl of Hunsdon ; the houses of Ircrowm and Lanarth, and all the Powells. Out of this house also, by the female line, came the Duke of Beau- fort.' And pray, sir, who lives there now?' I do, sir." Then pardon me, and accept a piece of advice: come out of it yourself, or you'll soon be buried in the ruins of it.'

div.head: MURDER WILL OUT.
div.p: MURDER WILL OUT.

I remember," says Lord Eldon, "in one ease "there I was counsel, for a long time the evidence did not appear to touch the prisoner at all, and he looked about him with the most perfect unconcern, seeming to think himself quite safe. At last the surgeon was called, who stated deceased had been killed by a shot, a gunshot in the head; and he produced the matter, hair, and stuff cut from and taken out of the wound. It was all hardened with blood. A basin of warm water was brought into court, and as the blood was gradually softened a piece of printed paper appeared—the wadding of the gun—which proved to be the half of a ballad. The other half had been found in the man's pocket when he was taken. He was hanged. "I remember another man taken up twelve years after the deed. He had made his escape, and though every search was made he could not be found. Twelve years afterwards the brother of the murdered man was at Liverpool in a public-house. He fell asleep, and was awoke by some one picking his pocket. He started, exclaiming, Good God 1 ;be man that killed my brother twelve years ago Assistance came to him, the man was tried, and condemned."

div.head: FAMOUS PIE IN THE NURSERY
div.p: THE FAMOUS PIE IN THE NURSERY
RHYME.

"Sing a song of Sixpence" is a favourite nursery thyme; but every child who knows it probably thinks it a rhyme, and nothing more. It has a meaning, however, of a very beautiful kind, and I am sure you will be delighted with it. The twenty- four blackbirds are said to represent the twenty- four hours of a day. The bottom of the pie is sup- posed to be the world, and the top crust the sky. When the pie opens day breaks, and the birds began to sing; and then such a sight becomes a "dainty dish t set before the king." The king counting money in his chamber is the sun, and the golden coins he so lovingly.handles are golden sunbeams. The spun in her parlour is the moon; and, of course, the honey represents moonlight. The busy maid in the garden is the peep of day, the clothes which she is hanging out are clouds, and the blackbird that takes such a liberty with her nose is the sunset. And thus in the homely and prosaic figure of a pie we have a representation of the whole day.

div.head: Ettters to the Obitor.
div.p: Ettters to the Obitor.
GRAPPENHALL AND THE HIGHWAY AUTHORITI S.

Hir,—l presume there is such a person as the Surveyor of Highways for the district. Who he is, where he lives, or how he spends his time is best known to himself. That there is such a thing as a highway rate, levied twice during the year, is a fact with which the ratepayers are well acquainted. And many of us who are regularly called upon for our highway rates have not so much as a wheelbarrow with which to damage the roads, and it is evident we are simply paying our rates to keep the roads for the use of others. Personally, I would not complain if we could move about the parish with any degree of comfort on the footpaths. If the Surveyor will please consult his map, he may see that there is such a place as Bra.dshawe-lane,and any resident in the village will, I am sure, inform the gentleman where he may find it. Time was, some four years ago, when the Ship Canal Co. did a little in the way of repair- ing it, but I should think that very little work,had been done on it since that time. 're say that it is simply dis- graceful is using mild language. Perchance it is not fre- quented by members of the County Council, or the way- warden or the elite of the district ; but it is a regular and frequent resort of a great number of ratepayers in the parish, and as such we demand to know why this road is so sadly neglected, and at the next Vestry some- thing will be said about the matter. Theo, too, there are those beastly pebbles on the foot- path, Warrington side of the Dog and Dart. Why are those remnants of heathenism and barbarity allowed to remain ? Few pedestrians think of walking on them : they simply step on to the highway to escape the torture. Then there is the miniature lake by Turner's farm, near Mr. Percy Davies's, where a three inch pipe is expected to do the work of a nine inch ; the result is that when there is rain the road is next to impassable, and when there is frost there is a sheet of ice. That the matters referred to require immediate attention is the opinion of others beside

div.head: OFFICIAL STATSAIENTS.
div.p: OFFICIAL STATSAIENTS.

Sir,—So the Warringtonians are in their turn being treated to some of those miraculous official deliverances, which are commonly printed and widely circulated, at the cost of the ratepayers, when smallpox is about ! The latest literary curiosity of the kind which I have seen purports to be issued " By order of the Heath Commit- tee, and signed John 11. Gernall, medical officer of health." The Warringtonians are sapiently informed in this typical document, that the " enemy " (smallpox) is

" for the time being " (note the qualification) "strenu- ously and successfully with.stood by means of vaccina- tion." " Not a single person re-vaccinated in time," we are told" has taken the disease." "In time," moans of °muse the usual heads I win, tails you lose; because all re-vaccinated persons attacked would obviously be classed as not having been operated upon "in time !" The thing is transparent, and there is a fine commentary on it in the official report of the Health of the (Royal) Navy for 1891, in which we find recorded 17 cases of smallpox in that place last year, with 34 cases of " chicken pox "—the latter probably (vide the late Sir Thomas Watson, president, Royal College of Physicians) cases of vaccinated smallpox. Some of these acknow- ledged smallpox cases occurred in a ship whose people bad been vaccinated within a few months of the out- break ! As to the statements that " the unvaccinated and the insufficiently vaccinated have had severer forms of smallpox " with other evils, similar statements where they have been tested, notably so at Leeds, Black. burn, %%est Ham, and only lately at Birmingham by General Phelps, have been shown to be utterly untrust- worthy. And what word can adequately describe the Warrington Health Committee's statement that vaccina- tion" would have prevented all the trouble," knowing as they ought that revaccination does not exempt our revaccinated soldiers and sailors from the disease ? In 1889 our troops in Egypt suffered 1,750 times more from smallpox than did in that year the population of Eng- land. And they speak of vaccination as a " trivial oper- ation." In every text book on the subject which I have seen, in all official directions to public vaccinators, &c., the exact contrary is explicitly stated, or implied. Have the Health Committee ever read the Imperial German Commission Report on vaccination (1884) ? Or the Makuna Committee's " Transactions" Part 1 (1883) ? Have they ever heard of Professor Crookshank's and D. I C.Creighton's recent works? and do they Snow anything of the late Mr. W. White's "Story of a great Delusion ?" Apparently all these things are Greek to them, and hence we see this body in strong contrast to their brethren at Leicester, sending forth wild and absurd statements, which in the end can only result in covering their authors with ridicule. Warrington in this matter is living in the 18th century.—Yours .1. 11. 14 Dec. 1892.

div.head: LAST SHOT FROM A BORROWED BLUNDERBUSS. Sir,—Did I seek to snatch cheap victory from small op-
div.p: THE LAST SHOT FROM A BORROWED BLUNDERBUSS. Sir,—Did I seek to snatch cheap victory from small op-

ponents, I might raise the shout of triumph, and call your readers' attention to the way in which our "Learner" • retires from the contest, snarling with tail depressed,but with a parting salute from his borrowed blunderbuss. It would be easy to show that this too backward "Learner," like the naughty boy, is good only at "calling names." But I very much prefer to attempt to draw good from our correspondent rather than perpetuate rancorous evil. I quite expect many to differ from me in my presentation of things as they strike me ; in doing so let them only give a reason for their dissidence, and I shall have no com- plaint to make.

The essential features of this correspondence are Ag- nosticism and Evolution. My contention is,that Agnos- ticism is, in the present stage of human knowledge, the bourne and final destination of all consistent and con- tinuouS reasoning on the subject. As to evolution, it is the only rational explanation of the appearance of things around us ; its alternative, specific creation, being now relegated tothe limbo of detected delusion. No one,un- prepared with a sound alternative explanation of natural phenomena, can reasonably reject evolution. But let it be noted that I spoke of consistent and continuous rea- soning on the subject. It is the want of this continuous and consistent reasoning that makes the world so full of other than Agnostics and Evolutionists. When men mount the Car of Logic,it should be with the full determination to go with it whithersoever and as far as ever it will carry them. Instead of this,they use it—if used at ali— as they would a railway, to take them where they wish off, and allow the conveyance to to go, when they drop go on without them.. New,logic is like the ever-progres- sive steam leg of Miss Kilmanseg ; when once started it carries its owner (or present occupier), nolens tolens,' whithersoever it will, until the motive power is spent. The denominations affort. excellent examples of this ratiocinative suicide by jumping from the onward- moving vehicle of rational thought. From Roman Catholicism through Anglicanism anil Unitarianism up to Agnosticism, we have a fine gradation illustrating the "go as you will "in place of the" go as you ought " mode of logical conveyance. All these fprens of religious thought have been in advance of their times. They have each one of them being the more or less logical termini of their Periods. To change the metaphor, each by standing upon the ratiocinative ruins of its prede- cessor has got a better view and more extended hori- zon. Greekism and Romanism are the negation of religious thought ; Unitarianism is the acme of Christion reli- gions thought. But while the latter sect claim to be the summit of religious thought, they have but dropped from the car at a convenient halting place. The vehicle of thought is still moving and has left them to die, de- nominationally, where their parents or guardians placed them. This essentially human feature of sticking where our early training left us is no virtue, but merely the result of an instinctive attachment to the habitual.

Now where, among all the sects, our inchoate friend " A Learner may be I know not, but certain it is that he, like the small-beer toper an "get no furrarder." Nor can we wonder at this, remembering the astound- ing specimenc cf unreasoning with which be has favoured us. To my thinking" A Learner "is to some extent a type of the times. We are in a state of transition. The

div.head: NEMO.
div.p: NEMO.
RUN CORN SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.
RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.

It is too commonly supposed that in Board Schools no religion is taught, that the Scriptures are a sealed book to the young people who are receiving their education in such institutions. Undoubtedly, the advocates of Denominational ' education are to a great extend the cause of this erroneous belief because of the prominence they give to their claim to teach children in their schools religious doctrines, and the manner in which they ignore alto- gether, or very curtly refer to, the fact that religious teaching also finds a place in most, if not all of the Board Schools of the country. The cry of a" Godless education" which is sometimes se powerfully used to influence votes at an election time has no foundation in fact. There certainly is a material difference between the denominational and the School Board system of religious education. In the former case the scriptures are taught as interpreted by the creed or catechism of the sect which controls the school, and in the latter case the instruction is free from all sectarisn differences, or prejudices, and is so broad and pure that no parent who believes in a God or a here- after need be afraid of any heresy being learned there, or of any doctrine being inculcated which is-contrary to the faith professed by lather or dottier. Take for instance our own Board Schools in Runcorn. The schemes of religious instruction in force there, is exactly similar to that which pertains under.the Man- chester School Board. There is a book of specially selected hymns, and we quote the first verse of one for infants The busy day is nearly dune. The dark, still night is coming on; I pray Almighty God to keep His care around me while I sleep. The plan of instruction requires that the infants shall " learn by heart " six hymns, three moral songs, the " Alphabet of texts," the Lord's Prayer, the fifth com- mandment, and morning and evening prayer. The first standar3 have to -learn in addition, the ten com- mandments, and forty verses of Scripture (set out from the New Testament. Those in standards two and three have to learn four Psalms and four parables from the Gospel of St. Luke. In the higher standards the children have to learn by heart the Lord's prayer and ten commandments, St. John xv, or Ist Cor. xi, or Ephesians vi; six hymns and morning and evening prayer. The scholars are besides instructed in -Scrip- ture history, are given examples from Holy Scrip- ture of the observance or breach of the Ten Command- meats ; proof of the Ten Commandments by texts from the New T,stament ; and the petitions of the Lord's prayer exemplified by other passages from scripture. The Alphabet of Texts, is a series of 28 texts, the initial letters of the texts making the alphabet. The first five read.
A soft answer turneth away wrath ; but grievous words stir up anger. Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the Law of Christ.
Children obey your parents in the Lord ; for this is tight. Depart from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it.

Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil, avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it and pass away. The morning prayer, in which there are appropriate responses for the children, concludes : " Bless,o Lord,in mercy all our dear parents,relations. teachers, schoolfellows, and friends, may we be kind one to another, and so live together in this life that in the world to come we may have life everlasting. We ask all in the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, who hath taught us when we pray to say "—Then the echolars re- peat the Lord's prayer. 'rho evening prayer includes the following :-0 Heavenly/Father, we thank Thee for all Thy mercies during Guts day, and all our lives hitherte ; we bless Thee for oar food and clothing, cur health and strength our kind friends and teachers,and all the benefits of Thy I hand, but above all for Thy holy word and the know- ledge of Thy grace and mercy in our Saviour, Jesus Christ. May we praise Thee both with our lips and in our livea,and serve Thee day by day.—The scholars res- ponded with the words" Hear us, good Lord." '2,ould a parent wish for better instruction in religion for his children than that sketched above, in a school which is most assuredly approved and supported by the Government of the country as an institution for impart- ing knowledge ia secular subjects? But the champions of denominationalism do claim more. They claim that they shall be allowed to use money obtained from the taxes of the country for the purpose of inculating their own peculiar dogmas or doctrines,: into children sent to their schools to receive instruction in what is commonly known as the three r's. The denominational schools are practically entirely supported by public money, for without it they would not exist a single day, and yet the public have no voice whatever in ;their management. Through the exigences of the situation many children in Runcorn are sent to a denominational schools,where they I are taught a religious faith opposite to that which is held by the parents and also contrary to what the children themselves receive on the Sabbath. It would be inter eating to know what proportion of the children attending the National Day Schools attend there on the sabbath. Would the Vicar kindly vouchsafe us the information ? We have it on what may truly be called reliable authority that a considerable proportion of the scholars are not found within the walls of the schools on the Sabbatk. e A religious census of school going childrea would yield some surprising results. It is well known that children of other denomiaations are, for instance, attending the National Schools, probably because there is not accom- modation in the ratepayers' own schools, and the parents are being taxed by school pence to maintain a 1 system of which they do not approve. It cannot be too widely known that every parent, no matter what his means, has a right to free education, and he may demand it from the National School, the Holy Trinity School, the Wesleyan School,or the Catholic School and if the managers of these several schools refuse to provide it, a complaint to the Educe- tion_Department will soon bring about a remedy. One admirable means for bringing about universal free edu- cation in Runcorn, would be to return as members of the School Board on the 30th of the present month gentlemen who have advocated and will advocate free education, and who will see that as far as possible it is obtained under the present laws. It is true that the Board Schools are now free, but they were declared free not with the aid, but in spite of the denominationalists, on the present Board. Those who were behind the scenes can describe what pressure was necessary before the Board Schools were declared free.

The question of denominational education has been described by the Vicar as a question of religious liberty. Would not license have been a better word ? Why should any sect, no matter what it be, receive hund- reds of pounds of the nation's money yearly, to aid in teaching its particular dogmas. Even in these days one has to look very closely for religious liberty or religious fairness. At Moulton, the Bishop of Chester sought to prevent the establishment of a School Board, by induc- ing the ratepayers to build a school in which they should have an equal share of the management, but, when the crucial, point came, the impartial committee of management was to consist of the Vicar of the parish,as chairman, three of his nominees and three gentlemen elected by the parents of the scholars. In Ditton township the Nonconformists were induced to join with the Church party in an endeavour to raise £eoo towards enlarging the church school of that place, by the promise that they should be represented on the Committee of management. At the outset of the work one of the Nonconformists, evidently more wide awake than his fellows, asked to see the deed of the school. It then appeared that no person unless a member of the Church of England, could be allowed to have a voice in the management of the school. It is small wonder therefore that the Noncon- formists withdrew and are prepared to support a Board School where there is religious liberty-, and no sectarian prejudice existing. In these two examples one searches in vain for common fairness. We have no persoaal quarrel with the Vicar of Runcorn, or with the Church party as a whole, but in the interest of the town, and in the in- terest of education, we contend that it is better that there should be a School Board, composed of men who are believers in the School Board system and who will work for its extension as circumstances de- mand ; and not of men who view School Boards and their work with ill-concealed aversion, and who would retard their growth in order that their own sectarian establishments may progress unchecked. A majority of Denominationalists on a School Board acts simply as a drag on the coach of educational progress—it means not stagnation but worse—retrogression. Four o'clock on Monday next, the 19th inst., is the last hour in which gentlemen can be nominated as can- didates for the School Board, and the ratepayers ought to see to it that a sufficient number of gentlemen of pro- gressive and unsectarian ideas are nominated and sup- ported at the poll. Withtjrawals may be made up to the 21st,the list of candidates will be published on the 23rd, and the election will take place on Friday, the 30th inst.
A train of empty carriages at Craigendoran, on the North British Railway took fire on Thursday, and four new carriages were consumed. Helensburgh and Glas- gow traffic was disarranged.
