div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 17, 1891 • NOTES ON GAMES AND ARUNDEL CASTLE. j MARRIAGE OF DR. TOISEY. ATHLETICS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 17, 1891 • NOTES ON GAMES AND ARUNDEL CASTLE. j MARRIAGE OF DR. TOISEY. ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

Most certainly the sparsity of sporting delectation about Warrington is becoming a little too common, not to say distressing. We had reconciled ourselves to the non-appearance of the first team on Saturday, and our hopes were buoyed with the announcement that the "A" teanr would give us a performance on the ground at Wildervool. But the day before the match, there came a fall—nay, two falls—there was the fall cf the snow and the consequent fall of our spirits. Then th 6 frost set in, and on Saturday the ground at Wilderspool bore more resemblance to a skating rink than anght else.

_ Football Wa.9 impossible and as the A team were not aware that the Manchester Rangers had got skates,they did not invite them down. Consequently a great num- ber of persons,who went down to the field to seek delec- tations, didn't find it. Neither did they get their money back; but this is chieflybecause they did not tender any.

At a meeting connected with the Warrington Football Club, on Saturday night, Mr. Pemberton read a letter from an anonymous correspondent, in which was en- closed 30s. for the benefit of the club. After a little dis- cussion, it was decided to hand the money over to the treasurer, juct to keep his "hand in," in the way of keeping accounts.

Since then I have heard that the club, now that their treasurer is not too busy in dealing with "gate" money, would not refuse to gratify any other gentlemen who could discoversome little pleasure in sending anony- mous letters and presents to them. They have a greater preference for the presents, however ; and besides, tiat.y like to indulge in a little fun when they are not busy at Wilderspool. They don't mind how many times they go to the Post Moe to change P.O.'s. It's all in fun.

A certain juailor team in town who had intended to play on Saturday„,but, who were prevented by the frost, spent all their peat up energies and money,on a "feed." It was held at a ,certain hostelry in town. From a whisper which I received from a little oherub, it seems all went as merry as the bells for a time. n. mean contained amongst other things "tinned lobster." While this was being demolished a discussion cropped up res- pecting the deaths which had been caused by tinned fish. Whilst this was going on one of the members, who is reputed to be a humourist, was seen to grow very agitated, then writhe and wriggle in his chair, and finally fall to the floor.

" What's the matter IP— ?" was the anxious query of everyone. P tremblingly scrambled yo his seat and said he had been overcome by a terrible fart about tinned lobster which he had just remembered. The canned food he said, had caused some thousands of deaths this year. And juer. when the party began to exchange anxious looke,lie said he remembered that the number of deaths caused would probablybs repeated next year—they were the death of the lobsters which had been tinned Now that was a very clever jok e for a junior club footballer.
As there doesn't appear to be any more Warrington football items we wilt turn to the" goings on "of con- temporary teams. The results of the Lancashire Cup Competition are as follows :

For. Agst. Pld. Won. Lost. Dm. G.T. G.T. Pte. Swinton 6 5 . . 1 . 7 9 ... 1 2 ...11 St. Helens liecreation 6 ... 5 ... 1 ... 0 ... 8 10... 2 3 ...10 Warrington Mean 6 . 3 . 2 . 1 . 2 3 ... 3 3 ... 7 Rochdale Hornets Salford
FyWesley Oldham Broughton Rangers Broaghton 9 . 1 . 6 . 2 .. 3 2 ... 712 ... 4

On Saturday Swinton meet St. Helens Recreation, at Swinton. The Recs are expected to give their oppo- nents a warm gamo. And when it is taken into consideration that the !secs have beaten Tyldealey, Oldham, and Salford, we imagine the Swintonians will not have to waste any time in winking " the other eye" at their laurels. St. Helens have certainly done well this season, and if Warrington don't, by some stroke of luck come away with the cup, the Recs are likely to do it.

In consequence of having to cancel the match with Warrington, on Saturday, the Manchester Rangers have agreed to meet Salford. This fixture takes place at Fat- lowfield, and Is expected to draw a large "gate."

The ten games in the last round of the qualifying ties for the English Cup have been brought to a satisfactory conclusion,and it can hardly be said that there was any- thing in the nature of a big surprise. Only in one case was extra time required, and here Northwlch Victoria came out victors over Liverpool Caledonians. The tie was played at Liverpool, and the success of the Victoria was largely due to the excellent goalkeeping of Penning- ton, the Rovers' cast-off. Had it not been for his safety the Caledonians must have won. The victory was won by three goals to two.

Houghton,of Runcorti,is in a fair way for International honours once more. He is on his test now, and we hope that at Richmond, next Saturday,he will perform a little better than he did last season in the match between Eng- land and Ireland. In that match, however, there was no doubt that Houghton was completely " off colour," not through incapacity, but through indisposition. By the way I was reading the other day of the results of the annual meeting of several large Scottish teams. The Third Lanark, the Celtic,and Glasgow Rangers have all large liabilities on hand, the causes of which have been described more or less in a misty—Scotch misty —way. The Celtic have a debt of over £2,000.

A correspondent writes with regard to Association football in Warrington, as follows :—" It will no doubt have been noticed by many of your readers that the game is rapidly gaining popularity, and that several good clubs are cropping up in the town. Warrington are certainly the senior club, and it is lamentable when it is considered that they have barely enough funds to keep themselves as they should be with a good field. There is an opportunity for some benevolent gentleman to step forward, and do the necessary. Next year Everton will visit Warrington and play a week day match with a picked team from the district, and it is to be hoped that the people will recognise that there is enough talent in Warrington to establish a club which will bring credit to the good old town."

In our Almanac illustration this year we present our readers with a view of Arundel Castle, one of the most ancient strongholds and feudal courts in England, the seat a the illustrious Ifowards, Earls of Arundel and Dukes of Norfolk.

The castle of Arundel, in Sussex, is one of the old- est fortresses in England, and perhaps no feudal stronghold has clustered around it so many historical and legendary associations. It was a Royal fortress in Saxon times, and its origin is so remote as to have been ascribed to Bevis of Hampton, one of the misty heroes whose prowess is sung by the medieval romancer. History has no record of him; but tradition, with that circumstantiality which is Ickmacteristic of legendary lore, has much to say of hie life and doings. He is described iu the early romance as

Bevis of rennun, The Right Heir of Southarnptoun. Like :meat legendary heroes, Syr Bevis was of gigantic stature ; and his sword, six feet long, is said to be still preserved at Arundel Castle. The old baronial seat has undergone many modifications and renovations as the centuries have rolled on., each 'successive owner having vied with his predec- essor in embellishing it.

After the battle- of Hastings it was granted to Roger.de Montgomery by William the Conqueror, along with the Earldoral of Arundel and Shrews- bury. On the death of its warlike owner, which took place in July, 10144, at the Abbey of Shrews- bury, whither he had retired on feeling his end approaching, his son Ilszgbassumed possession of the earldom, and appropriately ended a life of turmoiland fighting upon the battlefield. He was shot through the brain with an arrow at Anglesea, in resisting an invasion of the King of Norway. The earldom passed to hie brother Robert, but all the poaseesions were subsequently forfeited to Henry I„ and the Castle became an appanage of the Crown. aenry dowered his second Queen, Adeliza, with these,possessions,ond on his death, by a second marriage, they came to William d'Albini, Loid of Butkenhara, in Norfolk. From the Albinis the earl- dom passed to the Fitzalane, who were also of Norman origin, their ancestors having fought side by side at Hastings. It would. be tedious to follow the genealogical stream throuli its many meander- ings down to the present time. It will suffice to say that Philip Howard, sou of Mary, Duchess of Norfolk, one of the sisters of the fourth earl, was invested with the title of Arundel in 1531. Eight years later, the eerl was attainted, and the estates were forfeited, to the Crown; but.in 1604 they were restored to Philip's son Thomas byKing James, and henceforward the liowarde have enjoyed uuinter- ruptedly the Amaral possessions. The Castle has been the scene of many an historic event, aril its owners—who, it may be said in passing, are Earls of Arundel by the simple right of ownership—played a prominent part on the his- torical stage. Here lived William d'Albini, one of the barons who signeiL Magna Charts.; and here, exactly six hundred years after this solemn ratifi- cation of English liberties—on the 111th of June, 1815,the anniversary of the great meeting of barons at Runnymede—a memorable feast took place. The Barons' Hall, ow of the finest banqueting rooms in the country, and which was designed to .commemo- rate the triumph of the barons over King John, was thrown open on that date, and was the acene of a gorgeous festival. Dr. Beattie, in "The Castles and Abbeys of Englannd," thus described this bril- liant spectacle :—" For the joyful celebration of this glorious epoch in the old baronial style, a brilliant assembly of rank and title had arrived from various parts of the country, among whom were twenty-two representatives of the ancient Howards. Complete suits of armour, in which the ancient chivalry of England had gathered the spoils of victory, some at Agincourt, others at Cressy, were arranged in military order around the walls. Swords, that by the evidence on their blades had 'done the State some service' helmets that had I been worn by the Howards at Flodden or by j • Belted Will' in some of the border forays ; chain and scale armour; spears and lances that had often gleamed in strife and tournament—all the imple- ments of ancient warfare, from the thick iron jcasque of the archer to the elaborately and richly gilded harness of the baron, were all reburnished and brought into unexpected light for this occasion. Nothing, in fact, was omitted thatcould increase the interest by giving an air of striking reality to the scene. If the spirits of the ancient barons could have looked down upon the hall in this hour of gorgeous festivity, they would have rejoiced to see what a bright inheritance their patriotic struggles had bequeathed, and have felt that they had become, indeed, immortal in the hearts of their descendants." It was at Arundel Castle that the Empress Matilda, mother of Henry 11., lodged when she landed in England in 1139. Stephen, the usurper, laid siege to the place, but Matilda, through the good generalship of Albini, succeeded in getting to Bristol and escaping to Normandy. Henry 11. when he came to the throne, showed his appreela- tion of the services just rendered to his mother, by confirming to Albini and his heirs for ever the bon- ' our and Castle of Arundel. Traditien assigns a small chamber over the inner gateway as the sleep- ing room of Matilda, and a worm-eaten walnut bedstead is preserved as the couch whereon lay the daughter of a King, the wife of an Emperor, and the mother of a King. William de Albini, above referred to, enjoys the rare distinction in a warlike community of having prevented a war by arbitra- tion. When Henry Plantagenet landed in England ' to assert his rights to the throne, Stephen went forth to meet him. The two forces were drawn up in line of battle, and Stephen while reconnoitring, fell off his horse three times in succession. The adroit Earl of Arundel, who was near him, encour- aged the notion that this was an unfavourable omen. Being a " bold and eloquent man," says the historian, he urged Stephen to arrange for peace, land went so far as to advise Stephen that the claim of Duke Henry was just. Stephen and Henry there- upon met in front of the two armies, and a recon- ciliation was effected and a treaty made, by which Stephen accepted the young Plantagenet as his successor.

Arundel Castle has been the abode or visiting place of other regal personages besides Matilda, among them being Alfred the Great—who in his will bequtaths Arundel along with other demesnes to his brother's son. Harold is also said to have lived here, and William Rufus celebrated tile least of Easter within its walls. Edward 1. in 1302 re- sided at the Castle for a short time. Caraccioli says, "So great was the hereditary fame of Arundel Castle, and so high its prerogative, that Queen Adeliza's brother, Joceline of Lorraine, though a lineal descendant of Charlemagne, felt himself honoured in being nominated to the title of its Castellan."

The Castle has undergone many sieges, and may be said to have ceased being the theatre of tur- moil and strife at the close of the Civil Wars. It was garrisoned at this time by the Parliament, but was captured by the Royalists in 1643,and subsequently re-taken and dismantled as a place of defence. Origi- nally the walls enclosed an area of 950 feet in length and 250 feet in width. In the centre was the Keep, now overgrown with ivy, and the reeort of owls and bats. It stands on an artificial mound, and is surrounded by trees and verdure. It is an exceedingly picturesque object in the landscape. The restoration of the Castle was commenced in 178 G by the then Duke of Norfolk, and was con- tinued by him till 1815, and in this work, though left incomplete by the noble proprietor, no less a sum than six hundred thousand pounds was expended. On the Grand Entrance, the Baron's Hall, the Library, the Great Drawing-room, and the Dining-room—formed out of the ancient family chapel—the highest skill of the architect has been expended, and the sculptor and painter have en- riched the interiors with some of the noblest speci- mens of their art.

-- On Wednesday, the 7th December, Mr. Clement Bernard Voisey,M.D. (London),F.R.C.S., and D.P.H. (Cantab), eldest son of Mr. Lewis Voisey, of War- riingtAn; urai "tharriell -arlfbchester, to Miss Edith Somerville Burns, second daughter of Dr. Burns, R.N.and that city. The bride,who was given away by her father, wore .a tasteful and becoming close-fitting costume of fawn cloth, trimmed with narrow beaver fur, therbodice of the dress having a yoke of white brocade. She wore a !fawn felt hat trimmed with feathers to match, and carried a lovely bouquet of ,britial flowers. She was at- tended by two bridesmaids, Miss Mary Burns and Miss Gertrude Voisey, who wore very pretty cos- tiame.s of pink cloth trimmed with green shot velvet and pink silk sashes, and large white felt hats trimmed with feathers and velvet. They each carried a large bouquet of white and ,pink flowers, mad wore gold bangles, the gift of the 'bridegroom. The bridegroom was assisted by Mr. Guy'Reynolds, of Warrington. At the conclusion of the service the notes of the Wedding Marcia burst forth from the organ, and the church bells rang out a merry peal. After leaving the church the bridal party and wedding guests drove to Dr. Burns's house at Borstal, and later in the afternoon the bride and bridegroom left for Brighton for the honeymoon. Among the invited guests to the "At Home" besides the fathers and mother of the bride and bridegroom were—Dr. and Mrs. Buchanan (sister of the bride), Dr. Albert W'. Burns (brother), Mr. Lotlis Yoisey, (brother of the bridegroom). Dr..a.nd Mrs.. Boucher,Dr.and Mrs. Beaumont, Capt.and Mrs. Christie, Dr. and Mrs. Walker, Rev. C.E. Crellin, Rev., Mrs., and the Misses Duke. Mr. and the Misses Wickham, Mr. and Mrs. I. Winch, Rev. and Mrs. A. J. Thorndike, Dr. and Miss Maguire, Mr. and Mrs. Sturdie, Dr. and Mrs.Tanna- hill, Mrs. S. Reynolds (Warrington), Mrs. and the Misses Packham, Col., Mrs., and Miss Plummer, Mr. and Mrs. Padwick, Dr. and the Misses Packman, Dr. Dakin (London), Dr. A. Fackman, Dr. Hutchinson (London),

The following is a list of the wedding presents, so me of which were very handsome. Bridegroom to Bride, diamond and moonstozenbangle. Bride's father, sliver canteen, Miss Mary Burns, carriage repeater clock. Dr. Albert Burns, silver biscuit boa. Dr. and Mrs. W. Buchanan. silver fish carvers. Mrs. soisey, and Household Furraure. A LECTURE ON PALESTINE BY MR.

GARINETT. At the Y.M.C.A., Friars Green, on Thurday night, Mr. Robert Garnett gave a lecture upon his visit to Palestine. The chair was taken by the Rev. T. Reed, who drew the attention of the audience to the present attention which Palestine was drawing upon itself in consequence of the condition of the Jews, and a scheme which was being promul- gated for the purpose of reinstating the Jews in their native country.—The Lecturer prefaced his descrip- tion with a few general historical and geographical facts. He then proceeded to describe the city and surroundings of Jaffa or Joppa, which stands on a prominence out of the sea. Amongst other features of the city he mentioned the house of Simon the Tanner. He and his party had stood on the roof of the house where the mar- vellous vision was said to have appeared. Although many sites had been selected as the correct place on which Simon's house stood, Dean Stanley had adduced such facts as to almost undeniably prove the identity of the house. On the way to Jerusalem the lecturer said the scenery was of a most magnificent character. The lepers outside the gates of Jerusalem were described. The Speaker said the distorted faces', decaying hands and feet and limbs of those unfortunate people were most repulsive, and made it difficult for a European to believe that they were human beings. They were rigorously excluded from the city, and were pro- vided with settlements on one side of the valley of Jehoshaphat near En Rogel. In Jerusalem the customs of the people were quaint and biblical, and he was on many occasions impressed by the manner of salutation which existed between men. When they met their salutation and bows, and gesticulations occupied many minutes. And it was when observing this that the speaker could for the first time realise the possible meaning which Christ had in bidding his deciples " salute ye no man by the way." (Laughter.) Reaching Bethel the lecturer said ore particular thing which struck him often was the method of grinding corn. This was done by two women crushing corn be- tween two large stones. Women were always employed at this or other equally arduous work—they were little better than slaves to the male sex.—The lecture was well illustrated with limelight views, and after its con- clusion the lecturer was accorded a hearty vote of thanks.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

Deep down into the depths of hot Dot pies did the Cycling Club members obtrude their spoons—not the silver ones—on Tuesday night. They met at a hot pot supper and a" smoker," which went off in fine style under the direction of their jovial and respected chair- man, Mr. Thomas Morris. About the most enjoyable part of the proceeding was a humorous sketch given by Mr. Percy Davies. It concerned a gentleman named Shaw, who lived at Market Gate four hundred years ago, about which time, according to Mr. Davies's ren- dition, the Central Station was in good working order. Mr. Davies had to tell of some very funny things about Mr. Shaw's saw, which appeared to be the only one in the country at the time. The Central Station, indeed, was the one "taking " point of the sketch.

Speaking of the Cycling Club by the way reminds me that the members are about to play off a billiard handi- cap at the Norton Arms, and amongst the prizes are three presented by Mr. T. Morris, Mr. P. Davies, and Mr. J. Sampoon.

"PLEASANT SUNDAY AFTERNOONS FOR. MEN." FORMATION OF A WARRINGTON SOCIETY. An attempt is being made to form in Warrington a Pleasant Sunday Afternoon class for men. If the Class is formed, which it is almost certain to be, it will form a branch of what is now a national insti- tution, for there are branches in almost every town in the United Kingdom, all of which have been highly successful in their object. The Society was formed about seven years ago, in Derby, by Mr. Reginald Hodder, a well-known philanthropist, and and the lines; which he laid down were that the class should be open only to persons over 18 years of age,that the proceedings of the class should, whilst adhering to things sacred, be made bright and instructive, and serve both as a religious and educative institution to men who could not be dealt with by denominational Sunday Schools. Sectarianism is not introduced into the classes, the chief object of the religious teaching &c., being solely to promote feelings of christian brotherhood amongst the members. The motto is "Brief, Bright, and Brotherly." There are various kinds of mutual improvement and aid societies connected with the classes, and there is a system connected with them for supplying the members with first class literature at small prices. The members are asked to contribute a penny a week, and those doing so who put in twelve attendances out of 13, are presented with a standard work of some kind, usually worth three or four shillings. Ministers of all denominations are invited to address the classes, and the members usually visit, on the Sunday evening, the church of the minister who addresses them in the afternoon. We believe that Mr. Taylor,tho Police Court missionary, first set about organizing the local branch, and as he was connected with Mr. Hodder in forming the first branch at Derby. he is likely to lend some valuable assistance. The Y.M.C.A. rooms will be the meeting place, and it is intended to open the class on the second Sunday in the new year, when Mr. Reginald Ilodder will deliver an inaugural address. Mr. Lunt, of Padgate Lane has consented to become secre- tary, and Mr. Kent of Legh-st. will act as treasurer. A , Committee consisting of Mr. Taylor and others has been formed, and several local ministers have offered to con- tribute their assistance. It is not intended to ask pre- sent Sunday School workers to join. It is said that there are close upon 18,000 members of the Society in England alone.

div.head: BUILDING SOCIETY SCANDAL.
div.p: THE BUILDING SOCIETY SCANDAL.
FURTHER ARRESTS EXPECTED.

Further arrests in connection with the Liberator Spciety are expected. Three warrants were issued from Bow-at. on Saturday last, and only two of them have been executed by the arrest of Hobbs and Wright. The authorities are reticient as to who the third is intended for. It is stated on authority hardly to be questioned, that one of the chief witnesses in the case had been threatened with shooting by a close relative of one of the prisoners. The death is announced of Mr. J. Edmunds, grocer, Port Dinorwic, one of the Welsh agents of the Liberator Society. The deceased, who was highly respected throughout the district, was prostrated with grief when he was informed of the collapse of the society in which many of his friends and acquaintances had invested their money. Mr. Edmunds, who was also an investor, never recovered from the shock, and his sad death is greatly deplored. It is stated that a certain gentleman of Carnarvon is a creditor of the society to the extent of £l,OOO, while there are scores of quarrymen and others residing in the parish of Llanddeinolen whose total investments in the society represent something like £9,000.

div.head: __•._._. PENKETH.
div.p: __•._._. PENKETH.

RETURN OP THE REV. E. S. JACKSON. The people of Penketh and Sankey will doubtless be Riad to hear that the Vicar is now on his way home, and is expected to arrive in a week or two. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. On Wednesday evening last, the weekly meeting was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom. Mr. Wig. field acted as chairman. The meeting took the form of a social concert, songs, readings, &c., being contributed by various friends. The ladies and gentlemen assisting were Misses Fanny and Hilda Garnett, A. Moses, L. Routledge, E. Hobson, and Mabel Garnett. Also Messrs. J. Smith, A. Seed, D. Ellison, R. Posnett. The Rev. J. Gunnell, resi- dent minister, gave some interesting facts as to the commencement and growth of Mutual Improve- ment Societies. Arrangements were also made for the coming conversazione, and committees formed to take charge of the several departments. The meeting closed with. the Doxology. THE VYRNWY WATER SUPPLY. At the fortnightly meeting,of the Vyrnwy Works Committee, held at Liverpool, on Tuesday, at the Municipal Offices, reference was made to the visit paid by members to the Mersey crossing on Satur- day, and it was stated that the works would be en- tirely completed at the end of the present month, by which time, it is thought, the contractors will be in a position to remove their plant. We I understand that at the present time the city is get- ting two million gallons of water from the Vyrnvvy lake, and, that if necessary, Rye millions could be obtained. But in the meantime the committee contemplate providing a supplemental pipe line between Prescot ieservoirs and Liverpool, in order that a much larger supply may be procured.

div.head: "MILLER OF THE DEE " AT THE ROYAL COURT THEATRE, WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE "MILLER OF THE DEE " AT THE ROYAL COURT THEATRE, WARRINGTON.

With the arrival of the Christmas season come the annual entertainments given by the children of most of our public schools. These entertainments formerly consisted of purely vocal or instrumental performances; but during the past two y ears a great advance has been made. And this has been in the direction of operetta, and if we mistake not was first initiated by the Roman Catholic Fathers of the town, and supported by Mr. Corney, bead master of Wrcliffe schools. The perf-qmances last Christmas season were all of an exceptienally clever character, and the public have been looking forward to the inauguration of this season's entertainments with a considerable ameunt of interest. Accordingly when the children of St. Albans' Catholic Schools appeared at the Public Hall on Monday night to submit an original operetta—" The Miller of the Dee "—they were welcomed by an exceedingly large house. The operetta, which has been written by the Rev. Father Craven, of St. Albans' Church, is a very meritorious piece of work and lends still further credit to the composer and his colleagues who have entered so ably upon their work of providing , this special kind of entertainment. The piece consists of three scenes ; it has a combination of opera and panto- mime in its plot, and is exceedingly smart and humorous in its dialogues, especially as many of these have a local bearing. The locale of the piece,of course, is the banks of the river Dee, and the two chief scenes are the Mill and the Castle of the Yellow Dwarf. The latter individual' is a remarkable character,and was well impersonated by Master William Hind. He was a kind of Richard HI but wasn't quite so bloodthirsty ; simply because he was I unwell and had no appetite. He was very ugly also. The only thing his chef could recommend was a strong healthy country man or woman, not over 25 years of age: who had to be plump and be bled to death slowly, after having been "probed " with a silver fruit knife.Theycaptured a woman,Miss MargeryMuffin,an old maid, impersonated by Miss Edith Turner. She thought of a matrimonial catch, and said she was not 25 ; but eventually refused to die as she was over 50 and only good for serving up spare ribs. She goes out to insti- tute a summons against the dwarf for breach of promise, &c. The story goes along pleasantly until a scene arrives where the dwarf, still in quest of human food, makes what is termed aB. line for Billy Peck, the Miller's son. William doesn't fall in with the dwarf's officer, when. on the question of hucnan sacrifice, he said for the benefit of the dwarf, " England expects every man this day to do his duty." William would not do it. So he was taken away to the castle ; eventu- ally rescued, and had the felicitous pleasure of seeing the dwarf sentenced—to be married to Miss Margery Muffin. The two things which were most conspicuous about the piece were the splendid training which the childrens' every action showed, and the artistic arranging of the scenes. The characters who most dis- tinguished themselves were John Feck,the Miller (Master George Browne), Tabitha Pack, his wife (Miss Annie Knight), and Jack, their youngest boy (Miss Annie Burns), Miss Margery Muffin (Miss Edith Turner), and the Yellow Dwarf (Master Wm. Hind). The remainder of the caste consisted of :—Billy, the Fat Boy (Albert Stokes), the Four Milkmaids (Maggie Lawton, Lizzie Cooper, Nelly Mather, Nellie Brophy), Miller's Girls and Peasants (Jane Pemberton, Mary Fagan, Winnie McCey, Nellie Hardman, Flo Turner, Lilly Mather, Maggie Bar- rett, Sarah Costelloe, Mary A.Lee, Maggie Brophy,Jennie Corney,Evelyn Conley, Rebecca Walsh, Mary F. Darton, Milly Pemberton, Annie Stirrup,Katie Jones),Miller's Men (George Darton, Alban Richardson, Joseph Marsh, T. A. Diskin. T. Regan), Lawyer Sharpe (John Vernon), the Cook (James Costellee),Varlet (Walter lA'arren),Sergeant of the Guards (Jno.Cunningham),the Royal Guards (Thos. Devlin, J.Coleman, E.Toole (drummer), Thos Jeffries, A. Walsh,Jos.Murton),Butcher,Jester,and Bailiff (Rt. Lowe The band in attendance was Mr. Caldwell's well-known orchestra band. The Rev. T. I. Craven acted as promp- ter and stage manager, and succeeded very well in both capacities. One of the local hits was worthy of mention. It concerned the medical profession, and was to this effect :

" If you're bad and have the spasams, Then go to Dr. Adams, If you're pale with haggard looks, Then go to Dr. Brooks. If you've measles or smallpox, Then go to Dr. Fox. If Indigestion makes you weary, Of course you go to Dr. Oeary.." and so on, Dr. Spinks being recommended for " kinks," Dr. Peacock for " chincough," and Dr. White when you don't " feel quite right."

div.p: MRS. MA.YBRICK'S HEALTH.

-- The Central News learns that Mrs. Maybrick has so far recovered from her illness, and is making such favourable progress, that the " sick visiting permit," enabling the Baroness de Rogues to visit her daughter in the hospital at Knaphill Convict Prison, has been withdrawn.
THE HEALTH OF SIR ANDREW WALKER. Yesterday morning the bulletin from Gateacre was to the effect that Sir Andrew Walker had passed a bad night; but that otherwise his condition remained the ss,me.

div.head: JUDGE LYNCH.
div.p: JUDGE LYNCH.

NASHVILLE. KENTUCKY, FRIDAY.—A negro assaulted a white girl, Miss Emma O'Brien, on Tuesday,and escaped to the woods. An infuriated mob went in pursuit of him, caught him, and after hanging him to a tree in a churchyard, built a bonfire and cremated the body.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE.

Mr. Gladstone left Ha warden for London yesterday morning, joining the 9-57 train at Chester. The right hon. gentleman was accompanied by Miss Helen Glad- stone. Mr. John Morley met Mr. Gladstone on his arrival at Chester from Sandycroft, and travelled with him to London.
THE WHOLESALE MURDER OF BABIES.

The inquest on the remains of four infants which had been unearthed at Redfern, on the premises occupied by John and Sarah Makin, who already stand committed for trial on the charge of murder in connection with the discovery of numerous other bodies cf infants at various residences occupied by them, wag proceed with at Syd- ney on Thursday. John and Sarah Makin, and two of their daughters, named Florence and Blanche, were brought before the Court on the charge of causing the deaths of these infants. Another daughter of the accused, named Clarice, was called as a witneas, and identified the clothing found on the bodies, while the mothers of two of the babies likewise recognised some of the clothing produced as belonging to their children. The proceedings were interrupted more than once by painful scenes, especially when the girl Clarice was giving evi- dence against her parents and sisters. The female pri- soners displayed great agitation, and all three fainted at different times while the inquest was going on.
CRITICAL ILLNESS OF MR. BLAINE.

Naw• YORK, Thursday. A special despatch from Washington to the " New York Times" says that it is believed that Mr. Blaine is on his death bed. The ma- lady from which he is suffering has assumed a farm which warns the family that a speedy and fatal termina- tion is at hand. The disease recently attacked the lungs and baffles the skill of the physicians. The visit of Dr. Janeway, who was summoned from New York, indicates the anxiety of the family. It was planned to take Mr. Blaine to California, but the physicians declared it dangerous to move him from the h)use. Inquirers at his residence, on Thursday, were told that he was better. The only persons outside of his family who have been permitted to see him since his last seizure have been Cardinal G ibbons, and Father Ducey. Mrs. Damrosch, his daughter, has arrived at the house.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL,

_ Another fatal accident occurred on the Ship Canal works on Wednesday. About seven o'clock in the morn- ing, a man named William Baker, alias William Brown, 54 years of age, better known amongst the fellow-work- men as " Old Billy," was on his way to "No Man's Land," on the Ship Canal works at Runcorn, and while crossing from the new engine shed to the old one he stepped in the way of the locomotive Cadogan, was caught by it, knocked down, and his right lag was out off, the other being badly injured. He was placed on the engine, which started at once for the Ship Canal hospital at Latchford, to which all persons suffering from accidents in the district are conveyed, but the old man had been so badly injured that he died when Moore had been reached.

div.head: WATER GAS.
div.p: WATER GAS.
A .LIVELY _MEETING OF SHAREHOLDERS.

At the general meeting of the Yorkshire and Lanca- shire Water Gas Company at Leeds on Thursday, the proceedings were somewhat exciting. The report., though it mentioned a loss of £BOO in the year's work- ing, was sanguine in tone, the Directurs.expressing the opinion that there was an enormous field for water-gas operations in the country. One of the shareholders, however, was anxious to know if the Board intended to refund the money with which theyhad been speculating. Another shareholder, amid much commotion, thought the Directors hed no right to gamble with the money.. An amendment in favour of rejecting the report and statement of accounts was carried, but the report was ultimately adopted, the Chairman using proxies of greater value. On the question of reappointing auditors a shareholder exclaimed," What do we want with audi- tors? We have nothing to reckon up.'

div.head: PREPARING FOR FOR CHRISTMAS.
div.p: PREPARING FOR FOR CHRISTMAS.

A NEW INGREDIENT FOR THE WASSAIL BOWL._ As usual at the festive season of the year, enormous quantities of spirits are being delivered out of bond for home consumption. The Liverpool Customs " 13111 of Entry "on Wednesday reports as so delivered 8,573 gallons of British spirits, 1,234 gallons of brandy, 7,107 gallons of " imitation rum." This last entry has caused some speculation among the curiously inclined, and it would be interesting to know under what guise this spirit finds its way to the consumer. Under a recent Excise order all rum other than that from Jamaica and Demerara is entered officially as " imitation ram," and hence the description under notice. The liquor, which is not even first cousin to" Old Jamaica " comes largely from Hamburg, and does an immense trade in "spirits " o suit all palates.

MANCHESTER TRADE, THURZDAY.—There is little change in the market from yesterday, but there is not much chanoo. as yet of getting prices for cloth that will cover cost of mak- ing on the day. Exchanges are again slightly lower and cotton is hardening, and the estimate of the clay's budness has been raised from 8,000 to 10.000 bales. Brazilian 1-164. dearer. Yarns are steady but not active, and neither in twist nor weft is there a large trade doing, In cloth the mar- ket is much as yesterday. Moderate inquiry is iound for Calcutta, but buyers hesitate to pay advances, thouizh that is occasionally done. COUNTY OF CHESTER. 'MEDICAL OFFICER OF REA LTIL THE Public Health Committee of the Cheshire County Council invite APPLICATIONS for the above ,APPOINTMENT, the salary, duties, terms of appoint- =sent, and qualifications being as follows. viz. : SALARY. The Salary will be at the rate of £l4O per annum pay- able quarterly, in addition to out of pocket travelling enpenses. DUTIES. "To attend all Meetings of the Public Health Commit- tee, and to aderise them on all Sanitary matters. To,receive upon behalf of the County Council the copies of the periodical and special reports of the Medi- ALOfficers of all the Sanitary Authorities in the Admin- trative County, and to tabulate and summarize such crts, for the information and the guidance of the Public Health Committee and the County Council. To generally advise the Public Health Committee and the County Council on all questions affecting the public health.of the County. TERMS OF APPOINTMENT. To be permitted to hold other public appointments, but not to engage in private practice. To bold office subject to three months' notice in writing en either side, and not to be entitled to com- pensation, pension, or other allowance on ceasing to hold office. To generally act under the direction and control of the Public Health Committee. QUALIANICATIONS AS REQUIRED BY TIIE LOCAL GOVERNMENT Acr, 1888, SECTION 18. To be legally quallified for the practice of medicine, surgery, and midwifery, and also either to be registered in the medical register as the holder of a diploma in sanitary science, public health, or State medicine under Section 21 of the Medical Act, 1886, or to have been dur- ing three consecutive years preceding the year 1892, a Medical Officer of a district or cnmbination of districts with a population, according to the last public Census, of not less than twenty thousand, or has, before the passing of the Local government Act 1888, been for not less than three years a Medical Officer or Inspector of the Local Government Board. Applications should be sent to the undersigned, at his office in Chester, so that they may be received by him not later Ulan Saturday, the 31st day of December Instant. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Counsil. Chester, 13th December, 1892.

This Company has been tormed for the purpose of erecting and working a Promenade Pier and Landing Stage. with Pavilion. Concert Hall, Open-air Band Kiosk. Refreshment Rooms, Shops, and Lavatories thereon, at the West End of Morecambe, immediately opposite Alexandra Road. Morecambe, by reason of its picturesque surroundings and healthy situation, is unquestionably entitled to a place in the foremost rank of the pleasure resorts ef Great Britain. At the present time, in close proximity to the site of the proposed pier, new streets and roads are being made, while a vast numb lr of dwelling-houses and shops are being erected to meet the requirements of the fast-increasing number of visitors who annually favour Morecambe with their presence. In addition, the Promenade and carriage drive is being im- proved and extended from Alexandra Road (the site of the pier) still further west in the direction Of Heysham. I In view of the above facts, it is confidently anticipated that a pier on the site proposed will be highly popular, and I yield excellent dividends, The plans of the proposed pier have been carefully prepared by Mr. J'. D. Harker, A.R.1.D.A., of Manchester. The pier will have a total length of 850 yards or thereabouts. According to estimates prepared from Mr. Harker's plans by Messrs. Butler and Co,. of Stanningley Iron Worke, Leeds, the contractors for the pier at South Shore, Blackpool the cast of the proposed pier, complete, will be from £35,000 to £36,000. Application is being made to the Board of Trade for the 'necessary provisional order for the erection of the pier. The only contract entered into is dated tile 16th day af December, 1892. and is made between the Company of the one part and William Devitt of the other part; arrangements to none of which is the Company a party, have been made with various persons in connection with the above-mentioned expenses which it is not -deemed material to Specify; but in order to avoid any question which might arise under section 38 of the Companies Act 1867, ,or otherwise, applicants for shares will be deemed to have had due notice of such arrangements, and to have assented thereto, and to have agreed with the Company (as trustees for the directors and other persons liable) to waive any further compliance with 'the said-section. The above-mentioned ixintract can be seen at-the office of the Company's solicitors. -Copies of the memorandum an d articles of association may be seen at the offices of the Company's solicitors. Prospectuses and forms of applications may be obtained from the Company's bankers, solicitors, auditors, and secretary. Should no allotment be made, the deposit will be returned an full. 17th December, 1892.
